en: Record of the Commentary on the Mahāyāna Śāstra,
Volume One:
Following the Explanation of the Title.
Fascicle Second:
The Explanation of the Section on Exposition Concluded;
Fascicle Third begins below.

Having explained the meaning of the subsequent "reliance on the capacity," the fourth fascicle below explains the section beginning with "the failure to realize the source" and continuing with the "gate of manifesting faults."
Fascicle Five:
Having explained the characteristics of arising and ceasing,
Fascicle Six follows below.
The Explanation of the Characteristics of the Path of Progression, from here until the end;
this concludes the Table of Contents for the *Commentary on the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
(End) *Commentary on the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by the Great Master Puguang of the Glorious and Solemn Imperial Song Dynasty.

The Explanation of the Treatise is divided into two parts: first, the title; second, the main text of the treatise. In the first part (the title), there are again two sections: first, the primary explanation of the title; second, the indication of the volume number.

Within the primary explanation of the title, the first five characters explicitly state the title, while the final three characters indicate the volume sequence. Regarding the explicit statement of the title: first...

Regarding the last two characters, which translate the Sanskrit into Chinese, the middle three characters still retain their original Sanskrit form. There are three interpretations of these characters:

First, "shi" (釋) means "to explain" or "to interpret," which carries the sense of "dissolving. This refers to how this treatise refutes the heterodox and establishes the orthodox, thereby dispelling accumulated doubts;
it is like casting ore into a blazing furnace, where its hardness and stubbornness are dissolved away. Second, "shi" (釋) means "to speak" or "to expound. This refers to the flow [of the teaching]....

"Penetrating Meaning" (*tongyi*) means that by means of this treatise, the commentary (*yanshi*) elucidates the profound essence (*aozhi*), just as ice melts into a long river so that what was frozen and accumulated now flows freely.
"Three" (*san*) refers to "establishment" (*cheng*); it means the establishment of the meaning, referring here to the structure of the treatise's text:

the brief indication of the meaning and its detailed explanation. This is like a skilled craftsman constructing a great mansion, establishing it with skillful artistry. As for "Mahāyāna": [it is so called because...]
This is called the Mahāyāna; "Mahā" (Great) is named according to its essential nature, and "Yāna" (Vehicle) is designated as such because it functions as a conveyance.

This title is established as the central tenet (*śāstra-mūla*) of the treatise; thus, it refers to the non-dual *mahāyāna* dharma, for this is the common basis upon which all vehicles rely, and it also encompasses the thirty-two specific and general dharmas that depend upon it.
The treatise has two meanings: first, it provides instruction and admonition to disciples.

It is named as such because it definitively determines essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, one takes either the four dharmas—namely, sound and so forth—which are the expressive designators (*vācaka*), or the four sense objects (*viṣaya*)—namely, form and so forth—which are their bases.
This is because the substance of sound is discontinuous while the nature of form is continuous; for this reason, it does not employ spoken language but rather uses only calligraphy.
It is just like casting metal or carving wood to serve as the maintenance of the Buddha-Jewel (*buddha-ratna*); therefore, the four sense objects are taken.
Regarding the structure of this treatise, following the *Yongtai Shu*, the title of this work is understood to encompass five characters that fully express ten meanings:

First, the thirty-three dharmas are named *Mahāyāna*; the Buddha’s sūtras are named *Vyākhyā* (Exegesis); and the primary treatise is named *Śāstra* (Treatise). Since the secondary treatises follow the names of the primary ones, there is no contradiction with the original source.
Second, the Buddha’s sūtras are named *Mahāyāna*; the primary treatise is named *Vyākhyā*; and the secondary treatises are named *Śāstra*.

1. Regarding the three [aspects]: the five-part main text is called *Mahāyāna* and is termed a *śāstra*; at the end of the ten fascicles, the supplementary treatise (*paryanta-śāstra*) refers to it as a *vyākhyā*. 2. Regarding the four [aspects]:
the main treatise is named *Mahāyāna*, while the supplementary treatise is collectively termed both *vyākhyā* and *śāstra*.

3. Regarding the five [aspects]: the Dharma-gate and the Buddha-sūtra are both *Mahāyāna*; the main treatise is termed *vyākhyā*, and the supplementary treatise is termed *śāstra*. 4. Regarding the six [aspects]: the Dharma... [text ends]
1. Both the sūtras and the treatises are Mahāyāna; although they cite Buddhist sūtras, these serve merely as supports rather than being the direct exposition of the Mahāyāna teachings themselves.
2. Both the sūtras and the treatises are Mahāyāna; since both the support (the sūtras) and that which is supported (the treatises) belong to the Mahāyāna, they are both Mahāyāna.
3. Both the sūtras and this very treatise are Mahāyāna; as for the three dharmas [of teacher, teaching, and retinue], they are mutually interrelated and all belong to the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the Mahāyāna, the final three meanings are explained by the *Mūla-śāstra* (the root treatise) as a dual interpretation; the *Śāstra* (treatise) consists of nine parts:

first, the single part of "establishing the thesis" (*pratijñā*) is named *Mahāyāna*; second, the single part of "explanation" (*vyākhyā*) is termed *Vyākhyā*; the remaining three parts belong to the *Śāstra*.

Tenth, all that is explained—the natures (*dharmatā*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), teachings (*deśanā*), and principles (*nyāya*)—are the *Mahāyāna*, while the final part of the *Mūla-śāstra* which explains them is the *Śāstra*.

If both the teaching and the principle are referred to as "Explanatory Treatises" (*śāstra*), then the nature and endowment are explained by means of the teaching, while the characteristics are explained by means of the principle;

the nature is explained by means of the principle, and the characteristics are explained by means of the principle. Setting aside the specific for the general, this constitutes a single interpretation (and so forth). That [work] provides a comprehensive commentary, which I shall not elaborate upon here;

however, those who wish for detailed clarification should consult it. Furthermore, according to the Liang translation, the *Awakening of Faith* (*Qixin lun*) has been added to this, which is based on a broader scope.
The underlying principle is likewise unerring.
Regarding the two sections on the translators: first, the title indicates the person who composed [the work]; second, it clarifies the translator. Within the first section:
Nāgārjuna is his specific name, which thus manifests both the Chinese and the Indic. In the Indic language, *Nāga-ācārya* means "Dragon Tree" (*Longshu*) in Chinese.
This refers to the fact that this Bodhisattva was born from beneath a tree and attained enlightenment within a nāga palace; thus he was given this name. The Great Master Zhi (Zhiyi) said:

"The tree represents the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), and the nāga represents the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*). He is also called Longsheng (Dragon-Victorious) or Longmeng (Dragon-Fierce). The two characters "Bodhisattva" are his general title;
in full, it should be *bodhisattva*, translated as "enlightened sentient being. As for what is meant by "enlightened": (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly here.)
This refers to the fruit sought; "sentient beings" (*sattva*) refers to those capable of seeking, for they possess the nature (*gotra*) that seeks enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Furthermore, there are two types of bodhisattva practice: first, that which prioritizes self-benefit through great wisdom (*mahājñāna*);

second, that which prioritizes benefiting others through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). *Bodhi* means awakening, the fruit sought by wisdom; *sattva* refers to sentient beings, those to be delivered by compassion.

The term "produced" (zào) is used here in a concise sense; it simply means that the Bodhisattva composed [this work]. The *Weishi shu* states: "The author is called 'producer' (zào) because he has newly initiated [the work];
when one expounds principles based on what already exists, it is called 'narrating' (shù), as it follows what has previously existed."

Second, regarding the translator: Vaidharmatras (Vaiśramaṇa), whose background remains unclear, translated this treatise into Chinese at Dazhuangyan Temple in Chang’an on the first day of the ninth month in the third year of the Hongshi era of the Yao Qin dynasty, completing it in ten fascicles.
The composition of this treatise is divided into three major sections: first, the section on the preliminary clarification of the ultimate refuge;

second, the section on the formal exposition of the chapters; and third, the section on the exhortation to propagate the work. Within the first of these, there are two parts: first, the causes and conditions for taking refuge;

and second, the actual expression of homage. Regarding the initial expression of homage: it means that because the Three Jewels are the field of auspiciousness, they are designated at the very beginning.
This is for the purpose of manifesting excellence.

Within the text, there are again two parts; first, regarding the sincere expression of reverence, the term "prostration" (*namas-kṛ*) refers to extending humility and respect by touching the head to the ground.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that there are three types of ritual salutation: first, verbal salutation, which is the act of inquiring after one's well-being.
The second, bowing with the knees bent but the head not touching the ground—this is *jang-kwi* (long-kneeling)—is called the medium-grade prostration (*chung-pin li*).

The third, the head touching the ground—this is *ting-li* (prostration from the crown)—is called the superior-grade prostration (*shang-pin li*). Among these three types of prostrations, this is the highest.

Nevertheless, regarding the three modes of action (*san-ye*), it mentions only the physical gesture (*shen-i*) because this serves as a representative illustration that implicitly includes the other two grades of reverent practice.

Second, regarding the supreme virtues to which one takes refuge: first, within the Jewel of the Buddha, "Perfectly Awakened One" (*samyaksambuddha*) refers to one who has fully realized the ultimate state of fruition.
Because he possesses all virtues, he is praised as "perfect" (*yuan*); because the four virtues are manifested simultaneously, he is termed "complete" (*man*).
This embodiment of virtue is tranquil and ethereally fused, yet luminously penetrating; thus it is called "perfect."
"Full" (*man*) signifies that it is perfect because it is free from the three and four marks; "complete" (*yuan*) signifies that it fulfills the virtues of the three and four.

Because the Buddha can illuminate and penetrate all things, he is called "Awakened" (*jue*). Furthermore, by combining the two characters "perfect" and "complete," both the manifest and the hidden, the remote and the subtle, the transcendent and the wondrous—which are difficult to name—are revealed.

When one is detached from those specific capacities and faculties, attaining the state of both ordinary beings and Buddhas, this is precisely the ocean of the perfection of inherent virtue (*xingde*).
Regarding the two aspects of the Dharma Jewel, that which is realized through awakening not only takes refuge in the Buddha but also takes refuge in the Dharma;

thus, one clarifies the Dharma with respect to the Buddha itself to demonstrate the universal taking of refuge in the Three Jewels of identical essence. "Awakening" refers to the fruit, while "that which is realized" refers to the principle-Dharma.
"Dharma" refers to the teaching-Dharma, and "Treasury" (pitaka) refers to the practice-Dharma.
Among the three Jewels, the first phrase "and" (*ca*) carries the sense of inclusion and extension. The Great Being who composed this treatise is the Master Aśvaghoṣa;

as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, if one wishes to compose a treatise, one must first pay homage to the two venerable teachers before beginning the exposition, because this is the method for showing respect.
Therefore, one should first pay homage to the Great Master of the treatise’s root, and furthermore, one should pay homage to him in the sense of showing reverence.

The Master who Expounds the Meaning says that a "Mahāsattva" (Great Being) is so called because they awaken to the Great Dharma, give rise to the Great Mind, cultivate the Great Practice, and realize the Great Fruit;
thus they are designated as "Great. Taking "one" and multiplying it by "ten," one is named a "Sattva" (Being).

One is the beginning of numbers, and ten is the end of numbers. There is no undertaking that does not have a beginning, yet few are able to reach the end. Only those who possess both a beginning and a conclusion may be called "Great."
In the second phrase, "O Śrāvakas," by citing one to include the rest, he says "and all the worthy ones. This refers to the three grades of worthies and the ten grades of sages.
Thus, the mind of faith permeates all other stages; it encompasses the four vehicles and includes both the two vehicles. Whether Great or Small, nothing is omitted.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva maintains a mind of equality and shows respect toward all beings; their manifestations of the Real and the Expedient are difficult to fathom.

Out of compassion, there are two parts to the exposition of the fundamental intent. First, regarding the initial verse in the section on verses, the first line states, "Opening the gate of *dāna* (charity/giving)," which means that for the sake of enabling those sentient beings of sharp faculties who dwell in confusion to realize [the truth], the *tathatā-mukha* (gate of suchness) is opened and explained. The second line states, "Provisionally manifesting the past..."

Regarding those at the stage of "heading toward" (*ābhimukhya*), because it is intended to cause those sentient beings of dull faculties to practice the successive stages, the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*) is displayed.
By means of a metaphor involving separation and heading toward, the two gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and arising and ceasing are revealed.

That is to say, within the great ocean there is a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) endowed with all merits that produces all manner of treasures; the Dragon King places it within a secret treasury.
The protection provided by a thousandfold gate signifies that the Dragon King cherishes it to the utmost;
furthermore, this is due to the power of the jewels and the natural law of such things. The gate closest to the jewel is named "The Barrier" (*Gedan*);
when the various dragons open this gate, one immediately attains mastery and unimpeded access to the treasury of wish-fulfilling jewels. This is like a practitioner entering the Truth.
Because one can directly realize the single essence through this gate, one naturally and mysteriously accords with the non-dual source of the mind;

whereas the other gates are termed the "position of heading toward" (the goal). Although the various dragons pass in and out through them and know that such a treasury of wish-fulfilling jewels exists, they have not yet personally attained it—just as a practitioner who, from the gate of birth-and-death, merely maintains their mental discipline and conduct, yet remains [separate].

True Suchness (tathatā) acts as the skillful means; because the Door of Arising and Ceasing is provisional while the Door of True Suchness is real, entering from the provisional into the real is what constitutes excellence.

This is stated thus in the "Section on Exposition" (*vyākhyāna-bhāga*). However, according to the "Section on Establishing the Meaning" (*siddhānta-bhāga*), there are sixteen kinds of dharmas that serve as doors of entry:
eight are real and eight are delusive. The real serves as the barrier (*pratisedha*) and the delusive serves as the direction of movement (*gati*).

Because of the differences between the mundane and supramundane, as well as the gradual and sudden approaches, the fundamental reality entered through the eight gates of truth is all capable of being darkly realized as the non-dual Dharma;
therefore, these are called the "Gates of Isolation. The fundamental reality entered through the eight gates of delusion is understood through skillful means as the non-dual Dharma;
therefore, these are called the "Stages of Orientation. Within these, the Mahāyāna Dharma of non-duality serves as the basis for all phenomena.
Because it serves as the basis for all that is penetrated, it is like a precious gem that can serve as the basis for all other jewels;

thus, this "gem" refers exclusively to non-duality, which simultaneously encompasses both understanding (*parijñā*) and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). If one explains the section on "Analysis" (*vibhaṅga*) according to this treatise alone, where it exclusively elucidates the four dharmas, then the former interpretation is correct.

However, if one incorporates various other treatises, such as the section on "Establishment of the Meaning" (*vyavasthāna*), where it universally elucidates all dharmas, then the latter interpretation is superior.

In the third phrase, the superior benefits of the two preceding gates for engaging with sentient beings are revealed; while "benefit" (*li*) and "advantage" (*yi*) differ in name, they are identical in meaning.

To explain them separately, they possess manifold meanings: pertaining to body or mind, cause or fruit, great wisdom or great compassion, present happiness or future happiness, abandoning evil or gathering good, dispelling delusion or realizing truth, and merit or wisdom, as well as mundane excellence.

Regarding the meaning of this contemplation: "this contemplation" refers to the realization of the contemplation; "according to what is appropriate" means it is applied to all sentient beings by encompassing those in the three categories of beings (*tri-nikāya*), as it is the subject matter addressed by the treatise.
Since the distinctions among the various classes and types of sentient beings are numerous and vast—and because they are not uniform—it is therefore said "all.

The fourth phrase, "repaying the kindness of the teacher," explains that the author himself acknowledges having personally received the teacher’s instructions and guidance, and thus feels a profound sense of gratitude.
Reflecting upon this profound kindness, how could one ever fully repay it? Therefore, it is said that [the repayment] is "partial.
Second, the long prose section has three parts: first, the heading; second, the demonstration of the characteristics; third, the concluding reference.

Regarding the heading at the beginning and the conclusion at the end, these run through the middle five sections, which are explained by following the appropriate correspondences throughout the upper and lower parts. Within the first part, the current re-explanation refers to what the original master of the treatise has already [stated].
The composition of this commentary on the *Mahāyāna-artha* has already been explained previously.

Second, regarding the manifestation of the characteristics [of the teaching] in the following text, there are five intended meanings: first, to reveal the profound and wondrous nature of its essence and function; second, to manifest the sudden and gradual modes of revelation;

third, to repay the profound and great debt of gratitude for the teacher's virtue; fourth, to clarify the cessation of disputes and arguments; and fifth, to demonstrate the direct reception of the master’s instructions.
The initial statement regarding the "Self-Teacher" refers to the Dharma that this treatise takes as its fundamental principle.
This means that because the non-dual Mahāyāna Dharma is inherently perfected from the beginning and does not rely on external rules or regulations, it is called the "Self-Teacher.

Its essence consists of the perfect and eternal nature-virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*), which are profoundly mysterious and beyond fathoming; its ultimate function is all-pervasive, subtle, and inconceivable. It may indeed be taken as the standard for realization.
When the general totality of the two levels of "that which is entered" (*praveśya*) is exhausted, there are the two levels of the specific gates of "that which enters" (*praveśaka*).
This is because all thirty-three dharmas—consisting of the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*)—are what is accepted as the primary tenets of this established doctrine.

Furthermore, when the single essence of the two fundamental dharmas—the threefold nature and the twofold [nature]—is exhausted, they are the two specific gates of True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Arising-and-Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*); for these are explained separately only as interpretive expositions.

For this reason, the phrase "those who have not yet attained" and so forth relies on the person to manifest the Dharma, thereby establishing the profound and wondrous meaning of its essence and function.

This means that those in the ten stages of faith and the three stages of worthiness have not yet personally realized [the truth], while those of the two vehicles and non-Buddhists have not yet abandoned error.

Regarding the terms "vague and obscure" (*mo-mo ming-ming*), there are two interpretations: first, in reference to the deluded mind, it refers to a state of dullness and lack of clarity; second, in reference to the object of delusion...
The realm is vast and boundless in its appearance; it is profound and hidden in its nature. To "peer into" [the cave] means to gaze directly at it. "Contemplation" refers to discernment.
Because it is silent, desolate, empty, and expansive, it cannot be grasped through form or name;
because it is subtle, wondrous, and signless, it cannot be known by a conscious mind.
Within these two [gates], for those of sharp faculties, the gate of immediate entry is opened and named "Direct Access" (*pratyakṣa*);

for those of dull faculties, the stages of gradual progress are revealed and named "Tending Toward. As for the principle that is the referent, it is the fundamental dharma entered through these two gates;
because it is manifested by means of the gates, it is called "entering" (*praveśa*).

The phrase "nurturing within the three" carries the meaning of impartial nourishment; it refers to how our Master, the Founder, impartially sustained and nurtured our Dharma-body and wisdom-life, surpassing the Yangtze and Han rivers in depth and equaling Mounts Qiu and Shan in weight.
How could such benevolence and virtue not be considered great? If this were not transmitted and propagated, how could one speak of repaying it?
Now that this commentary has been composed, it may be called a repayment of his kindness. The Master spoke of it as a "small repayment" out of humble modesty.

Among these four, the Master Śākyamuni entered into profound meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and contemplated that in the future, during the degenerate age (*kaṣāya-kāla*), there would be much contention and the Wheel of Dharma would lose its course, with the nectar of immortality turning into poison;
he now explains this once more to bring an end to such faults.
Among the five [factors], the Sanskrit term *āśaya* means "intention" (*yi-lao*).
Having personally received the original intent, he composed this commentary for circulation so as to demonstrate that his own exposition does not contradict the original intention.

The three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) are as explained below. To provide the causes and conditions for initiating this treatise, there are actually many types [of categories]; however, these five are presented briefly, which is why the word "etc.

(*ādi*) is placed [at the end]. Second, to pre-emptively clarify the basis and the inclusion: first, the distinctions of the initial treatise; second, first, concluding the preceding and generating the subsequent; concluding what has already been stated.
This shall be explained after [the discussion on] birth.

Regarding the two treatises, there are questions and answers below that explain and establish them. This is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation of the various treatises to clarify the two; second, the specific analysis.

The first part consists of opening three questions and returning with three answers. Within the first section, the verse summary provides the answer: the first line answers the first question, followed by the total ten [lines].

The response below consists of three parts: first, answering the subsequent question; second, answering the final question; and third, an expository explanation in prose. Regarding the first part, which indicates the number and explains the opening line of the verse:

it refers to the total count of treatises—both fundamental works (*mūla*) and commentaries (*vṛtti*)—composed by Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and others, beginning from the time of the Buddha and extending down to the era of the Master [Vasubandhu].
Thus, it is said that there are "one hundred and nine thousand sections" (*śatasahasra-navasahasra*).
Regarding these two points, the following section clarifies the "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*) explained in the third line of the verse.
The text from that point onward indicates that the ten thousand nine hundred treatises mentioned above, in their general characteristics, do not exceed ten types of inclusion:

(1) *yathāruci* (according to preference), (2) *vistara-saṃgraha* (extensive inclusion), (3) *mūla-vistara-vyākhyā-saṃkṣepa* (the root being extensive while the commentary is concise), (4) *mūla-saṃkṣepa-vyākhyā-vistara* (the root being concise while the commentary is extensive), (5) *ekāntārtha* (exclusively meaningful), (6) *vyañjana-vistara-saṃgraha* (extensive inclusion of the phrasing), and (7) *miśra-śāstra* (miscellaneous treatises).
The *Aṣṭapada-cakra*, the nine divine mantras (*navadeva-mantra*), and the ten verses correspond respectively to the [ten] treatises listed below;
however, as these titles are all accompanied by their scholastic designations, they are mostly omitted due to the constraints of the verse lines.

Furthermore, regarding these ten treatises, although the master Yongtai cited them based on the translations of Ārya Dharmarakṣa, many of the names and meanings still reside in India (Zhugan), and few have been transmitted to this land.

Third, regarding "Three Mahā-": this refers to the three characters at the end of the verses of this treatise’s commentary, meaning that among the ten types [of treatises], this present work belongs to the first, the *mārga* category. Second, regarding "Aśvaghoṣa":
this specifically reveals the works composed by Aśvaghoṣa. This has two parts: first, opening with four questions; second, responding with four answers. Second... [text continues].
First, the verse summary provides answers to the four preceding questions in the order of the four lines of the verse.
Second, the prose commentary explains them: first, it generally presents the four meanings;

second, it specifically indicates the textual passages and meanings to explain the two middle lines of the verse, stating that among the one hundred treatises, ninety of them constitute the nine [sections].
The *Kusumalatā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Flower Garland) subsumes the remaining ten categories of the *Śāstrārtha-saṃgraha* (Compendium of the Meaning of the Treatises).

This [classification] is divided into two types based on their exegesis: "Flower Garland" refers to those that adorn the scriptural text to inspire delight; "Compendium of Meaning" refers to those that collect and synthesize sublime meanings to inspire resolute conviction.
The former are commentaries (*vyākhyāna*), such as the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; the latter are treatises (*śāstra*), such as...
Regarding the three categories such as the *Yogaratna* (Jewel-like Yoga), this treatise is classified below [in that category].

The commentary on the final phrase of the verse states that "Jewel-Volume" (*ratnapustaka*) is a title specifically designated because it is held in high esteem in the Western Regions (India); its text and profound principles are as wondrous as volumes composed of precious jewels.
Thus, among the ten types of treatises mentioned in the preceding text, it belongs to the *Makara-maniprabha* (Wish-fulfilling Jewel) class, like a jewel.
The *Liang Jing Zhangzhen Lun* (Treatise on the Precious Seal of the Sūtras) and other works comprise twenty types.
Below, ten treatises are specifically distinguished. First, the opening; second, the question; third, the restatement; fourth, the answer.

Within the initial section of the verse-answer, the first five lines answer the question regarding the expressive names (*nāman*), while the final line answers the question regarding the identity or difference of that which is expressed (*vācya*).
Question: Regarding the two prose explanations of the two [sections], first is the interrogation and listing of titles to explain the first five lines of the verse;

second, from "In this way" (*evam*) onwards, is the conclusion pointing out the similarities and differences to explain the final line of the verse. This means that among the ten types of treatises listed above, within the section on the "Establishment of Categories" (*vyavasthāna-mukha*), the original total number is fully indicated for each identical type;
however, within the section on the "Prose Exposition" (*vistaravyākhyāna-mukha*), they are each deficient according to their respective systems of tenets.
These verses merely clarify what is common while also including what is distinct.

Second, "Having already explained... and below concerns the distinctions between the two collections (*piṭaka*). This section has two parts: first, concluding the previous topic and introducing the subsequent one; second, the question-and-answer explanation establishing the two collections. The first part, "The two collections exist...
and below, consists of opening with three questions and returning with three answers. Within the first [part], the initial two lines of the verse provide the answer.
The first question is answered with the third line, and the subsequent question is answered with the final line.

Second, the prose explanation has two parts: first, a general clarification of the three meanings; second, [the specific explanation]. First, clarifying the number. First, clarifying the various collections (*piṭaka*) to explain the first two lines of the verse.
Within this section, there are two parts. First, within the fifty-one collections, first, the presentation of the meaning has three parts. First, the individual [explanation].
1. "Cause and effect" means that there are numerical categories to distinguish the differences in the superiority or inferiority of causal practices and resultant virtues. 2.
"Manifesting two kinds of merit" means to reveal the functional capacities and virtues of faith and the other stages regarding the obstacles to knowledge and their transformative efficacy.
3. "Guiding practitioners" means to lead and gather practitioners from the state of ordinary beings to sainthood, and from causes into the fruition. Next, following the words "Vajra," it is cited:
The explicit text establishes the first meaning, while the implicit contains the latter two.

Regarding the second [section], "Or there may be," which increases the number to ten *piṭakas*: first, the heading and inquiry; second, the specific demonstration of the text, which consists of ten sections.

These are established because the Tathāgata, through his skillful means, adapts to the faculties of beings with freedom in opening and closing [the teachings], thus proceeding sequentially from one *piṭaka*.

Furthermore, because they increase to ten kinds, first, regarding the Tathāgata’s sound of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*): the true reality (*dharmatā*) of speech and sound is itself the Wheel of Dharma;
therefore, this sutra should belong to the *Avataṃsaka* class, as such a statement exists in the new translation from the Great Zhou dynasty.

Second, it distinguishes between the higher and lower vehicles (*yāna*), each comprehensively encompassing both cause and fruit so as to include all phenomena exhaustively. Third, regarding the aforementioned higher vehicle:

the first gate is the sincerity of the one who takes refuge, and the second gate is the supreme virtue of the object of refuge. Regarding the second [the detailed explanation following the summary]: first, the section on the summary;

within this, first, the citation and presentation, and second, the entrustment of the text. Regarding the second [the section on taking refuge]: as above, it consists of the citation and the entrustment.

The second part, the extensive explanation through the questions and answers of the two masters, has two sections: first, the introduction of the inquiry; second, the response that establishes the explanation. The introduction of the inquiry has two questions:
the first asks about the number of virtues, and the second asks about the characteristics of those virtues. The response that establishes the explanation has three parts:

first, the verse summary, where the first two lines cite the number of virtues, the next four lines indicate the characteristics of the virtues, and the final two lines reconcile the numerical count; second, the prose commentary; third, [the further analysis].

First, the general manifestation of the number of virtues explains the first two lines of the verse; second, the reconciliation of the numerical quantities from the "Buddha-fruit" section below explains the latter two lines of the verse.
Fearing that there might be a question as to how the Buddha’s virtues, being boundless, can be limited to such a number, this section now provides a comprehensive reconciliation:

although there are immeasurable and boundless merits, when categorized by their common characteristics, they ultimately do not exceed these [categories], which serves to allow for the appropriate manifestation of the response.

In the *Jìyìzhī lùnshī* (The Treatise on the Easy Understanding of the Limits), the master first cites the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as a praise in three parts. Regarding "How so? and below, there is the second section: the detailed explanation of the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

This is divided into two: first, analyzing the virtues according to the text; second, [the specific analysis]. Within the first, there is a general question-and-answer regarding the merits of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) across the seven stages.

Regarding "How so? and below, there is the second part: the specific inquiry and explanation of the six categories of non-form (*arūpa*) merits. There are six [sub-sections] therein. The first states that one is free from the three kinds of defilements (*saṃkleśa*).
The "Ten Perfections" refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the three realms and the six destinies (*gati*), which constitute the defilement of fruition (*vipāka-saṃkleśa*).

Since the fixed attachments to the false views of the two vehicles and externalists are also of the nature of retribution, they are included therein. The "evil armies of the ground-dwellers," the "groves of error," and the "entanglements" constitute the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*).

Among these, the member of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) constitutes the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*). These two [categories] are explained here in terms of the two types of retribution: the primary (the self) and the secondary (the environment).
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities belong entirely to the karma of mind; the perfection of speech and sound constitutes the karma of speech;
and the thirty-two marks belong to the karma of body. His ability to manifest transformations as the Honored One within the triple world fully encompasses all three types of karma.
That which is above—namely, the auspicious dwelling place—is the *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant retribution). Within this, the number of Brahma-sounds is either...

There are differences [in the accounts]: the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra* states there are sixty-eight qualities of Brahma’s voice, while the *Mahāvyutpatti* and other teachings frequently clarify eighty-eight qualities of the "wonderful sound" (*svara*).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* speaks of sixty kinds of sounds, with each individual sound having five hundred sub-varieties, and so forth.

This is because what is heard differs according to the faculties and dispositions of beings; therefore, the various explanations vary in their increase or decrease. Regarding the three [types of speech], they are categorized as follows:
The two aspects clarify that the ten karmas are in equal correspondence, sharing a common basis of arising and being free from weariness;

these five kinds constitute the aspect of inconceivable karma, for through the wisdom of *yathābhūta-jñāna* (knowledge as it is), one provisionally contemplates conditions in accordance with the conventional to accomplish the benefit of others, thereby fully possessing the two types of unattached karma.
This is the aspect of pure wisdom, for through the wisdom of *tathatā-jñāna* (knowledge of suchness), one contemplates emptiness in accordance with the ultimate truth to accomplish self-benefit.
Because it is utilized, it is naturally inexhaustible; it penetrates the three types [of realms], and its principle and measure are equally reflected in the two preceding aspects.

This is the Middle Way contemplation of conditions, which accomplishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Regarding the four [types of] utilization, they pertain to the Tathāgata’s body, mind, merit, and retinue, all of which are universally pervasive.
Within that pervasiveness, there are places and times, as well as the fullness of persons, dharmas, faculties, and roots.

When the three—object, consciousness, and [the subject]—are vast and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, they pervade all places; when life-span is pervasive throughout inconceivable eons, it pervades all time.
Their retinue and merits encompass both time and place; their compassion pervades the faculties; their speech pervades all phenomena;

and their realized wisdom pervades all principles. Because they are peerless and universally pervasive across all dharmas, with nothing equal to them, four of these five aspects constitute the Wisdoms.

When combined, they form two pairs: the first pair, consisting of the first and third [wisdoms], is the wisdom of suchness (*yathāvad-jñāna*); the second pair, consisting of the second and fourth, is the wisdom of things-as-they-are (*yathā-mātra-jñāna*).

Furthermore, these four types establish the designation of "wisdom" by transforming and relinquishing the names of the [eight] consciousnesses: the first is the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); the second is the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*);
the third is the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*); and the fourth is the great perfect mirror wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). The lecturer should [explain this].

One should understand in detail that among the six [analytical knowledges], the four types—of phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), expression (*nirukti*), and eloquence (*pratibhāna*)—are designated as "unimpeded" (*pratisaṃvid*).

These four are all the objects of cognition (*ālambana-viṣaya*), while "unimpeded" itself refers to the wisdom (*jñāna*) that takes them as its cognitive subject. Furthermore, they are called the "four analytical knowledges" (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*):

the first two involve knowing the phenomena, and the latter two involve expounding the Dharma. The former specifically refers to the thorough comprehension of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; therefore...
To speak of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) and the true nature (*svabhāva*) is to subsequently realize the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena;

thus, it is called "differentiation," referring to characteristics such as suffering and emptiness, or arising, abiding, and so forth. These two types of characteristics can be understood through verbal expression. Liberation (*vimukti*) is precisely a designation for non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*).

Second, the meaning of "mastery" (*vaśitā*) in the subsequent assembly is explained in detail. First, the initial assembly provides a general reconciliation regarding mastery, fearing that there might be a question such as:
"Why is the term 'mastery' not explained individually here as it is in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, where there are ten kinds of mastery and so forth?
Now, the general explanation states that it applies to all because mastery pervades the six aforementioned categories by means of all the various merits.
Because "emerging from obstructions" and "being free from bonds" both signify mastery (*vaśitā*), these two aspects of form are not separately distinguished.
Below, regarding the enumeration of the eighty-four thousand distinct varieties of the marks of form, the details are so vast and extensive that it is difficult to describe them fully;

therefore, one should refer to what is explained in the *Mahādhāraṇī-śāstra*. Furthermore, there are differing accounts regarding the Tathāgata’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*); the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, for instance, states that there are ten lotuses.

The *Huazang* (Flower Treasury) Sūtra describes the infinite ocean of marks and signs as being like the atoms within it; the *Wuliangshou* (Infinite Life) Sūtra speaks of the eighty-four thousand radiant marks and signs of Amitābha Buddha;
and the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtras speak of the thirty-two major marks and so forth—these differ only in their breadth or brevity according to what is seen or heard.

Regarding the second section, "The Dharma and Saṃgha," which consists of one verse already explained, there are two parts: first, the summary introduction; second, the detailed exposition. Regarding the first, the summary introduction, there are two parts:

first, the recitation of the root verse; second, the composition of the commentary. Regarding the second, the detailed exposition, there are two parts: first, the marking of divisions and a brief indication; second, the sequential explanation.

Regarding the first, the marking of divisions and brief indication, there are two parts: first, the classification of gates; second, the inclusion within the essence. The latter is precisely the utmost sincerity of the one who takes refuge. That is to say:

Because one pays homage to all the physical forms and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all those infinite sentient beings, the "body" (*kāya*) is the basis; thus, it is collectively termed "characteristics.
As for the specific meaning of "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*), since it encompasses the multitude of bodies, it is difficult to avoid the arising and ceasing [of those bodies];

hence it is said that transmigration is impermanent (*anitya*) due to birth and death. Furthermore, the "body" is the substantial reality (*dravya-svabhāva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*); the four or five aggregates together constitute its substance.

Therefore, the physical characteristics (kāya-lakṣaṇa) are the provisional functions that manifest [the mind]; the three types of action (trikarma) and the four stages are collectively termed "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa).

Specifically, bending and stretching, bowing and looking up, greeting, praising, and the discernment of applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra) are called the characteristics of the three types of action. Their continuous circulation, agitation, and unstable transformation are called the characteristics of the four stages.
Because one seeks to use what is subject to arising and ceasing to trade for the true and eternal, the masters of the treatises provisionally speak of these four.

The discourse on mutual overcoming and the cultivation of reverence likewise possesses the three types of action (*trikarma*). Furthermore, the gateway of universal penetration is precisely the supreme virtue to which one takes refuge.
Thus, "various bodies" refers to those subsumed above—the profound treasury of the Dharma, namely the four dharmas of teaching, principle, practice, and fruit.
"Practicing according to reality" refers to the assembly of Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Moreover, by taking refuge in and revering the Jewel of the Buddha and the Dharma...

The two preceding and following verses are integrated to clarify that there are three ways of taking refuge—namely, by life, essence, and appearance—and that there are three objects of refuge—namely, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
One takes refuge in the Buddha with one’s life, in the Dharma with one’s essence, and in the Saṅgha with one’s appearance. Because these have symbolic significance:

one pays homage to the Buddha as the one capable of sustaining [the teachings]; one pays homage to the Dharma as the basis for reliance; and one pays homage to the Saṅgha because they possess physical form.
Because they seek [refuge], they pay homage by means of the marks; since three are paired with three, there should also be nine.

However, because the resolute understandings (*adhimukti*) of those who take refuge differ, the three matters are taken collectively as the agents of refuge, and the Three Jewels are taken collectively as the objects of refuge. "To pay homage" (*namas-kṛti*) refers to the completion of what is to be honored;

"what is to be taken as refuge" refers to the full detail of the virtues possessed. To explain: "to take refuge" (*śaraṇa-gamana*) means "to reach" (*prāpti*), and "to arrive at" (*gati*) means "to penetrate" (*praveśa*). Taking these three together...

The matter of the "equality" (等) that penetrates the Three Jewels does not merely refer to seeking refuge and entrusting oneself to their majestic protection; it also signifies a profound union with innate virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), wherein subject and object are mysteriously identical—this is true reverence.
Regarding the second phrase, the word "equal" (*等*) is further explained:

as for its comprehensive scope, it applies proximately to the two gates and distantly to the two verses, because both the one who takes refuge and the object of refuge are entirely equal. There are two meanings of "equality": first, equality in measure (*samatā*).
"Equal" (sama) refers to being level and uniform; it comprehensively encompasses many dharmas, while "level" (samatā) means being a single essence without differentiation.

This means that although the sublime virtues to which one takes refuge—the distinct categories of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—are all objects of reverence and admiration, they are free from conceptual discrimination; thus, they are called "equal.

Furthermore, although the wondrous practices of those who take refuge—whether noble, holy, or ordinary—are distinct, they equally accomplish devout devotion, severing all notions of self and other; thus, they are called "even" (sama). The following treatise discusses this.
The phrase "this very profound homage" (*namas*) refers to the act of paying respect.
Regarding the two masters’ subsequent questions and answers that extensively clarify this, there are first the introductory questions, which consist of two parts:

(1) questioning the number [of dharmas], and (2) questioning their characteristics. Second, the answers that provide an explanatory resolution, which begins with the summary verse; within this, the first line provides a general overview.

The heading answers the first question; the second line provides a specific explanation answering the second question; and the final two lines reconcile and resolve contradictions and obstacles. This is explained in two parts:
first, the general exposition of the first half-verse, which consists of two sections. First, the general indication of the two dharmas; second, the specific explanation of those two dharmas.
Regarding the first, the explanation of the "dharma within dharma"—that is, the teaching—it means that by means of the *sūtras*...
Because the sūtras and śāstras produce understanding through phenomena, there are two kinds of principle (*li*): first, the principle of meaning (*yi-li*), and second, ultimate truth (*zhen-li*).

Now, the nature of true suchness (*xing-zhenru*) corresponds to the latter; the false and provisional corresponds to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is called "true" because it is free from [intrinsic existence];

the reality of attachment corresponds to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which is called "such" (*ru*) because it is utterly transcended. Since these two are both free and transcended, they are the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the very essence.

The "Ocean of True Suchness" refers to the dharmas of fruition; because the merits of the fruition stage are perfectly complete and each accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), being profoundly deep and vast, it is likened to an ocean.

The "Treasury of Immeasurable Virtues" refers to the dharmas of practice; because they are maintained according to their respective applications without contradiction, the two are like [the ocean and its treasury].
Below, the term "Saṃgha" is explained: practicing in accordance with principle is called "practice in accordance with reality" (*yathārtha-caryā*); "reality" (*yathā*) refers to that which is...

The realization-wisdom (*pramāṇa-jñāna*) is precisely that which can realize true wisdom; this establishes the name "Saṃgha," distinguishing it from those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), as they lack true realization.
Regarding the phrase "wisdom and principle, etc.," the following provides the formal explanation of the meaning of Saṃgha.

Second, for what reason does the lower section connect with the preceding question and answer? Part three: first, the inquiry and explanation regarding the distinct meanings of "body" (*kāya*) and "life-force" (*jīvita*).

Within this, first, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is explained: because it is of the same substance, it serves as that which is subsumed; because it is vast and perfect, it is designated as the ten directions. Next, the characteristics of the body are explained:
one desires to exchange the body of birth, death, and transmigration for the firm, solid, true, and eternal essence. Although [the text] in its wording...

This clearly elucidates the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) in their meaning, which also implicitly contains the three karmas (*tri-karma*), for [salutation] such as bowing, stretching, and so forth would not be accomplished [otherwise].
Second, regarding the inquiry and explanation of how body and life are shared with others: first, the inquiry is made based on the distinct natures of self and other;
next, the explanation is given based on the identical nature of self and other. "Of one flavor" (*eka-rasa*) means they share the same taste of equality. "Of one mark" (*eka-lakṣaṇa*) means...

Because they share the same true nature (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), the master of treatises Aśvaghoṣa, although he knew that all sentient beings are a single-body continuity (*eka-kāya-santāna*), now incorporates them [into the lineage] without contradicting the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of mutual support as a distinct-body continuity (*nānā-kāya-santāna*).
In the verse, the term "extremely profound" refers to this [point] in order to establish the meaning of equality. Third, the section beginning with "Why? provides the interrogation and explanation.

Regarding the initial inquiry within the section on "Taking up the Characteristics of Accomplishment for Others": since one already knows that body and life are identical in all respects, why is it necessary to embrace others to form the characteristic of *vandana* (homage)?
In the subsequent explanation: because one embraces sentient beings in accordance with one’s original vow, the Buddhas rejoice and sustain them;

because they give rise to sympathetic joy as they share the same essence (*samatā-kāya*), Bodhisattvas offer praise. By practicing in reliance upon this, one accords with both teaching and principle; thus, the Dharma is not... [omitted].
Severance.
Second, the explanation by Aśvaghoṣa of the second half of the verse. Part one: Question and answer resolving objections. First, within the question and answer concerning the lower stages:
first, the question asks that since the Master currently resides in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) and dwells in the mind of abiding, he should only take refuge in the emerging mind of his own stage.
Furthermore, regarding the verses concerning the two higher stages (*bhūmi*), why must they universally refer back to the previously deceased monastics of the lower stages? To answer this in turn:
it is because, by relying on an intention of "identical essence" (*ekātmya-samānārtha*), one universally encompasses both self and others to express reverence;

those persons so encompassed include all levels from the lower stages down to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), as there is none who is not included. This is because they are all not the same as the author of the treatise himself. The second [point]...
This is because it refers to those dwelling in the stage of the eighth bhūmi; if one does not include others, it refers exclusively to those of superior status.
If this is so, why does the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* state that Kāśyapa Bodhisattva prostrates to those who have first resolved their minds? Does this not constitute honoring those of the lowest of low ranks?

It is because the intent of "taking refuge" (*śaraṇagamana*) and "prostrating with reverence" (*namas-kāra*) differs: taking refuge seeks the empowerment of their majestic spiritual power, whereas prostration merely manifests respect toward another.

Because there is no pride, the various stages differ in their universal or specific application. Second, "If that were so" (*yadi cet*) and below concerns the question and answer regarding the stages prior to the [first] ground (*bhūmi*).

First, the question: "If all are subsumed as those who can take refuge, why do you not take refuge in the multitudes of those prior to the grounds? Second, "It is not that there is nothing to which one takes refuge" (*na tu nāsti*) and below is the answer:

it is not that there is no object of refuge. Third, because the three types of worthy persons (*pudgala*) and others are indicated only by way of a shadow (as representative examples), they are not mentioned individually.
In the section concerning the fulfillment of the stages following the "Dharma-Cloud" (*dharmameghā*) ground, within the initial formal question and answer, the first question asks:

by what kind of *saṃgha* is one to take refuge, now that the stage of the Dharma-Cloud—the culmination of the causal path—has been reached? The subsequent answer, beginning with "The Sublime," states that although the causal stage of the Dharma-Cloud is complete, the fruit-stage has not yet been attained;
therefore, one takes the Sublime Awakening (*samyaksambodhi*) as the object of refuge and veneration. Thus, within the *saṃgha*, the Buddha is [the ultimate object].
Because he is the foremost leader, [the author] subsequently raises a further inquiry and provides an explanation regarding the initial inquiry. The intent of the initial inquiry is as follows:

"If the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is that which is to be taken as the object of refuge and veneration, why is it not mentioned separately in the verse? The subsequent response and explanation states:
"Because these ten stages (*bhūmi*) include the aforementioned stage of wondrous enlightenment; through this method of 'shadow-brief' and 'shadow-manifestation,' nothing is omitted."

Second, because the subsequent section points back to the verse, citing the verse to authenticate the present exposition; the "reflection" (image) encompasses both the preceding and following sections, as the monastic community consists of many types. Question:
Since the body and life-force that take refuge are identical in both cases, how can there be a distinction between the preceding and following sections?
Answer: That [preceding section] refers to its own school’s continuity as being the same, whereas this [following section] relies on the distinctness of separate continuities; thus, the texts differ.
"Emergence" refers to the manifestation of the reflection.
Second, having already explained the two fundamental intentions of the original text below, the first part concludes by pointing to the fundamental intent of the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa:
for the benefit of the three groups of sentient beings, and so that the Three Jewels may not be severed. Second, the proclamation of the explanation, part one.

The Chanting Text (Sòngběn) has two parts: the verses and the commentary. The commentary has two sections: first, the general indication through a structural outline; second, the detailed explanation. The first section, the structural outline, has two parts:

first, the division of topics; second, the sequential explanation. Within the first, the "Section on Severance" (Duànjué mén), there are three parts: first, the heading and inquiry; second, the enumeration and explanation;

third, the synthesis with the root verses. Regarding the root verses, there are four general meanings: first, the three categories of sentient beings who are the recipients [of the teaching]; second, the four kinds of obstacles to be eliminated.

Regarding the three types of bondage, the four kinds of pure faith that arise from them, and the three supreme lineages of the Triple Gem that continue from them—these four sections sever doubt and abandon the four obstacles of false attachments in their respective order.
Within the two sections concerning continuity, the three parts are as previously explained:

the *dharmadhātu* of suchness is designated as the "abode" because it is the essence in which practitioners dwell, the "reliance" because they settle their minds therein, and the "path of travel" because they traverse it.
Regarding the two types of monks situated directly behind the palace, these refer to the stages of the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Because they directly realize and indirectly transform the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), both are said to "dwell" [in it]. While one could say that all three—Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha—are uninterrupted, because the phrasing of the treatise is concise, it simply says "the lineage of the Buddha" (*buddhagotra*).

Furthermore, the Dharma is the word of the Buddha, and the Saṃgha are the sons of the Buddha; by mentioning the persons, the words are subsumed, and by clarifying the father, the offspring are encompassed.
The son merely says, "Because the lineage of the Buddhas leaves nothing behind.

Second, the verses on the assembly’s subsequent question and answer separately clarify two points: first, posing the question to provoke inquiry; second, providing the answer to establish the explanation. First, within the verse response:
the upper two lines answer the initial question, and the lower two lines answer the subsequent question. Second, the prose commentary.

The second part [of the commentary] explains the two [halves of the verse]. First, it explains the first half-verse. Second, it provides a general explanation of how the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*) serve as the universal object (*sāmānya-ālambana*).
This means that within the three categories of the three aggregates, one takes the first category as the universal object of perception;
because this single category exists entirely within the stage of the cause, it is said that "the perfect fruit has not yet been attained."
Second, the detailed explanation of the three [categories] through two sections and three subsections: first, the heading and inquiry; second, the enumeration and demonstration.

Regarding the first [of the three], the category of those lacking faith—whether already fixed or not yet fixed—the term "prior to faith" refers to all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Although they may possess a general, superficial faith regarding the results of karma, this is still termed "lack of faith," and they are all classified as those of wrong certainty (*mithyātva-niyata*).
Second, the two groups of those who have or have not yet fulfilled their lack of roots; herein, these three groups encompass the stages of fruition.
Third, the group of those who have or have not yet realized the state of being free from seeking; the texts for both are clear and may be understood accordingly.

Third, regarding the designation "definite" (*niyata*): although the stage of the Buddha’s fruition (*buddhatva*) is called "definite," it is not subsumed within the categories of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), or elements (*dhātu*).

How could it then be said that [this teaching] is intended for sentient beings? Furthermore, although the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) have not yet attained direct realization, they have already realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and are free from all doubt and fear;
they also practice the skillful means of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and their conduct in the present stage is immeasurable. How could they be so designated?
Because it is indeterminate, the Master of the Commentary (Śāstrin) adopts the first interpretation.
Second, with the desire to explain the second half of the verse below, there are three parts: first, the initial statement and inquiry; second, the detailed presentation; and third, the conclusion.

Second, having already explained [the preceding], the detailed exposition of the essence and the conditions has two parts. First, the opening clarification of the essence, which has two parts. First, the opening of the general essence, which has two parts:

first, concluding the previous section and indicating what follows; second, reciting the root text and providing the commentary. Regarding the second part, reciting the root treatise and composing the explanatory text, there are two sections.

First, briefly clarifying [the essence] by dividing the categories; within this, first the indication, and next, from "that which can enter" onwards, the citation and explanation of the gates of entry. Within the gates of entry...

Regarding "elucidating the principle": "elucidation" (*vyavahāra*) refers to the act of elucidating or manifesting; it is called "elucidation" because one manifests the principle by means of a gateway. It does not mean taking sound and so forth as the essential body of the gateway.
Within the gateway through which one enters, that which is skillful toward it is the "entrance," meaning that which is capable of entering.
This refers to the dharma that is entered, which serves as the basis for that which is capable of entering.

Second, the extensive explanation based on the meaning, in three parts: First, a general explanation of the gates of meaning and text. Regarding the function of the Dharma-gates: based on these gates, one gives rise to faith;
that which is believed is the essence of those dharmas. As for the function performed, it is simply the arising of faith, because this faith crowns all practices and pervades all stages.
Question: Within this, the Mahāyāna essence is non-dual; now that it is described as the object of faith, why is this so?

The treatise below states that it is "independent of the sense faculties" (*indriya-vinirmukta*). If it were truly independent of the faculties, one should not understand it as existing merely because those dharmas are inherently accomplished;
rather, it is not designated in accordance with the faculties. For this reason, the treatise says it is "independent of the sense faculties."
Second, the definitive explanation of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). This has two parts: first, the explanation of its name and stage in two successive cycles.

In the first cycle, "determination" (*niścaya*) is itself "resolute conviction" (*adhimokṣa*), which serves as the cause of faith; "progression" (*pragati*) is "diligence" (*vīrya*), which is the fruit of faith;

and "mind" (*citta*) refers to the mental sovereign (*cittarāja*) that functions simultaneously as the basis. Because it reveals the self-substance of faith through those causes and fruits as well as the mental sovereign, [the faculty of faith is established]. Furthermore, by virtue of...
The "faculty of resolute progress" (*adhimukti-indriya*) is so named because it serves as the basis for manifesting the essence of faith;
its meaning is that of being the support for growth. The six perfections and the myriad practices arise from this faculty and enter into the ultimate truth without departing from these two [aspects].
First, the stages of practice are correlated; subsequently, an analogy is raised to explain them. Within this, the practice of faith has not yet been fully detailed.

Because it has been established, it is called the "initial fulfillment of the stage of faith"; because it has already reached completion, it is called the "subsequent. Regarding the analogies, the Sanskrit terms have not yet been identified for their Chinese counterparts;

the first analogy should correspond to the category of duckweed and parasitic plants, while the second analogy should correspond to the category of the King of Medicines (Bhaiṣajyarāja), the pine, and the cypress.
Second, the ten meanings below the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) reveal its functional capacity. This section has two parts: first, the posing of the question; second, the explanatory answer.
Within the verse response, the first line answers the number of meanings, and the second line answers the characteristics of the meanings. "Clarity and purity" is the primary meaning of faith;
"turning toward" is the primary meaning of a faculty (*indriya*). The word "etc. indicates that each [term] is equal to the remaining nine meanings.
Second, the prose explanation has two parts. First, regarding the ten meanings of faith: the first one belongs to the general function, while the remaining nine are specific functions.

Within the general category, all treatises state that its nature consists of mental factors (*citta-dharma*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "Deeply enduring, delighting in, and desiring [the real, the virtuous, and the capable] constitutes the nature of the mind.
Among these, the first three pertain solely to self-benefit; the next four pertain to the benefit of others; and the final two [pertain to both].

It penetrates both types of benefit and fulfills the general function mentioned previously by universally remedying all obstacles; it subsequently remedies specific obstacles individually through its particular functions, namely:
doubt and regret, indolence, envy, pride, lack of faith, stinginess, distraction, and malice.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Faith can forever extinguish the root of afflictions; faith can transcend the paths of all Māras."

Among the ten meanings—severing the web of doubt, emerging from the stream of craving, extinguishing pride, and the two roots of reverence and its basis—the first five meanings correspond to the stage of the Three Worthies (*trividha-ārya*).
Within the "Lower Worthies" (the Ten Abodes), one leaves behind pride and realizes the nature; this corresponds to the first two meanings.

Within the "Worthies of the Ten Practices," one cultivates the virtues of long-term practice; this corresponds to the meaning of "giving birth. Within the "Higher Worthies" (the Ten Dedications), one maintains and upholds meritorious virtues.
As it repeatedly increases and develops, it shall emerge as four or five; the three meanings of "integration," "flourishing," and "prosperity" apply universally across the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

While the explanation of the names and the assignment of positions within the stages reach only up to the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi*, this is because the *Samantaprabhā* (Equal Enlightenment) and *Svayambhū-jñāna* (Wonderful Enlightenment) are implicitly included within the tenth stage when speaking from the perspective of their unification.

Third, "The three [categories] can enter" refers below to the capacity to enter and that which is entered. That is, the sixteen gates are the capacity to enter, and the sixteen dharmas are that which is entered.
Because this is abbreviated here, it is referred to in the subsequent text.

Second, "Having already explained" below clarifies the establishment [of the categories]. This has two parts: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, citing the original text and providing an explanation. Regarding the first: [End of section]

The Chanting Text of the Treatise has two parts: the commentary on the text. First, the inquiry and the explanation; second, the detailed exposition. Regarding the first [the inquiry and explanation], there are two sections: first, a brief indication; second, a broad explanation of this meaning.

Regarding the first [the brief indication], there are three parts: first, an illustration by means of a parable; second, the "The Transformer" section and below, an explanation by way of the Dharma; third, the "Faster than before" section and below, the application [of the analogy]. Regarding the first [the parable], there are three parts: first, the parable itself; second, the "The Transformer" section and below, the Dharma-explanation; third, the "Faster than before" section and below, the synthesis. Regarding the second [the broad explanation of this meaning], there are five sections. Regarding the first [section], there are three parts: first, the inquiry arising from what preceded;

second, the "In order to" section and below, the sequential narration and explanation; [and so forth]. The text consists of five segments. In the first [segment], there are three parts: first, the parable; second, the "The Transformer" section and below, the Dharma-explanation; third, the "Faster than before" section and below, the synthesis.
Regarding the first of the two similes among those [two], the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) is explained as follows:

because it produces all manner of precious treasures at will, such jewels exist only within the great ocean, capable of producing all the various gems found therein. Yet, the substance of these jewels is exquisite, dignified, and perfectly square;
the Dragon Kings place them in the most profound and secret locations, so that all ordinary beings, as well as the various *nāgas* and spirits, cannot reach them.
"One must not see the subsequent Mahāyāna teachings as being merely equal to the Dharma of the Śrāvakas.

This means that although the non-dual Dharma is of a single essence, it manifests as thirty-two kinds of Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; for this is the common basis upon which all vehicles rely.
Following this, the section on "Reiterating the Majestic Power" concludes by summarizing the "Majestic Power of the Great Dragon," referring to the Great Dragon King and his precious jewel.

Because the jewels produced therein are gathered, stored, and utilized with mastery, those of sharp faculties and wisdom—namely, the great bodhisattvas—comprehend and understand their essential nature and various dharma-gates, thereby becoming free from doubt and slander. Among these three, the first is illustrated by means of a simile:
the wish-fulfilling jewel is placed within a secret treasury and sealed and protected by a thousandfold gates, which serve to exclude [unauthorized access].

The keys for understanding the various classes of dragons and so forth consist in thoroughly knowing that these jewel-treasures exist. Next, regarding the Mahāyāna, the fundamental teaching is joined with the Dharma:
although this foundational Dharma is capable of giving rise to Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, those of dull faculties cannot attain comprehension through it alone.
Only by means of detailed explanation, analysis, and extensive exposition can one finally achieve clear understanding; even though this single treatise provides such an explanation...

In the section [discussing] the divisions, it is explained that there are only four dharmas. Since the subsequent treatise states, "Based on the single dharma of the one mind, there are two gates," this single dharma of the one mind is precisely the non-dual substratum upon which all things rely.
Therefore, the treatise declares it to be the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, because this is the common tenet of all the treatises, the treatise itself states that its essence is one. Nevertheless, its...
The basis also has two types: first, the general, and second, the specific. Generally, all arise from the non-dual dharma;

specifically, they take as their basis that which is proximate to their function. Furthermore, while the principles of the preceding metaphors are broad and pervasive, regarding their ultimate source and profound logic as elucidated by the two treatises:
the fundamental dharma is solely non-duality, whereas that elucidated by the discourse on the "one mind pervading everywhere" and so forth is different.
This fundamental dharma is precisely the dharma of the single essence and the single mind; each follows its own primary tenet as the definitive standard.

Thus, among the four [sections], the first relies on a metaphor to demonstrate that although the various nāgas may see and hear the wondrous jewels with their eyes and ears, and their minds likewise understand them, they further manifest the majesty of their tongues to proclaim the virtues of the jewels, yet they do not compete with one another to enter into them.
The gate opens, leading toward the vicinity of the *dāna* (charity) where one may obtain the wish-fulfilling treasury (*cintāmaṇi-kośa*), yet there is as yet no means to ascend the palace terraces.

To definitively synthesize and recite the teachings is the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*); to investigate them in both their extensive and abbreviated forms is the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*);
and to encourage the application of practice is the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*). Although these three wisdoms are possessed, they have not yet given rise to firm resolve.
When faith increases toward the stage of supreme progress, one may compare it to attaining the Vajra-dharmadhātu-garbha;

yet by what means could one otherwise realize and witness this most excellent, profound, and wondrous principle? Having examined the textual meaning and its correspondence to the Dharma herein, I suspect that the translator’s rendering of the phrasing was incomplete;
it should rather have been stated: "While reciting and upholding the venerable words of the teachings through speech, one contemplates them within the mind."
Regarding the profound principle of the extensive and concise [teachings], one is exhorted to apply diligent practice;

yet, if firm faith does not arise, there will be no means to attain the treasury of jewels of the *dharmadhātu* within the Vajra [Vehicle] when progressing toward excellence, nor to realize the profound principle. Therefore, the fourth section establishes the "Chapter on Cultivating Faith in Practice.

In this regard, the student should further reflect and discern for themselves; as the Yan edition of the treatise states: "Diligently apply diligent practice" (the Li edition reads "diligently apply practice").
Regarding the exhortation, within the appearance of the tongue in the analogy, the character "quán" (exhort) should be used.

Among the five [sections], the first indicates the method of extensive and abbreviated exposition, which is the gateway for entering the two preceding divisions. It is the section on faith (*śraddhā*). Sentient beings who are timid and weak, upon hearing the extensive [teaching], become weary of its complexity;
their minds grow indolent and lack the capacity for further advancement in practice. As for sentient beings of dull faculties who hear...

Briefly stated, those sentient beings whose minds are difficult to enlighten and who give rise to renunciation [of the path] such that they cannot receive or understand it, may—if they encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who exhorts them—immediately cultivate the causes and realize the fruit.
However, if they do not obtain the conditions of such exhortation and encouragement, they will for a long time follow their habitual tendencies, becoming estranged and falling away.
Their afflictions will blaze fiercely, burning away their roots of goodness, and they will become icchantikas.
Because there is no lineage (*agotra*), the subsequent section from "Aśvaghoṣa" onwards concludes [the discussion].
