Regarding the second [section], the extensive explanation of the subsequent [part], there are two [subsections]: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, the meaning of that which is based upon it. First, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent:

herein, the headings of the gates are stated as "general characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) because they correspond to the subsequent differentiated characteristics of that which is based upon them. If viewed in relation to the preceding gate of the "basis," this [general characteristic] belongs to the general consciousness that serves as the basis.
The "dependent" is also called the "distinctive characteristic" (or, according to some versions, the "distinctive characteristic of differentiation").

Second, explaining the meaning of the two dependencies. Third, the three gates: first, the gate of awakening that opens the fundamental and the initial to manifest virtue; second, the gate of non-awakening that reveals faults upon the fundamental;

third, the gate of the similarities and differences between awakening and non-awakening. Within the first [of these], there are two parts: first, a brief explanation of the establishment of the two types of awakening.

Section Two: The Gate of Extensive Explanation of the Determination of the Two Awakenings. This section has two parts: first, the presentation of the root text; second, the commentary. The first part [the presentation of the root text] has two sections: first, the division of the categories; second, the explanation of the meaning.

"Root" (*mūla*) carries the sense of "sustaining," because it can sustain the sands-of-the-Ganges number of merits, ensuring they are never lost. "Fundamental" (*maula*) means natural, not derived from...
Because it arises through the construction of causes and conditions, it is remote; because it is free from temporal duration and is boundless, it is not established as something proximate.

Thus, these four virtues collectively subsume the ten meanings: the "root" (*mūla*) is the virtue of bliss (*sukha*), as it sustains and gives rise to true happiness.

Thus, this belongs to the category of "purity through the means of severing afflictions," rather than being inherently luminous and pure from the beginning.
How could it be otherwise? This concludes the section on practice; as for the phrase "affliction and awakening," this concludes the first [section].

Regarding the phrase "the difficulty concerning the hidden and the manifest," this refers to the conclusion of the subsequent objection: if delusion and awakening are mutually dependent as the hidden and the manifest, how can the doctrine that they are inherently existent (fundamentally present) be established?

Second, the phrase "if it is made" introduces the investigation into initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). First, this restates the words of the response, meaning that the previous objection is refuted by turning back to provide another answer.
It is said that all afflictions are fundamentally and eternally severed, and all merits are fundamentally and eternally complete.
Because of this fundamental severance and these fundamental merits, the principle of "original existence" (benyou) is established. Now, to reaffirm this, it is stated:
if one makes such a claim, there are two points; below, a refutation is extended, indicating that the proposed thesis itself is not established. That is to say, if...

If original enlightenment (*prakṛtistha-awakening*) does not depend on the severance of delusions, but is by its very nature luminous and pure, endowed with all virtues, then the meaning of its being "originally present" can be established.
However, if one says that it only comes to possess these virtues after the severance of delusions, then it would follow that there are no originally inherent virtues;

this would constitute a great error. Since the "original severance" and "original virtues" were previously established [as the nature of] beginningless purity, how could they be the "commencing awakening" (*ādikarmika-awakening*)?
Is it falsely claimed that this is the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*)?

For this reason, the following citation of scripture establishes that the severing of fundamental afflictions and the realization of fundamental virtues constitute *ādikṣaya-bodhi* (initial enlightenment); it is not the original enlightenment, because it is the awakening to the initial delusions.

Third, regarding the section "By what means... and below, which concludes by returning to the intent of the question: because the Master [of the treatise] anticipates the doubts of the opponent, he provisionally initiates the discussion by asking, "Why is this so?

Second, regarding the section "The two types of original awakening" and below, which extends the answer: first, restating the question; second, the explanation beginning with "That is to say, like a horse... and so forth.
The first [of the two] is that which is fundamentally beyond thought and deliberation: this fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) has been non-arising and non-ceasing from the very beginning;
because it is free from origination and extinction, it is neither established nor negated, for there is no increase or decrease;
it is neither affliction nor virtue, for there is no defilement or purity. Fundamentally transcending names and signs, it is beyond the reach of speech and thought, and cannot be described.

Regarding the distinction of the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), there are two; here, the name is established in contrast to the "initial" [awakening]. This refers to what was previously stated:

that which is called "original awakening" (*mūla-awakening*) by way of being free from conceptual thought and so forth, is precisely because the pure initial awakening—arising from time without beginning—proceeds simultaneously with both serenity (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
As it serves as the antidote to the obstacles of affliction and possesses complete merit, the name of that pure original awakening is established based upon this initial awakening.
Therefore, the second section begins the explanation of the underlying cause, stating that because the two types of awakening arise from the same source yet have different names,
one may rely upon the *shijiao* (initial awakening) to manifest that pure *benjue* (original awakening).
2. Thus, the following section generally distinguishes the two types of perfuming (*vāsanā*). This consists of: first, the posing of the question; second, the response and explanation.
Regarding the first [the response], there is the verse summary: the first verse displays how [the mind] has been free from defilement and pure since the very beginning;

the subsequent verse displays that there is only the perfuming of virtues (*guṇa-vāsanā*) and no perfuming of afflictions (*doṣa-vāsanā*). Regarding the second [the prose commentary], there is the explanation of the verse text, the first part of which explains the preceding seven lines.

Next, as explained below regarding the final phrase: although there are differing meanings of "perfuming" (*vāsanā*)—in that the defiled and the pure mutually support and depend upon one another to achieve accomplishment—here, both are accomplished as the true virtues of one's own nature; therefore, it is said to be "perfuming through complete transformation.
By the power of this perfuming, the illusory nature and the various phenomena that follow that illusion are all made to be of a single flavor, such that they do not allow for defilement.

Because they are established through mutual dependence, these perfumings are described as "white" because they are pure. Regarding the two bodies (the Reward and Transformation Bodies) below, the scripture is cited as proof:
since the fundamental twofold awakening-nature is unchanging, there is only the perfuming of qualities (*guṇa-vāsanā*), for it does not follow after delusion; thus there is no affliction.

Because the perfuming of qualities is eternally ultimate, there is only the revolution of fulfillment (*paripūrṇa-parāvṛtti*), which is devoid of ascending or descending; thus there is no revolution of partiality (*bhāgaśaḥ-parāvṛtti*).

The second section explains the nature of detachment from the two types of awakening. Regarding the first part, which clarifies the fundamental and the initial [awakening], there are two sub-sections:
first, a general restatement and indication; second, a specific attribution of the text. Following this, the meaning is interrogated.

Because non-awakening exists by depending upon fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*), the cause is revealed through its fruit: fundamental awakening serves as the basis, and only through the turning of non-awakening does [the latter] arise.

The meaning that original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) possesses the quality of being free from [delusion] is revealed by relying on non-enlightenment (a-bodhi); thus, it is said that there is "initial enlightenment" (ādi-bodhi).

Because the antidote is revealed by means of the obstacle, one speaks of the "initial enlightenment that is free from nature" only in relation to that which is to be remedied—the fundamental and derivative non-enlightenment.
Second, the explanation of the meaning based on the *benjue* (intrinsic awakening) below is divided into two parts. First, regarding *benjue*:

because the function of intrinsic awakening penetrates [all things] yet follows along with delusion, it is called "departing from nature" (*li-xing*); because it does not maintain its own natural purity, it is called "not abiding in its own nature."
Second, the initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodha*). This has two parts. First, the direct clarification of being free from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vimukta*):

because the initial awakening penetrates the functioning of [the mind] that undergoes defiled perfuming, it is able to counteract defilement; since it is deceived by what is defiled, it is called "free from intrinsic nature. Second, the successive interrogation and explanation.

Within this, first is the interrogation and explanation of the meaning of deception. Herein, first is the interrogation regarding how the initial awakening is well able to sever defilement and realize [the truth].
Why does the Pure One say that one is deceived by defilement? For all dharmas are from the beginning of a single flavor, equal and without distinction;
they are neither defiled nor pure, and possess neither merit nor fault. Now, this initial awakening (ādikṣānti-bodhi) conceives a notion of differentiation within that which is undifferentiated.
To perceive distinctions such as abandonment and realization, or merit and fault, is precisely to be deceived by other defiled dharmas. If this is so, then the original...
Since the Awakened Mind (bodhi) does not form such conceptualizations of superiority or inferiority regarding phenomena, why is it also described as being "free from nature" (*niḥsvabhāva*)?

It is because the essence of that original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is identical to that of this initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*); thus, by contrast with initial awakening, its original awakening is manifested.
This is like a perfect mirror, pure and stainless, which is called "original luminosity," yet later, due to the obscuration of clouds and dust, must be polished again until it shines forth.

"Crystal" (yìng) is immediately designated as "Newly Illuminated" (xīnmíng); although the names differ, the essence of illumination is no different. Using this metaphor to correspond to the meaning of the Dharma, the principle is clearly evident.

If this is so, [the text] below raises a question to explain when [this awakening] is separated from time: "At what time can this initial awakening, which has coexisted with defilement since beginningless time, become separated from it?
It refers to the moment within the Path of Liberation when one realizes non-thought; at that time, one ultimately becomes separated from all [defilements].
Because it is false.
Second, "fulfillment" refers below to fulfillment, which is the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*), while "division" refers to the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*).
This will be explained below in the treatise.

Second, the section on the detailed explanation of the two types of awakening through the gate of definitive discernment (*viniścaya*), which has already been introduced. This consists of two parts: first, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one;
second, explaining the characteristics according to the text. Regarding the first [the detailed explanation of initial awakening], there are two parts:

Regarding the section "Marking the Two and Four Characteristics," below is the specific exposition, which begins with the general establishment.

First, within the establishment of the four characteristics, there is first the marking and listing, followed by the explanation of the two types of coarse and subtle, both of which take the nine types of defiled phenomena as their substance.

These are merely divided into two—namely, the permanent and the impermanent—based on the duration of time; both are essentially the merit of *prajñā* (commencement-awakening) that accords with conditions.

The essence arises solely through the nature of conditions; because it is originally complete yet divided into two, there are "awakening following [conditions]" (*anubodha*) and "non-awakening" (*abodha*).

Within the establishment of awakening following [conditions], first the headings are listed and then their characteristics are explained. Because awakening and non-awakening are non-dual in character, it is called "complete awakening" (*pūrṇa-bodhi*);
because awakening and non-awakening are distinguished by way of mutual dependence, it is called "divided awakening" (*vibhakta-bodhi*).

Second, how are the four characteristics explained individually below? First, the inquiry and explanation of the four characteristics: first, explaining "long duration" in terms of the path of cultivation (*pratipakṣa-mārga*).

From the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) up to the fulfillment of the fruit, it is only when the causal virtues are complete and perfected that one is finally able to transcend [the characteristics];
therefore, it is called "long duration. Second, explaining "short duration" with respect to its causal conditions: the successive replacement of moments (*kṣaṇa*) is termed "short duration."
Third, regarding the three explanations of impermanence: in contrast to the faults that are their opposites, the four characteristics are established as remedial virtues.
As the faults arising from the objects to be remedied—namely, change (*jarā*) and destruction (*vināśa*)—are extinguished, the change and destruction of the remedial virtues subsequently arise.

As the faults arising from the objects to be remedied—namely, duration (*sthiti*) and production (*utpāda*)—are extinguished, the duration and production of the remedial virtues subsequently arise. If this is so, why are there only the two characteristics of change and destruction?

Although their names as virtues are manifested through their distinct modes of abiding and arising, because the power of these virtues remains slight during the stages of cessation (*nirodha*) and difference (*anyathātva*), they are not mentioned there in brief.
It stands to reason that the names of these virtues should also be established for this stage [of duration], as the meaning can be inferred by applying the subsequent cases to the preceding ones.
Thus, since all four characteristics arise from conditions, they are called the "four characteristics of initial arising"; the explanation of the permanent [dharmas] will follow later.
That which exists from the beginning is the nature-virtue (*dharmatā-guṇa*); therefore, it is said to be the four marks of permanence.
Second, regarding the inquiry and explanation below concerning "subsequent awakening" (*anubodha*): first, the full awakening is clarified; next, the partial awakening is clarified.
If one undergoes defiled perfuming, one is then able to counteract defilement; that is to say, one is able to awaken to that very non-awakening. Therefore, it is called "awakening to non-awakening."
Alternatively, "awakening" (bodhi) is so called because it either undergoes perfuming, thereby manifesting the presence of the "non-awakening" that is its object of remedy;

or, because it does not undergo perfuming, thereby manifesting the characteristic of the "remedy" itself. Thus, awakening and non-awakening are named according to their two functions: undergoing perfuming and remedying obstacles.

Third, as for the conclusion and exhortation below it: regarding the four characteristics previously explained, one should observe them in their respective order as they are associated with awakening.

Second, "In this regard" and so forth, explains the characteristics; first, the brief presentation and enumeration, then the actual explanation, followed by "Since those [characteristics] do not exist," and so forth.

To further explain the sequence of before and after: when one relies on that initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) as an antidote, first there is no characteristic of cessation and later there is no characteristic of arising;
in the interim, there is no abiding or change. Therefore, "before and after" constitutes their sequence.

first, the verse; second, the prose commentary. Within the prose, first the headings and enumeration; next, the explanation of the characteristics. As for "acting alone" (*kevala-kriyā*) and so forth:

the former two are extremely subtle and are unable to assist one another in combining to produce movement, hence they are called "acting alone. The latter one is somewhat coarse and arises with a distinct, superior function to accomplish [the result].

The following passage summarizes these points below to conclude the name. These three characteristics arise first, and are thus termed "arising.

Among the three subtle states explained in the subsequent text, the first one; among the six defilements, the last one; and among the five mental faculties (*manas*), the first one—all are included herein.
It is subsumed under the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).

Second, the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). This consists of two parts: first, the question; second, the answer and explanation. The first part has three sections: first, the verse; second, the prose commentary; third, the general explanation of the verse.

Regarding the four aspects of the characteristic of abiding: first, the aspect of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to the movement and transformation of the preceding state due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), resulting in non-awakening.

1. The characteristic of the capacity for seeing (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*): because it depends on the aforementioned capacity for seeing, it falsely manifests as objects when the signless realm (*animitta-viṣaya*) is not clearly perceived.

2. The characteristic of manifestation (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*): because it depends on the aforementioned capacity for seeing, it falsely manifests as signs when the signless realm is not clearly perceived. 3. The characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*): because it depends on objects, the mind gives rise to the discrimination of the characteristics of defilement and purity.

4. The characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*): because it depends on the aforementioned discrimination, further recollections arise in succession without interruption. Among these four, the first two and the first [characteristic] are [as described].

The characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) belongs to the three subtle [states] subsumed under the *ālayavijñāna*, and is also included within the three types of non-associated defilements (*viprayukta-saṃkleśa*).

[Section on] "2. Thus" and below: A detailed differentiation of names and meanings. This section has two parts: first, the inquiry; second, from "In this regard" (*atra*) and below, the explanation of the transformation (*pariṇāma*).
The characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) itself is the seeing mind; therefore, it is able to sustain the perfuming of the mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).

"Sustaining" refers to the activity of the perfumer (*vāsaka*), while "perfuming" refers to the infused portion (*vāsya-bhāga*). Because the manifestation of the mind (*citta-pravṛtti*) perfumes the infused portion of the mind, the manifested characteristic (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*) is form (*rūpa*).
Although the perfuming of the infused portion of form also extends to the mind, because it is contrasted with the evolving characteristic (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), it belongs exclusively to form.
Discriminative wisdom has the characteristic of discerning and selecting; among the six coarse [aspects], it occupies the first position.

The characteristic of the simultaneous arising of dharma-activity is extremely subtle, yet because it is able to sustain the characteristic of discriminative wisdom, it gradually brings about the latter five.

Therefore, it is said that the sustaining of the six kinds of gradual continuity belongs to the characteristic of the simultaneous arising of dharma-activity, which is progressively coarser than the former.
Therefore, it is able to abide in and maintain the *vibhava-vijñāna* (consciousness of discriminating phenomena); these three constitute the selection of the coarse and the subtle.
This involves two points: first, the *vibhava-vijñāna* encompasses both the coarse and the subtle, yet here, the aspect of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*) only subsumes the subtle portion.

Second, these four aspects of abiding are called "subtle" in contrast to what follows, such as the aspect of difference (*anyathā*), yet this does not preclude their presence within the intermediate stages.
Furthermore, there are coarse and subtle [aspects].

Regarding the three distinct characteristics (*visiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*), there are two parts: first, the posing of the question; second, the answering explanation. Regarding the first [the posing of the question], there are two parts: first, the verse summary; second, the long prose commentary.

Regarding the first [the verse summary], there are two distinct characteristics: first, the characteristic of grasping (*parāmarśa-lakṣaṇa*), which is established by name based on the cognitive activity of the subject that perceives.

"Grasping" (*udgraha*) and "characteristic" (*nimitta*) are the two [aspects] designated by the term "name," meaning that names are established based on the objects of perception; such are the two characteristics.

These two characteristics are precisely the first type of self-grasping (*pudgala-grāha*), namely the innate (*sahaja*), and the second, namely the conceptualized (*vikalpita*). Below, these two are distinguished individually by name and meaning.
First, the inquiry; second, the explanation: "If we rely on... This means that the grasping-aspect (*udgraha-lakṣaṇa*) arises with respect to the various objective characteristics.

The distinction between different interpretations is precisely the distinction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), because they belong to the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*). Therefore, the treatise states that "difference is established as difference in itself.

Regarding the characteristic of names (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the fact that those names are each distinct; this is the characteristic of difference because it belongs to the objective referent (*ālambana*).

Therefore, the treatise states that "names are established in accordance with their characteristics. Furthermore, these two characteristics previously [arose] from the signified dharmas, such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
Following the grasping at birth, one further gives rise to grasping based on the expressive sounds, names, and phrases;

this is stated in terms of what is predominant regarding the two aspects. In reality, however, these two aspects mutually interpenetrate, and false conceptualizations arise with respect to all phenomena.
Furthermore, the conceptualization of a self—whether as identical to or separate from the aggregates—is not limited merely to that [specific form].

Because of names. Fourth, the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*). Part one: the initial inquiry; part two: the response and explanation. Part one: the verse summary; part two: the long prose commentary. Part one: the explanation of the characteristic of cessation based on the verse.
Therein, the first [verse] pertains to the cause, and the second is the result—namely, the karma that is able to summon out-flowing existence (*sāsrava-karma*).
The maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) thus summoned—these two combined are termed the "characteristic of cessation" (*nirodhalakṣaṇa*). Below, the names and meanings are distinguished:
logically, "destruction" (*bhaṅga*) should apply throughout all three phases; it is not mentioned for "arising" (*jāti*) and "abiding" (*sthiti*) because they are separated by an interval.

Furthermore, below, the meaning of "succession" (*anupūrvī*) is clarified through repetition. Previously, the meaning of "cessation" was explained as the time when one experiences the fruit of suffering, which oppresses the body.
The mind has no means by which to advance toward the good, even though humans and devas, as well as those in the realms of mixed reception, possess subtle and slight manifestations of suffering;
yet because deluded attachment entangles the mind, it is especially difficult to perform wholesome deeds, and for this reason they are all termed "extinguished" (*nirodha*).

Furthermore, when one truly initiates karma that leads to the three realms of existence, the Buddha-nature—the root of goodness—is lost and does not manifest, just as that which has arisen does not arise again; thus it is called "extinguished. Nevertheless, even while undergoing the wheel of suffering, the Buddha is also extinguished.
When the nature initiates activity, it also ceases wholesome qualities; this explanation is given because the treatise intends to manifest their characteristics.

Second, as for how these are specifically enumerated below, first the names of the stages are presented. However, regarding the stages and grounds (*bhūmi*) elucidated in various sūtras and śāstras, there are differences in whether they distinguish or combine the afflictions (*kleśa*);

for example, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing) has the "Five Patiences" (*pañca-kṣānti*), the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Yingluo jing) has the "Six Natures" (*ṣaḍ-gotra*), and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) has the "Four Grounds."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Seven Stages*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and other treatises speak of five stages (*pañca-avasthā*).

In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the stages of abiding, practice, and orientation (*vihāra-caryā-pratipatti*) are each expanded into ten, forming the "Ten Mysteries" (*daśa-guhyaka*), which constitute the forty-two factors; these encompass the ocean of fruition and penetrate the source of the cause, such that the differentiated and the equal are mutually unimpeded.
In this present treatise, the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) is expanded, while the three levels of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) are combined.

The stage (*bhūmi*) is divided into two parts, thus forming five positions (*pañca-sthāna*). Because the skillful means for training and guiding sentient beings as established by the various noble ones (*ārya*) differ from one another, there are these divisions.

Regarding the first four of the two [parts], the preceding four list the stages of practice (*caryā-sthāna*). As for the four matters within the first four [positions] concerning the causal stage (*hetu-avasthā*):
first, it clarifies the orientation toward the position, manifesting that there are fifty types of persons (*pudgala*) at the time of entry, wherein others come and rely upon oneself gradually.

Because of their progressive advancement, the latter three types are distinguished according to the person, meaning that bodhisattvas fulfill their respective stages and engage in cultivation and progress;
thus, having clarified the characteristics of the cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), since a cause must necessarily produce a result, the characteristics of the result (*phala-lakṣaṇa*) are clarified.

Furthermore, in order to manifest the modes of practice for the remedial paths of the aforementioned three, the characteristic of separation (*visaṃyoga-lakṣaṇa*) is clarified. Finally, as for the three matters in the stage of the result (*phala-avasthā*), they refer to the result itself.

The "Perfected" (pariniṣpanna) is not the fourth [nature], because there is nothing it does not perceive; nor is it the characteristic of cultivating causes for the sake of proceeding toward a state of non-existence;
thus, that which is established is different.
