In relation to the Buddha, all sentient beings enter the storehouse of ignorance; the various defiled and pure phenomena are established through mutual dependence.
If they did not depend upon one another, no distinction between the defiled and the pure could be found. The Buddha is named "Non-thought" because he is contrasted with "arising";

"arising" is named "non-awakening" because it is viewed in relation to the Buddha. Furthermore, while our own school establishes identity, within that identity there is also a sense of differentiation.
One may look toward establishing distinctions, yet within those distinctions there is also the meaning of sameness; such identity and difference should be carefully examined and contemplated.

Third, from this point downward, he exhorts one to observe the relationship between the Buddha and sentient beings: they are both eternal and defiled, both pure and non-defiled, both permeated by defilement and purity, and both neither defiled nor pure;
they are without birth and without Buddha, without accomplishment and without non-accomplishment, and are not constrained by existence or extinction, nor by mind or speech.
Do not rely on the present [text] alone; rather, this exposition of defilement and purity briefly indicates the general outline while simultaneously encompassing the profound meaning.
Second, from here below, the two awakenings are shown to be mutually pervasive. This has two parts: first, the heading and indication; second, the explanation and establishment.

Regarding the first, the explanation of the main text, there is first the fusion and the clearing away of the partial and the complete. This means that throughout the fifty stages, awakening is without any difference of superior or inferior transformation. One.
Because there is no ultimate limit to the gradual fulfillment of awakening, the following passage explains the reason for this:

it is by means of the *ārambha-abhisambodhi* (initial awakening) wisdom (*prajñā*) supporting those four marks (*lakṣaṇa*), and through their simultaneous coexistence, that [the stages] can be established.

If the four marks—cessation, difference, abiding, and arising—did not exist, that initial awakening could not establish itself; thus, there would be no distinction between the gradual and the complete fulfillment [of awakening].
Because it is equal to and of one mark with original enlightenment (prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna), without any distinction, it subsequently returns to its source as before.

In the second section, "The Two Great Summaries," which introduces scriptural evidence, the first part specifically clarifies that while the characteristics and the awareness are established such that awareness follows the characteristics, they exist simultaneously;

because they are fused and identical to original enlightenment, it is said that [awareness] "follows" [the characteristics]. Next, the phrase "Furthermore, because... provides a general explanation of the underlying reason.

Second, having already explained the brief [overview], the extensive explanation of the section on the definitive analysis of *mūla-awakening* (*mūla-awakening-viniścaya*) has two parts: first, concluding the previous section and introducing the subsequent one; second, the commentary that elaborates upon the meaning of the text.

Regarding the second part, the extensive explanation of the gate of *mūla-awakening* as it conforms to defilement, there are two sections: first, the recitation of the root treatise; second, the composition of the explanatory commentary. Regarding the second section, the composition of the explanatory commentary, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the divisions;

second, the explanation of the characteristics of *mūla-awakening* and its conformity to defilement. Regarding the second part, the explanation of the characteristics of *mūla-awakening* and its conformity to defilement, there is first a general explanation of the term "conformity to defilement," which applies universally to *mūla-awakening*.
Taking that which is able to follow the defiled dharmas of ignorance as the "follower," this refers to the "following" of defilement because it comes to depend upon others;
it is the awakening that follows defilement, distinguished from that which is pure.

2. From here below is the detailed explanation of the two characteristics that arise. This section has two parts: first, the heading and indication; second, the detailed explanation following the headings.
Regarding the first part, the general explanation of the two characteristics, there are two sub-sections: first, citing the text; second, from "In this way" onwards, explaining the meaning.

This means that due to this fundamental awakening (mūla-āśraya-parāvṛtti) following defilement, illusory discrimination gives rise to two characteristics. Fundamental awakening is the essence (svabhāva), and the two characteristics are its function (vṛtti). This is the relationship between essence and function.
Because they do not abandon or separate from one another, they are said to be "concomitant" and "co-evolving.

Second, the detailed explanation of these two characteristics has two parts: first, the gate of the originally existing nature of wisdom being pure, which contains two sub-sections—the sub-section on not maintaining its own nature while following conditions, and the sub-section on counteracting all karmic obstacles; second, the combined explanation of these two gates.

There are two parts to the initial section: first, the formal analysis of the two gates; second, the inquiry and its explanation. Regarding the first, within the verse, the first three lines correlate with the meaning:
because all obstacles are destroyed, the *dharmakāya* manifests; because all obstacles are extinguished, true wisdom is purified.
The phrasing of the verse is skillfully concise, displaying the sequence by leaping over it. The final line concludes the name; logically, it should be called "Dharma."

Regarding the purity of body and wisdom: here, the names are not established based on what is manifested, but rather are designated according to the characteristics of the antidotes that subdue afflictions.

Second, the long prose section has three parts; first, the general explanation: although this fundamental awakening (mūla-awakening) evolves in accordance with conditions, it does not abandon its original nature, and because it perfects the person through the adornment of the dharmas of merit, wisdom, and cultivation, [it is so named].

II. The Two Abandonments: A Detailed Explanation. This section has two parts: first, the treatment of obstacles to reveal the virtues; second, the power of the remedy. Regarding the first, the power of the remedy, there are two sub-sections:

first, the question and answer that introduce the topic; second, the enumeration of names and explanation of their meanings. That is to say, the abandonment of obstructive defilements must necessarily rely on two powers:

the first power resides in the fruit, while the latter power belongs to the cause. Because the nature of the heavens (*deva*) is originally thus, it is not something newly produced. Second, "In this way" and below concerns that which is abandoned.
Among the hindrances, the first relies on the method of the profound permeation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is supremely excellent;

thus, when the fruit of the ten stages is fulfilled, one is able to destroy the karmic characteristic of ignorance acting alone. Subsequently, the second relies on the power of the permeation of the true wisdom of the ten kinds of *tathatā*, which is next most excellent;

thus, when the causes of the ten stages are fulfilled, the ninth [hindrance]—the karma of conjunction—is extinguished, the eighth—the capacity to see—is extinguished, and the seventh—the manifesting aspect—is extinguished.

Upon reaching the second [stage], the wisdom that extinguishes conceptualization reaches the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), where the characteristics of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*) are extinguished.

However, according to the *Mūla-śāstra*, the objects to be countered (*vipakṣa*) are limited to the characteristic of continuity alone, because this is the final limit of the manas-consciousness and represents the ultimate point of what is to be countered throughout the ten stages;

furthermore, it is adjacent to and encompasses the three levels of the candidates for the stages (*tri-piṭaka-śaikṣa*). Alternatively, "continuity" may refer to the consciousness of continuity itself.

Although the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena) prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva] has been clarified here, its capacity to counteract [afflictions] is not yet complete, even though the objects to be counteracted are already sufficient;

this meaning is understood by inference. Therefore, the ignorance (*avidyā*) manifested in the lower roots—which was previously destroyed—is actually an obstruction to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Now, the manifestation of the *dharmakāya* through the destruction of ignorance is based on the comprehensive obstructions; thus, ignorance and the functional power of karma mutually depend upon one another to give rise [to phenomenal existence].

All defiled states are termed "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) because they manifest at the very beginning; thus, they are not designated by subsequent names, as later dharmas lack the meaning of conjunction.
Since its essence is severed from afflictions, it is called "pure" (*viśuddha*); because it illuminates objects with brilliant clarity, it is said to be "luminous" (*vimala*).
2. From "As in the original" (*er ru ben*) below, it is established by returning to the fundamental seal (*guibenyin*).

3. From "For what reason" (*he gu*) below, it is explained through the "good" [passage]. 4. Regarding the initial inquiry and explanation concerning the completeness or deficiency prior to the stages (*diquan juede*):

this refers to the previous clarification that the two powers (*erli*) only explain the fulfillment of the fruit (*guoman*) as well as the stages above the Grounds (*dishang*), without mentioning the three levels of worthiness (*sanxian*) or the ten levels of faith (*shixin*). This is because, compared to what preceded, these are merely the beginning.
In the state of awakening, these are clearly and distinctly manifest in their respective order; therefore, they are not briefly displayed here.

Alternatively, since the fruits and the ten stages have already been explained, the three levels of the *śaikṣa* (the three *pudgalas* of the stage of training) and so forth can be understood by analogy.

Second, why is it that the sequence of the investigation, explanation, and treatment of obstacles is as it is? It is because fundamental enlightenment (mūla-avabodha) turns its back on the holy and faces toward the ordinary, evolving through a sequential process;
this is different from initial enlightenment (ādi-bodhi), which turns its back on the ordinary and faces toward the holy.

If this is so, when fundamental enlightenment enters the storehouse of ignorance (avidyā-garbha), how can it still be said to be capable of severing all afflictions? It is because, though following along with defilement, it does not lose its own nature, just like water.

How could water that has formed lack the nature of moisture? Its self-nature is luminous and pure; it can purify and treat all defilements. Although its power has not yet been restrained, it will never abandon them.
Therefore, even when turning downward, it may still be said to "sever" [defilement], for it must await the mutual support of the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) as they turn together.

Third, why is this? This interrogative and explanatory passage regarding the upper and lower aspects of the two awakenings is thus: the sequence of the upper and lower of these two awakenings is actually due to...
Because the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus.

Fourth, regarding the phrase "Thus it is," there are two parts: the interrogation and the explanation. This section on the two periods of transformation has two sub-sections. First, the five questions and answers:

although the distinctions between the coarse and subtle, and the superior and inferior, manifested through the conditions of delusion and awakening differ, they do not depart from the one mind; therefore, there is no sequence before or after, just like a white woolen cloth.
Counting several *xun* [in length], they are painted to form images; although these images are layered one before another, they appear simultaneously.
Second, thus below, citing the teachings to establish the proof. Part one: answering the question regarding their arising. Part two: "At that time," etc., extensively citing the scriptural text.
Part one: pointing to the ancillary text.
Second, informing the subordinates to clarify the correct principle, in four parts: First, the command and exhortation to seek counsel regarding one matter:

namely, that the fundamental and initial enlightenment of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas appears in the world solely for the sake of the one great cause and condition—namely, to reveal, instruct, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision;
thus, the nature of this knowledge and vision is precisely fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), while its manifestations are the aspects of knowledge and vision.
This is precisely *ādi-bodhi* (initial awakening).
Second, regarding the section "At that time" and below, which concerns reverently receiving [the teaching] and posing questions: first, it recounts what was previously heard;

within the twelve lines of the verse, the first ten lines specifically clarify the two turnings, among which the first line commands the audience to listen, and the subsequent four lines clarify the upward turning of initial awakening.

The first two lines of the verse on "Original Enlightenment" (*samyag-vākya-mūla-avabodha*) explain the subsequent two lines by generally clarifying the temporal divisions. Following this, the section beginning with "I and... formally extends the inquiry.
Third, from "At that time... onwards, there is the admonition to listen for the teaching; herein, the preceding verses are revealed to resolve those doubts, beginning with the initial presentation.
Next, from "Good son" onwards, the initial and final aspects within the explanation of the characteristics are presented.
From "The four therein" onwards, it is said that upon hearing this, all are awakened; this refers to the simultaneous negation and manifestation of one matter, one characteristic, and one essence.

That is to say, by brushing away diverse characteristics, one returns to the identical characteristic; yet, when there is neither one characteristic nor one essence, even the identical characteristic is eliminated.
When the single flavor of emptiness is realized, that very emptiness is also empty and beyond words; thus, one further brushes away the traces of the preceding expressive terms.

When the words of emptiness are also empty, one again uses emptiness to dispel the prior expression of emptiness. By using emptiness to dispel emptiness until there is nothing left to dispel, the profound and wondrous principle is thereby revealed.
All of this constitutes the meaning of the single method of negation (apavāda-pratiṣedha), and the nature of all phenomena is likewise the true reality (bhūta-lakṣaṇa).

Reversing the previous "absence of marks" reveals the quality of true bliss, which is also eternally abiding; reversing the previous "absence of essence" reveals the quality of true permanence, which is also definitive;
reversing the previous "absence of words" reveals the quality of true purity, meaning it is not like defiled phenomena that shift and are indeterminate, and thus it is also truly existent;
reversing the previous "also empty" reveals the quality of true self—this constitutes the positive definition of a single reality.

This is the meaning: since the preceding characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics (*animitta*), it is not translated separately. Because emptiness is negated, one expresses non-attachment to existence;
because existence is expressed, one negates sinking into emptiness. When emptiness and existence are free from doubt, a single matter becomes manifest;
through this *dhāraṇī*, all that is heard is clearly understood and fully awakened.
II. From here below, the remaining meanings are explained in detail. This section has two parts: first, a general heading indicating the scope; second, a detailed explanation of the characteristics.

Regarding the manifestation of causes and conditions, there are two parts: first, questioning and explaining the previous refutation of cessation; second, citing the text to apply it, and then explaining it according to the meaning.
"The consciousnesses of various conceptual proliferations" refers to the three subtle [consciousnesses] that involve grasping, objectifying, and cognitive deliberation.
That is to say, the wisdom of discrimination clings to objects and does not relinquish them; this is the characteristic of continuity.
The characteristics of wisdom and the continuity of those characteristics both arise based on the three subtle states and all various conceptualizing consciousnesses (*prapañca-vijñāna*).
Since all such phenomena are entirely the out-breath of that ignorance (*avidyā*), their defilement is particularly heavy, and therefore they must be destroyed.

Second, from here below, the demonstration of what is severed and what is not severed has four parts. First, the general introduction and the raising of the inquiry. Second, the general inquiry and interrogation. Third, the specific establishment of the objection.
Fourth, the detailed analysis of the objection that [the truth] can be severed. Regarding the first, the analysis of what can be severed according to the nature of phenomena:
it is said that all defiled phenomena are a synthesis of the true and the false; if the false can be severed, then the true should also be severed, because the true and the false proceed together.
Because they are distinct yet constitute a single dharma, the following analogy is raised to clarify this: for example, a single person possesses two functions;
when he is in a state of feigned sleep, it is called "sleeping," and when he is awake and alert, it is called "awakening. Although two terms are designated, there is in reality only one person.

One cannot say that by cutting off sleep, awakening remains, or that by attaining awakening, sleep perishes, because the continuity of their substance is one. This means that if one speaks of the functions of sleeping and awakening...
Furthermore, [the opponent] would incur the grave fault of asserting that the essence is distinct and that the realms of existence arise through false proliferation.

Second, if [ignorance] cannot be severed, it is impossible to bring about liberation; for if ignorance were indestructible, the fundamentally enlightened pure mind would be perpetually shrouded by defilement, making escape from suffering impossible—this fault as well is great.

Second, the following section provides an answer based on the treatise, which is divided into three parts: first, the explanation according to the Dharma; second, the general answer; third, the specific explanation.

Third, the initial part consists of an inquiry and a listing [of points], followed by the establishment of the argument. Second, the "same" [point] and so forth explain the two meanings. First, the dual explanation of the two meanings:

regarding the meaning of "sameness," the phrase "all are principle" means that because all phenomena are entirely constituted by the grasping of principle, their characteristics are identical to their nature; therefore, it is said they are "all."

Since this principle is in every case a principle, it cannot be severed. If that is so, the preceding passage—within our own school’s definitive resolution—states that because they share the same substance (*ekasvabhāva*), the severance of one is the severance of all. How then can it be said here that they do not share the same substance?

However, because there is a distinction between the identity of the phenomenon (*vastu*) and the identity of the principle (*tattva*), there is no contradiction between [the claims of] severance and non-severance. Next, regarding the virtues and defects within the section on "difference":

"Differentiation" means that because the entities of defilement and purity are not identical, they are said to be distinct; since they are distinct, it might follow that both [defilement and purity] could be severed.
Regarding all phenomena, the following two scriptural passages are cited in succession. First, to prove that they cannot be severed:

because the characteristics of all phenomena are not different from their nature, it is said that the three poisons are themselves *nirvāṇa*. This applies equally to views and non-views, as well as to attachment and non-attachment.

The primordial single characteristic is entirely without differentiation; because this single characteristic is devoid of all characteristics, desire, hatred, delusion, nirvana, and the Buddha-way are all non-existent.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "There is no Buddha and no Dharma.
If there are sentient beings who can understand this, they are called "wise ones" within the world. Second, the lower stage of the ground provides scriptural proof that [defilements] can be severed.
This means that because ignorance is able to sustain all defilements, it is said to possess great power;

because it can obstruct the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it renders one lacking in self-mastery; because initial awakening (*ādikṣānti-bodhi*) is able to sever and eliminate it, it is called a "sword";

because the myriad practices (*sādhana*) of the ten stages can adorn it, it is termed a "jewel"; and because ignorance is profound and vast, it is likened to an ocean within the context of the ten stages.

Because it is severed bit by bit, it is said to be "gradually exhausted. This means that since ignorance has both coarse and subtle aspects, the ten types of coarse functions are gradually severed across the ten stages (*bhūmi*), while their subtle essence is suddenly severed upon reaching the fruition.

Because the *dharmakāya* of True Suchness realized through the ten stages gradually increases in height, it is like a mountain slowly becoming visible; this is as explained in the third fascicle of the *Benji lun*.

Second, from here downward, there is an explanation by way of analogy. This has two parts: first, the general indication; second, the detailed explanation. Within the detailed explanation, there are two sections:

first, the arising of delusion based on the True [Nature], which uses analogies to correspond to the Dharma, each having four points; herein, the *ālaya* is the "great" that encompasses the secondary.

Second, the mutual support of the True and the delusive, starting from "next, the characteristics of water," and so forth. Finally, "water is not... explains the establishment of the fundamental nature, essence, and function of Original Enlightenment as being inherently present.

Detached from and liberated from the movement of thought and the bonds of conditioning, because the universal functioning acts as the permeation of ignorance, it moves and shifts according to conditions to produce all defiled manifestations.
Later, regarding the passage "if the wind below ceases," false [consciousness] is extinguished and the True remains. First, it clarifies the extinction of the false:

since fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) treats delusions in order from the subtle to the coarse, first ignorance is extinguished, followed by the treatment of karma and other conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of consciousness.
Later, to reveal that the reality truly exists, it is said that the nature of moisture is indestructible; this means that although wind and waves may cease, the nature of moisture remains constant.

Likewise, although the various consciousnesses may perish, fundamental enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) eternally persists. It is like salt and cinnabar, which remain distinct despite being mixed with nine other substances; or like fire and water, which maintain their own unique characteristics whether burned or doused.

The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is inherently thus and cannot be subject to further questioning. How could it be compared to the state of sleep versus awakening, where one might assume its substance is fixed?
Since a single instance that lacks uniformity is not a true similar example (*sapakṣa*), the previous objection raised against me is without fault.

Third, from here on, the two [examples] are explained together: first, the heading; second, the explanation of their characteristics, beginning with "The great ocean. Regarding the first, the explanation of the characteristics of the simile:
first, it explains what is produced by the wind and water, namely, that water issues from the crown of the head due to the power of the Dragon King’s mental intention.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that within the four great continents,
twenty-five thousand rivers flow continuously and without interruption into the great ocean. Furthermore, there are eighty trillion great nāga kings, such as Daśaraśmi,
along with the nāga king Sāgara and his son named Jambudhvaja, who each rain down great torrents of water that pour down incessantly.
The ocean and so forth are now explained here by way of the principle of the single characteristic shared between the dharma and its metaphor.

Second, as for the reason why [the waves arise], this reveals the causes and conditions for the movement of the waves. First, the inquiry and enumeration of the similar primary elements (*mahābhūta*) have two meanings:
first, because they occupy the same location and are inseparable, they interpenetrate one another without obstruction; second, they are in harmony.

Because they are mixed and inseparable, it is like various medicinal ingredients compounded into a pill; they abide in close proximity to one another without merging, yet they occupy the same location.
This refers to the coexistence of similar types in the same place.
Second, this meaning is explained and established below in two parts: first, clarifying the great elements; second, first, the actual demonstration of their mutual presence.

First, it is shown in accordance with the fact that because they are mutually present, water and wind interpenetrate, constantly producing waves that continue in an uninterrupted succession. Next, "If the water...

and so forth, which is a reverse demonstration showing that if they were not mutually present, there would be no waves. Second, "Why is this? and so forth, which further explains the reason for this in accordance with the sequence.
Regarding the "first class": it refers to the fact that when *vāyu* (wind) increases, there is only wind; when the kalpa is consumed by fire, there is only fire.

Since the increase of any one [element] results in the decrease of the others, these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) must logically exist together. Therefore, they are said to be co-arisen, co-occurring, and inseparable.

How can the great elements create derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)? It is said: earth provides stability and support; water provides moisture and nourishment; fire provides warmth and transformation; and wind provides motion and development.
The four primary elements mutually assist the derived matter by acting as its five causes: namely, the generative cause (*janana-hetu*), which can produce all forms;

the supporting cause (*niśraya-hetu*), because it serves as the basis upon which form relies; the establishing cause (*pratisthā-hetu*), because it is able to establish form; the maintaining cause (*dhṛti-hetu*), because it is able to sustain form;
and the growth cause (*vṛddhi-hetu*), because it enables form to increase and expand. Thus, these various forms would not exist without earth or space.
Because it has no support, it does not disperse like water; because it lacks fire, it does not decay or rot; because it is not constant, it is not moved by wind.
Therefore, these four are invariably and eternally present together. Furthermore, below this is explained the principle of *dharmatā*:
because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is originally thus, the ocean, wind, and water combine to constantly produce waves; this is called the principle of *dharmatā*.
Furthermore, it is like a dragon fighting over a boat made of camphor wood, or a fish dying upon entering water containing olives;
these are all natural laws (*dharmatā*), so how can one raise objections?

Second, below the section on ignorance, the teaching is shown to accord with the analogy of the dragon; "one mind as many" refers to the tail and the tip of the single mind, which serve as the metaphors.

Placing the head of conditioned sovereignty upon [the head of] unconditioned sovereignty serves as a metaphor to represent the difference in superiority and inferiority between the true and the false.
Second, this treatise intends below to indicate the meaning and exhort the contemplation of the distinct characteristics of the true and the false;

since this is its primary intent, it is called the "initial identical characteristic," while the latter is called the "subsequent" because it is supplementary. Within this, there is also a latent anticipation of external objections, fearing that someone might ask:
It was previously stated that ignorance is not separate from the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) and is therefore indestructible;

why, then, is it said here that "if the wind ceases, the movement ceases," and "if ignorance ceases, the continuity ceases," while the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*) does not perish? To resolve this, it is now explained that the distinct characteristics of the true and the false are the primary intent of this treatise;

for it is by means of the characteristic of the purity of wisdom that the characteristic of the harmonious consciousness (*saṃyukta-vijñāna*) is broken and its characteristic of cessation is extinguished.

Because the wisdom of the dharmakāya manifests as the continuity of the mind and is utterly pure, if they were of identical nature, then ignorance and the like could not be destroyed, and it would be difficult to demonstrate the two aspects of original enlightenment (mūlajñāna). Therefore, the identical nature is taught last, being mentioned incidentally.
In the section citing scriptures as proof, first it reveals that within the false there is the true; next, it clarifies that within the true there is the false;
finally, it praises the profound nature of this realm, which cannot be understood by ordinary or inferior beings.

Regarding the first, the gate of accord with the faculties and suitability: First, the arising of wondrous objects in accordance with the faculties—this refers to the spontaneous manifestation of six kinds of objects through the sovereign functioning of original enlightenment’s wisdom, which accords with conditions to benefit the practitioner, as stated in the second chapter of the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.
The verse says: "The bodies of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are like space, without marks;

Second, as for establishing auspicious names according to their qualities below:

because all six kinds of sublime objects are the function of original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) responding to conditions, they are called "Tathāgatas" by speaking of the function from the perspective of the essence.

As stated in the *Buddhanāmasūtra*, the names of Buddhas are also established based on these six objects, such as the Buddha Sovereign of Form-Dhāraṇī (*Rūpa-dhāraṇī-vaśitā-buddha*) and so forth; or, these may be the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation bodies).
The Buddha-body follows a single realm to transform sentient beings; the Sangha is supreme, establishing auspicious names within this very realm and differing from the six sense-objects of the world.

Alternatively, it may follow what is seen, being superior or inferior according to circumstances. "Equal according to the time" means that through original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), one differentiates the capacity for transformation and benefit based on the duration [of practice], purity or defilement, and sharpness or dullness of faculties, thereby remaining far removed from inappropriate times and places.

it is said that through the power of this "luminous pearl," the principle of the mirror manifests the images of objects without distinguishing between their similarities and differences.

By the force of perfuming (*vāsanā*), all things become entirely clear and pure. This is just as when various streams enter the great ocean, their flavors collectively become salty, and myriad forms are reflected therein.
The colors of Mount Sumeru are all identical to the azure hue of this jewel; the meaning of the mirror can be understood from this.
Furthermore, when all objects and the two—the jewel and the mirror—appear before one another, each appears in its entirety without exception.

Second, regarding the "perfuming of the cause" (hetu-vāsanā), the meaning is combined as follows: the intrinsically pure original enlightenment (prakṛti-viśuddha-mūla-awakening) perfumes the three worlds, making them one with awakening;
this perfuming of original virtue is not the same as the perfuming of adventitious afflictions. Question:

Is it that there was first defiled perfuming which subsequently becomes pure, or is it that there was originally no defilement which is therefore called "pure"? Answer: It is not that there was first defilement and it later became pure; rather, it is so named [because it is inherently pure].
Regarding "original perfuming": if one were separated from awakening (*bodhi*), it would follow that [the mind] is defiled; because it is originally perfumed by awakening, it is primordially pure.

Just as the afflictions of the higher realms should not be unwholesome (*akuśala*)—since they are suppressed by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and have always been established as obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) due to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—so too is this case:
it is primordially perfumed by the nature of phenomena and primordially pure by the nature of phenomena.

Second, furthermore, within the section on the meaning of "space" (*ākāśa*) and so forth, there are first the initial presentation and second the citation and explanation of the two meanings of space:

for there is no dharma of matter that does not possess the meaning of space, because space pervades all and matter is thus identical to space. This is like a flower.
The Venerable One explained: "For example, it is like space, which contains all forms within itself yet makes no conceptual distinctions regarding any objects;
or like space, which pervades everything and enters equally into all lands. The former refers to its capacity for reception, while the latter refers to its universal omnipresence."

If the flow of defilements manifests in this manner even within original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), how can one say that awakening is pure and free from faults?
[The commentary below resolves this: All defiled phenomena cannot defile it; the nature of wisdom is fundamentally pure, and defiled phenomena are fundamentally empty.

It perfumes sentient beings, causing them to attain awakening and purity, and enabling them to become free from all faults.

Second, the detailed explanation of the three [obstructions] below. First, clarifying the three faults to be abandoned:

although all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) are fully subsumed within the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), they are here distinguished because the three virtues (*guṇa*) that are obstructed possess specific differences.

All categories of coarse and subtle defilements produced by ignorance (*avidyā*) constitute the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), as they obstruct the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) regarding *tathatā*. Thus, fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) encompasses both the coarse and the subtle.

The subtle [afflictions] are all obstacles to wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), for they can obstruct the subsequently attained worldly knowledge (*laukika-pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); thus, together they are capable of obstructing the pure virtues of the *dharmakāya*.
For this reason, the two are explained separately. How so? The following reveals the three virtues that are accomplished:

because the *dharmakāya* is of a single flavor, equal and without differentiation, it is called "pure" (*śuddha*), which constitutes the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*). Because the *saṃbhogakāya* is free from defilement and every speck of dust has been swept away, it is called... [the virtue of purity].

Purity itself constitutes the Wisdom Virtue (jñāna-guṇa) of the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya), for it engages with sentient beings by remaining far removed from delusion and darkness; therefore, it is called "clarity" (prabhāsvara). This clarity itself constitutes the Beneficence Virtue (upakāra-guṇa).
Third, regarding the three types of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*), these are discussed below in terms of the virtues that counteract the three faults to be abandoned by clarity.
These three virtues are established as the direct opposites and antitheses of those three faults, because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

It is "muddy" because it is difficult to emerge from the afflictions of sentient beings; it is "impure" because, like the phenomena within water, it obscures wisdom and prevents one from seeing clearly;
it is "foul-smelling" because, even when combined with pure things, it carries the scent of base and mixed elements;

and it "surges to a height of one *vyāma*" because, having distanced itself from the afflictions, it rises high above the ten stages (*bhūmi*). It is "pure water alone" because [it is free] from these [defilements].
Because wisdom dwells in the palace of constant bliss and the chamber of emptiness and stillness, it possesses abundant merit; "gandha" (smell) here refers to foul-smelling water.

The appearance of fragrance obstructs that filth, meaning that the fivefold Dharma-body—consisting of precepts, concentration, and so forth—is able to leave behind the fetid vapors of all compounded things.
The two dharmas [fragrance and foulness] emerge below, joined according to their meaning; herein, the intended metaphor takes only the fundamental awakening and fundamental purity.

"Reality-as-it-is" (*yathābhūta-śūnyatā*) corresponds to the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahādarśana-jñāna*), which is equal to empty space and is exclusively...
The manifestation of the same lands as emanations clarifies that wisdom does not manifest as various heterogeneous defilements;
thus, the object of causal perfuming is the Wisdom of Equality, which permeates the three worlds to unify them into a single awakening due to their nature of equality.

The mirror from which phenomena emerge is the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, which is able to discern the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, selecting the three virtues and eliminating the three [defilements].
Because it has lost the excellence of observation, the mirror of the perfuming of conditions becomes the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (all-accomplishing wisdom).

It initiates the transformations of the three karmas to perfume all sentient beings, so that their activities are not in vain and are fully accomplished. This is because initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) is identical to original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).
Thus, the four meanings are correlated with the four wisdoms; however, this original awakening, which is free from faults and manifests virtues, entirely relies upon the pure initial awakening.

This is the explanation of the meaning; therefore, within this treatise, the four great meanings of the pure initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) are not separately revealed, as they are already fully manifested within original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). This concludes the third section of the treatise.

first, the explanation of the dharma; second, the explanation of the metaphor. Third, from "perfectly complete" onwards, it cites the sutra. "Wisdom" refers to that which is heard.
The wisdoms of reflection and cultivation are what cover that dhāraṇī-wisdom and clarity;

whether it arises as preparatory, fundamental, or subsequently attained, or as co-arising with phenomena, it is empty according to its respective application. Among these, the meanings of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are most directly relevant.

The three are all ignorance. [This section has] two parts: first, the question; second, the answer and explanation. The first part [the question] has two sections: first, the verse; second, the prose commentary.

Within the prose commentary, there is the explanation of the meaning, which includes the dharma, the metaphor, and the application. Regarding the metaphor, *kālakauśika* means "red-eyed bird" (*cakṣurlohitapakṣin*);
it refers to the monkey, which is originally of the rabbit lineage. These sentient beings are produced by their individual karma within the various darknesses.
Regarding "form" (*rūpa*) and "seeing luminosity," the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* cited below states that a single ignorance possesses two types of functions;

because it follows the distinctions among people according to their illusory qualities, it is called "substance" (*dravya*), which means either "the primary meaning" (*svārtha*) or "the essential nature" (*bhāva*).
Fourth, the ignorance that is neither [of the two]. Part one: the question; part two: the answer and explanation. Part one: the verse; part two: the long prose. Part one: explaining the meaning.

That is to say, its essence is luminous and profound, beyond description and definition; because it transcends both the object and the subject of cognition, it is called "neither-of-the-two" (*ubhayābhāva*).
Second, citing the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, there are six layers of questions and answers. Among these, the first four state that it is "not that."
Because it is a dharma that transcends the four propositions of existence and non-existence, the intention of the fifth questioner is as follows: ignorance is not any of those four propositions;
rather, that very "negation" (non-being) is itself ignorance. Thus, one says "it is not. Regarding the word "not" (*na*) used above, it means "neither" (*naiva*).
One does not employ that negation to constitute ignorance. The sixth question and answer explain and establish the meaning of the aforementioned "double negation" (*ubhaya-niṣedha*).

Because there is no phenomenon that can be clarified, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*). This means that if something were definitively existent, definitively non-existent, definitively so, or definitively not so, then phenomena such as existence and non-existence could be clarified.
Since, however, there are currently no phenomena such as existence or non-existence that can be clarified, both expression and conditions are transcended;
thus, it is termed "neither of the two. Nevertheless, the intent of this sutra does not merely consist in transcending its words.
Furthermore, because it eradicates and transcends both right and wrong, the term "neither" (俱非) encompasses three meanings: first, it refers to being simultaneously free from both mind and words;
second, it refers to being free from both existence and non-existence, as well as right and wrong; third, it refers to overturning the preceding state of "both being right.
Although the explicit text highlights only the first two, according to its underlying meaning and intent, it should also include the latter one.

Regarding the five emptinesses and ignorance, there are two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the response and explanation. Regarding the second part, there are two sections: first, the verse; second, the prose commentary.

Regarding the first section (the prose), there are two parts: first, the explanation of the meaning; second, the citation of scripture beginning with "beginningless. As for the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature):

it refers to how, due to ignorance, that which is empty by its very nature is falsely perceived by the deluded mind as existing. Although it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it has the power to serve as the root of all delusions, just like a fly [that perceives a wall as a net].
Although snakes, stumps, and ghosts lack both substance and function, they can cause sentient beings to flee in terror or even lose their lives;
yet, through deluded perception, one claims these snakes and ghosts exist when in fact they are originally empty.

Regarding the six types of fully developed ignorance, there are two parts: first, the question that raises the topic, and second, the answer that explains it. This consists of two sections: first, the verse summary, and second, the long prose commentary.
First, the explanation of the meaning: this refers to the essence of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is exclusively defiled and serves as the cause for all that is defiled and pure.

Because its designation is complete [in this sense], it differs from what preceded it, where both were considered "enlightenment" (*vidyā*). That [previous] teaching was based on the fact that the essence itself universally possesses the power of illusion;
thus, it is called the "two Buddha-natures. Below, the scripture is cited starting with "from ignorance," which means that by virtue of ignorance, regarding that...
Birth and nirvana are falsely conceived as objects of joy and aversion; because of this, one gives rise to the great bodhicitta.

Taking this mind as the substance, one gradually perfects the myriad practices until reaching the ocean of fruition. When one traces back the root cause of all this, it is entirely ignorance; therefore, it is said that [ignorance] is fully present.

Third, regarding the following reference to the treatise, there are two points: first, the *Ratnakośa* has already clarified this, as it is explained with explicit clarity in passages concerning the meaning of awakening and the meaning of non-awakening;
second, the arrangement of the subsequent verses is merely a brief summary of the presentation in the root treatise.
Since that presentation is already clear, there is no need for further elaboration in matching them to the commentary.
Second, first briefly darkening [the topic] and then separately opening ten kinds: first, the inquiry; second, the explanatory response. First, the verse response; second, the prose explanation.
First, clarifying the distinctions in meaning and function: first, a general clarification, wherein the names of the ten kinds are presented to explain the nine preceding lines of the verse;
next, the clarification that while the essence is one, the functions are distinct, explaining the final three lines of the verse. Now, as for the establishment...
The tenth is the reliance on the six meanings: 1. Reliance on the antidote (*pratipakṣa*): This refers to the "seeing" (*darśana*) and the "fulfillment of observation" (*bhāvanā-paripūri*).
"Seeing" is based on the name as it is established from what is realized; "fulfillment of observation" is designated according to the antidote itself. 2. Reliance on the meaning of cause (*hetu*):

It is called the "ground of abiding" (*sthiti-bhūmi*) because it acts as the cause for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and possesses great kindness (*mahā-anugraha*). 3. Reliance on time (*kāla*): It has no beginning but has an end. That which is fundamentally possessed is called "without beginning."

It should be stated that there is an end; the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*) arise and sustain it. The "birth" (*janman*) and "non-equalled birth" (*asamasama-janman*) constitute the "receptacle for the offspring" (*putra-garbha*).

The former two—growth and birth—are differentiated as general and specific; only "birth" (*janman*) and "arising" (*utpāda*) are mutually pervasive, as they both give rise to all phenomena. These two are distinct. The "receptacle for the offspring" (*putra-garbha*) is able to sustain the hidden and the manifest.
Regarding the five reliances, delusion and obscuration are precisely the obstruction of wisdom (*jñāna-āvaraṇa*); this non-awakening (*abodha*) pervades the delusion regarding all phenomena.
The obstruction to wisdom (jñeyāvaraṇa) specifically hinders the clarity of insight; it is based on the six [faculties] that can take objects as conditions for awakening and realization.

Because only those in the stage of Great Awakening (mahābodhi) can thoroughly comprehend and realize the object of ignorance (avidyā), and because the birth of the "unequalled equals" (asamasama-janman) attains wisdom while the "unawakened sons" (abuddha-putra) remain in their storehouse, these five types possess power relative to the downward-turning [process], whereas the single stage of "viewing fulfillment" lacks power relative to the upward-turning [process]; this position is established as the retribution [stage].

The grace has its end; having realized this, one understands that the three types of penetration exist based on the upper and lower [realms], and that there is the sense of the powerlessness of ignorance.
In terms of its actual function and principle, there are many such types; however, for the time being, following the sūtras, they are briefly divided into ten kinds.

The second section, "Explanation of the Ten," consists of two parts: first, the general overview; second, the specific explanation. Regarding the first, the "General Overview," there are two parts: first, the question; second, the answer and explanation. Regarding the second, the "Answer and Explanation," there are two parts.
First, the verse summarizes the vision, which refers to the wisdom that illuminates—that is, the cognitive faculty capable of perceiving.

"One locus" refers to the dharmadhātu, the locus of all meritorious qualities of the realized dharma, because it is established as relying upon the single locus of the one mind. Thus, by means of this "one locus," one is able to see. "One locus" [refers to] the locus of the one [mind].

The seer and the seen are of one locus; because the two names "sound" and "action" differ, this ignorance here is designated according to its locus, meaning it is the ground-abiding of seeing one locus.

The second part consists of the prose section, which has two sub-divisions: first, the explanation of the meaning; second, the citation of the sūtra. The following nine stages (*bhūmi*) should be categorized and divided accordingly.

However, in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, it is stated that all conceptual afflictions (*kleśa*) of the triple world are abandoned simultaneously and instantaneously upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); this is termed "seeing in one place.
That text speaks of what is abandoned first by the three vehicles, whereas this [present teaching] relies on the final, uncommon antidote (*pratipakṣa*) of the Tathāgata.
The explanation of the severance [of doubt].
Second, the dwelling stage of inexhaustible requital of kindness, which has two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the response and explanation.

First, the verse praises kindness as the cause of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dwelling stage; therefore, "requital" is explained as being inexhaustible because the response is infinite, or alternatively, it refers to the inexhaustible kindness [itself] that is requited.

The dwelling-ground (*sthiti-bhūmi*) is explained according to the *svāmin-vyākhyāna* (explanation by way of its master), or because it is inexhaustible, as the grace of the dwelling-ground is boundless. This consists of three parts: first, the prose;
second, the explanation of the meaning; and third, the citation of the sūtra.

Regarding the third point—that which has no beginning but has an end—there are two sections concerning the dwelling-ground: first, the posing of the question; second, the answer and explanation. Within the second section, there are two parts: first, the verse; second, the prose.
Within the practice, although it arises from the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) being manifested in dependence upon conditions, it is said to have a beginning;

yet because it reunites with the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), it is said to be without end. Since delusion has no source, it is called "without beginning. Because the Buddha-fruit is free from thought, it is said to have an end.
Thus, "having an end and no beginning" refers to abiding in the ground (*bhūmi-sthiti*); this is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (locative determinative compound).

Regarding the fourth [topic], "The Ground of the Arising and Abiding of the Peerless and Peerless": first, the question; second, the answer and explanation. First, the verse; second, the prose commentary. First, the explanation of the meaning:
the term "peerless" (asama) indicates that its essence is superior; "arising" (samudaya) reveals that its function is impartial, because it is able to impartially give rise to all defilements.

Thus, the peerless is precisely the arising; the essence sustains the function. Furthermore, the peerless is precisely... *(Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a scholastic commentary on the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* or a related treatise concerning the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*). The passage analyzes the compound "asamasamodayasthiti-bhūmi," breaking down the semantic layers of "peerless" (*asama*), "arising" (*samudaya*), and "ground" (*bhūmi*).)*
The various afflictions produced therein exceed the sands of the Ganges in number and have no equal; because they manifest all at once, they are called "equal-arising.
This "equal-arising" belongs to the sense of being peerless. Furthermore, it is both "unequal" and "equal-arising," as both functions are present simultaneously.
Next, citing a sutra, it says that within the sixth heaven of the desire realm, there exists a particularly sublime palace and garden.
The place where the Māra Pāpīyān receives his retribution is peerless and supreme among the heavenly hosts;
likewise, ignorance is uniquely predominant among the afflictions. Therefore, it is used as a metaphor.

Regarding the five births and the abiding in the stages: first, the question is raised; second, the answer provides the explanation. Within the answer, the verses are explained in detail as cited previously.
The three types of birth are defined by their association with karma; that is, because these three arise first, they establish the meaning [of "birth"].
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is well-established therein, and because it is obtained through birth, it is called "obtained through birth" (*upapatti-labdha*).

Although it arises in conjunction with the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), the power of ignorance is superior, and thus it alone receives the name. This is established by taking its initial arising as the proximate basis.

Regarding the statement that "attainment by birth" (*upapatti-lābhika*) refers to the "son" and so forth: the Sūtra distinguishes this term because it is prone to confusion. Fearing such confusion with the essential nature (*svabhāva*), it was initially designated as "attainment by birth.
However, this is not the case here; it is called "attainment by birth" based on the arising of the fruit.

As for the expression "son of a son," it refers to the produced dharmas which are established as "sons" in dependence upon the producing father. Because the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are not identical, it is called "son of a son."
The sixth is the stage of dwelling in the fulfillment of contemplation (*guanman zhuzhi*). "Guan" (contemplation) is pronounced with a level tone, meaning "to await.

Because one awaits the stage where initial awakening (*shijue*) is perfected and permanently severs [delusions] therein, that which is contemplated is fulfilled; hence it is called the fulfillment of contemplation.
The seventh is the stage of obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa-sthiti-bhūmi*), so named because it relies on the function of being an obstacle to knowledge;
although this obstructs all noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) in general, it is specifically emphasized here because it is particularly contradictory to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).
Regarding the passage from the *Aṣṭādaśa-avakrānti-bhūmi-sūtra* stating that "Prajñā is non-cognition" (*ajñāna*) and so forth:

it is because there is no agitation that it is termed "cognition"; hence it is called "non-cognition. If there is something known, there is necessarily something not known. Therefore, the sage’s mind is non-cognitive, and thus there is nothing it does not know.
This cognition of non-knowing is precisely what is called "non-cognition. All conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and consciousnesses are the absence of such knowing.
This is because the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the various consciousnesses is merely false ideation; it lacks that true knowledge which is free from ideation.
Ninth is the stage of awakened realization (*bodhilabdha-bhūmi*): its essential nature is subtle and profound, yet it is able to universally take all causes and effects as its objective domain.
This function of universal cognition is fully understood only by a Buddha; others do not know it. From that [stage], one is able to...
Because it manifests its own designation by means of these conditions, it is called the "Stage of Awakening and Realization" (*bodhilabdha-bhūmi*).
Regarding the "Stage of the Seed-Treasury" (*bījagarbha-bhūmi*), the "seed" refers to all the resultant seeds that are sustained;

that is, the aforementioned afflictions await their capacity to produce, and in relation to what is produced, they are designated as "seeds. This is because there is a distinction between the fruit-seed and the causal seed; however, this [stage] lacks that [distinction].
Because it is capable of containing and maintaining [the seeds], it is called a "repository" (*kośa*). Since it is the repository of the "sons" (seeds), it is designated by way of its master.
For example, various seeds contain both hidden and manifest sons; these "hidden" and "manifest" states are like the unripened and ripened [stages].
Among the fruits held by worldly seeds, some are able to produce fruit immediately, while others can only produce fruit after a long time; there are none that do not [produce fruit eventually].
The same applies to the "manifest" (*vyakta*): that which is sustained by it has already been moistened and is ripe, being close to producing fruit;

that which has not yet been moistened is still in the process of production, and its distance from the fruit remains great. Furthermore, the "sustained" defiled instruments—referring to seeds and manifest states—are respectively termed "concealed" and "evident.
Regarding the "son like a celestial net": all the banners, parasols, and palaces of the devas are covered by nets so that nothing may be lost.
The meaning of "maintaining the seeds without loss" is likewise. Furthermore, the various distinctions among the seeds held are like the number of mesh-holes in a net, being immeasurable.
Second, regarding the causes [of the names], the following explains the names of the stages (*bhūmi*). This has two parts: first, the inquiry; second, the answer and explanation. First, the verse:
Second, the prose section; first, the explanation of the meaning in four parts. Regarding "the heavy burden": "burden" means to carry, that is, to dwell upon it.

Next, citing the Sūtra, the "four dwelling grounds" included within craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) are: (1) the dwelling ground of craving for desire (*kāmarāga*), (2) the dwelling ground of craving for form (*rūparāga*), (3) the dwelling ground of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*)—these being, respectively, the innate afflictions of the three realms—and (4) the dwelling ground of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
This refers to the delusions of discrimination within the three realms, which correspond respectively to the ocean, the mountain, and the wooden man;
as these four types all rely upon ignorance, they are called "abiding grounds.
Second, regarding the section on the sequential detailed explanation of the scattered teachings: first, the summary reference; second, the citation of what was stated below.
The commentary on the second [section] begins with a rough description of the two characteristics. First, the indication; next, the explanation below.
Because the fundamental [characteristics] are extensive while the attendant [characteristics] are concise, it is urged that one should contemplate them.
Second, "not below" explains the establishment [of the meaning]. First, the extensive explanation of the fundamental [characteristics]. First, the general heading.

Regarding the second part, the detailed explanation of the four [topics] following the two fundamental [verses]: first, within the inquiry and response regarding their arising, there is first the question and then the answer, which consists of two layers.

Second, from the words "The two... onwards, the characteristics of the practice are investigated and explained; here, the first two characters indicate that which is deluded, and from the words "How... onwards, the third [section follows].
In Faxian’s account of his confusion, the initial heading provides the name, while the subsequent section on "actual knowledge" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) reveals its essential nature.

Actual knowledge of *tathatā* (suchness) is the gate of entry; by means of this wisdom and its object, one enters the fundamental dharma. That which is called the "single-mind dharma" (*ekacitta-dharma*) is the dharma that is entered;

it is the universal basis upon which both that wisdom and its object depend. Within this context, the character "dharma" (*fa*) designating the "single mind" takes a specific term as its general name, because—by means of... [the text continues].
Because the one mind is itself the dharma-realm.

Third, regarding the conclusion of the causes below, the phrase "in this regard" and so forth clarifies that the characteristics of ignorance’s delusive obscuration arise from being deluded regarding the true knowledge of all-encompassing awakening;
thus, one falsely recognizes agitated, turbulent, and frivolous conceptual discrimination due to being deluded regarding True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because of the principle of equality, one falsely imagines the defiled and illusory realm;

this arises from being deluded regarding the essence of the single-mind *dharmadhātu*, thereby erroneously grasping at the mind of objective perception that undergoes arising and ceasing. Because it cannot accord with this true knowledge and so forth, it is said to be "not as it is" (*ayathābhūta*).
Fourth, the detailed explanation of the single meaning of those three lower [categories]:

These three dharmas constantly maintain the nature of a single, middlemost reality, mutually supporting one another and never being separated, just as the three factors of a mirror [the mirror, the image, and the light] are neither identical nor different. The single mind is like the substance of the mirror;
true suchness (tathatā) is like the clarity of the mirror; and actual knowledge (vidyā) is like the function of reflecting. These three dharmas correspond to the three virtues (triguṇa).

Knowing is *prajñā* because it profoundly penetrates both principle and phenomena and excels in decisive discernment; True Suchness (*tathatā*) is liberation because, being of one suchness, all afflictions are utterly removed;
and the One Mind is the *dharmakāya* because it is the locus upon which immeasurable merits depend.
Second, from here below, there is a brief explanation of the derivative branches; that which possesses such thought refers to the defiled dharmas produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because the fundamental non-awakening is deluded regarding the three dharmas, these derivative false thoughts arise on this basis.

Second, from here below, the two gates are briefly distinguished. First, the division is indicated: herein it is shown that fundamental non-awakening arises in mutual dependence upon original awakening.
"To rely" means to depend; one depends on the true virtue (*tathatā-guṇa*) for the illusory phenomena (*māyā-dharma*) to be established.
This is because the true virtue possesses power and is the agent of establishment, whereas the illusory phenomena lack power and are the objects of establishment. "To cling" means to draw forth.
Citing illusory phenomena (mṛṣā-dharma) precisely reveals true awakening (tathatā-jñāna); thus, illusory phenomena possess power while true awakening lacks the power [to manifest itself].
This is because the manifesting subject and the manifested object have distinct characteristics.

Second, "Returning Merit" (*guīdé*) below explains the characteristics. First, within the section on the gate of the power and lack of power of the illusion established by returning merit, the meaning is first demonstrated.

The subsequent combined text states that ignorance has no substantial body; it manifests as illusory and false, lacking the power to arise of itself, and exists only by depending upon awakening (*bodhi*).

This reveals that while the reality of virtue possesses the power to manifest, the power to produce delusion belongs to the path, the regions, and the objects of confusion—these being metaphors for fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*).

The human mind that is deluded is like non-awakening (*a-bodha*). If one follows the previous explanation, it would not accord with the three dharmas; here, however, the formation of illusion is established solely [by this principle].

Because "original enlightenment" (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*) and "suchness-original enlightenment" (*tathatā-prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*) are shown to be identical names, [the former] is able to enter [the latter], for it is not separate from the dharma that is entered.
In the section on the gate of the power and lack of power of grasping at delusion to manifest the true, first the meaning is shown, and subsequently the textual structure is applied.
That the *dharmakāya* and *prajñā* cannot manifest themselves means that the True Dharma lacks the power of self-manifestation; it must await non-enlightenment (*abodhi*) before [it can manifest].
The "manifestation" indicates that false dharmas possess the power to reveal the True; this analogy and its application can be understood through the following.

Second, regarding the section "Having already explained," there is the gate of the ignorance-abiding-ground (avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi) as a subordinate member. This has two parts: first, the summary conclusion and the pointing-out of the heading; second, the explanation based on the gate.
Regarding the first, the gate of displaying the subtle subordinate members, there are two parts: first, stating the root; second, providing the commentary. First... [text continues].
Section Two: The General Outline and Brief Demonstration of the Exposition. Part One: Explaining this passage. Subsection One:

The Dharma’s failure to perceive its own three marks is termed "root and branch," because the root and branch, the lower and upper, and the upper and lower mutually exert power upon one another and are never separate;
thus, the branch relies on the power of the root, while the root receives the nourishment of the branch—this is the state of failing to perceive the *tathāgatagarbha* (awakened nature).
The final stage of the three marks acts as the productive cause; therefore, the final mark is established.
The initial stage of the three subtle marks serves as the sustaining cause for the branches of non-awakening; therefore, the fundamental substance remains abiding. To illustrate with a simile:
the father is like ignorance, because it is that which gives rise [to existence]; the son is like the three subtle marks, because they serve as the branches that provide sustenance.
Second, if—as in the previous case—it were to apply to other obstacles, there are two points:

first, the refutation that if the fundamental and the derivative mutually support one another to achieve abiding, then when Bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward gradually eliminate derivative marks, their fundamental non-awakening would lose its branches and its power would be nourished;
thus, they should sever it accordingly and become identical to the Subtle Awakening (the Buddha-stage). Second, the coarse [obstacles] are severed below this point.

Regarding the subtle existence that answers and severs the coarse characteristics: this refers to the fact that because the manifested forms transform, the characteristics of their arising appear extremely coarse.

As for the three subtle characteristics—namely, those that follow karma and coexist with it—although the coarse characteristics have been eliminated, the subtle characteristics still remain. Therefore, they are associated with non-awakening and are not separate from it;
how can you falsely interrogate me as if we were in the same stage of fruition?

2. From here below is the section on the "Gate of Simultaneous Establishment through Marking and Explanation. 2.1. First, the direct explanation of this text. 3.1. First, the explanation based on this [text].
3.1.1. First, the characteristics of karma. 2.1.1. First, indicating the meaning. 2.1.1.2. Second, correlating with the original text.

Because the characteristics of the karma of arising are extremely subtle, there is no distinction between subject and object or mind and realm; they cannot be divided. They are sovereign and subordinate, principal and attendant, yet uniquely refined and subtle.
The subtle, hidden movement and the meaning of its continuous flow are designated as "karma" (action). Because such karma arises based on non-awakening (*abodha*), it is called "moving flow.
It is precisely due to this non-awakening that the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*) is revealed to be fundamentally without movement.

Although the characteristics of karma are subtle, they are nonetheless the root of the birth-and-death of both the fragmented (*paricchinna*) and the transformative (*pariṇāma*) types. Therefore, it is said: "When there is movement, there is suffering; [this] karma..."

Regarding the first fruit [of realization], it is not separate from that initial cause of ignorance; therefore, it is said that "the fruit does not depart from its cause. Second, regarding the characteristics of transformation:

first, the meaning is demonstrated; next, it is correlated with the original text. Within the former, there are three parts: first, explaining in accordance with the preceding, how the aspect of karma transforms to become the "seeing" (darśana-bhāga); second, the section beginning with "If there were no...
which uses reductio ad absurdum to clarify that the meaning of this transformation of discernment (*vijñapti*) is identical to that of the seeing-part; third, [the conclusion].
Based on this, the names are concluded below.

Third, regarding the manifestation of signs (*nimitta*), there are two parts: first, showing the meaning, and second, correlating it with the original text. Within the former, there are three sections identical to those previously mentioned, with the addition of a concluding analogy.

Based on the aforementioned capacity for perception, the manifestation of various objective realms (*viṣaya*) constitutes the function of the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*); these objective realms, in turn, belong to... [the object of cognition].

The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the object-condition (*ālambana*), because it possesses both the capacity of subject and object within this context, is thus twofold. "As below" refers back to the previous determination (*viniścaya*);
that previous determination refers to the three subtle aspects within the *ālayavijñāna*, which are indicated by a common name.
"In this context" broadly distinguishes between the subject and the object.
Section Two: Distinguishing Other Meanings Below the Root Text. Part One: Question and Answer on Ignorance and Karmic Consciousness. Sub-part One: Raising the General Inquiry.
This refers to the initial karmic consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is indistinguishable from its object; yet, how does it differ from fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*)?
Next, "What is this... and so forth, specifically demonstrates the intent of the doubt: the intrinsic nature of ignorance is the faculty of non-illumination.
That which has not yet been differentiated is identical to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). Thus, how are these—the fundamental and the derivative—distinguished?
Second, the so-called "downward-turning" [section] consists of two parts: first, refuting false positions and establishing the correct;

second, explaining that the initial movement of the mind is not non-ignorance (*avidyā*). First, the provisional establishment: when the essence of the mind first moves, it is called "original movement" and designated as ignorance. Now...
The formal statement concludes: "If it were thus, [the following] would refute and dismantle this point. Now, the general negation states:
"This is not so," because it contradicts the treatise. Among the three characteristics explained therein, it says that the movement of the mind is itself termed *karma*;
from this, one knows that the primordial movement is not ignorance (*avidyā*).

Second, regarding the statement "if one says that the arising of a subsequent thought is not the *ālayavijñāna*": first, the concession and establishment [of the position] states that since this initial movement is not *avidyā*, it should logically belong to a stage of the *karmavijñāna*.

The uninterrupted continuity of its activity is called "permanent," just as the ocean constantly produces waves without interruption. Regarding the seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), the phrasing [of the original] is still inverted;

This means that because this sutra exists in three versions in total—among which the extensive version is found in the Dragon Palace, Khotan, and other locations; the intermediate version consists of thirty-six thousand stanzas and is currently transmitted in the Western Regions;

First, the headings and enumeration; second, the explanation and establishment of the first gate. Regarding the first, the "Gate of Citing Two to Manifest Three and Fully Enumerate":
although the initial sūtra only cites the two consciousnesses of manifest phenomena, it also implicitly reveals them by extension.

Since the latter manifesting consciousnesses belong to the fruit and the karmic-activating [manas] serves as their cause, once the subsequent fruit is clarified, the prior cause must necessarily exist. Because the treatise elucidates them in mutual relation, there is no deficiency. Second, regarding the subsequent section, it "summarizes" (*shuai*) what is above and "reaches down" (*da*) to what is below; this constitutes the complete enumeration of the gates.

because those *dharmacakras* establish that the *manovijñāna* and the *manas* each have their own distinct seeds, it is said that the *manovijñāna* arises only by depending upon the *manas*.

because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which takes the aforementioned manifest consciousness as its basis, could be confused with the manas, an opponent is established to exhaustively clarify the profound principle, namely:

Regarding these, two types of faults are derived from the preceding formal inference (*pramāṇa*):

What has been received [as a premise] is not truly capable of establishing [the conclusion]. The intention of the two parties' admissions is to reveal the fault of "concordance" (*sādharmya*).

Since the sacred teachings have already admitted that the manifest consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manas are of the same seed, the original formulation of the formal argument (*prayoga*) intended to contradict the opponent now finds no point of contention;
thus, its effort is wasted and it is not a valid establishment. Alternatively, the negation and the admission may be taken as having a single meaning, merely expressing the operation of concordance.
