Since each [of these] is fully endowed with the two meanings of cause and condition, this inquiry is raised; the subsequent answer states:

"If viewed in relation to the three consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), awakening (*bodhi*) is the direct cause (*upādāna-hetu*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) is the remote condition (*pratyaya*); therefore, the consciousness produced thereby has clarity as its predominance and darkness as its inferiority.

If viewed in relation to the three characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), ignorance is the direct cause and awakening is the remote condition; therefore, the characteristics produced thereby have darkness as their abundance and clarity as their scarcity. Thus, the fruit produced therein [is characterized by this predominance and inferiority].
Because their natures and obscurations differ, they are able to produce dharmas, and thus their causes and conditions vary.
Fourth, as for why the lower [realms] share the same coarse and subtle characteristics, there are two parts: first, the formal question and answer; second, the initial inquiry and explanation.

Regarding the seventh, within the previous discussion of arising and ceasing, it was stated that the six coarse characteristics all belong to the stage of the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) and are not the dharmas of the other consciousnesses; that *manas* consciousness is precisely...

Regarding why this subtle state of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is separately established as being subsumed under the *manas*—both in terms of its cognitive function and its continuity—it is because one establishes that the *manas* and the mental consciousness are of a single essence and not distinct.
Thus, while these two aspects previously belonged to the mental consciousness, they are now attributed to the *manas*. From this, it is known that they certainly do not constitute separate entities.
Sixth, the question and answer regarding "If this were so": If these two have no distinct substance, then they should fully encompass all six aspects to constitute the mind (*manas*).
Why, then, are the latter four coarse divisions omitted and not called *manas*, while only the aspect of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the aspect of continuity (*saṃtati*) are subsumed?
However, in terms of reality, all six aspects are indeed the mind; although only two are mentioned, the underlying principle is already exhausted therein.
Therefore, the scripture is cited stating that "there is nothing it does not perform" in order to demonstrate that it fully encompasses all things without exception.

Furthermore, if the *manas* consciousness already subsumes both the coarse and subtle levels, why does the treatise separately posit the transformation of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) as something external?

This is done to reveal the distinction between the gateways of the supporting consciousness and the supported consciousness; for both the coarse and subtle consciousnesses take fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) as their support.
Therefore, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is separately presented as the supporting basis (*āśraya*) for the manas;
this can also be understood in accordance with the *Dharmacakra-sūtra*, which distinguishes between different types [of seeds]. Thus it is established.
Second, from "raising this" onwards, he provides examples for other dharmas: suppose someone were to ask, "Since the manas already subsumes the three kinds of subtle characteristics, why..."

Therefore, the *ālayavijñāna* is established separately as the three subtle phases; it is pointed out by way of analogy as the "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) to clarify the meaning of the support (*āśraya*) and that which is supported (*āśrita*), and thus it is established separately.

This case should be understood in the same way. Since the three subtle phases universally depend upon the mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhicitta*), the preceding [phase] can give rise to the subsequent, and the latter functions as the support for the former.
Because the coarse mental consciousness depends upon the present mirror-like [wisdom], the three phases, although subsumed within the *manas*, [are so designated].

Because it reveals the meaning based on the [underlying] principle and because it establishes [the ālayavijñāna] as distinct, this consciousness is cited to resolve and penetrate the specific meaning of establishing the ālayavijñāna.

Second, "Furthermore" and below, there are two parts: first, harmonizing with the nature; second, subverting [dualistic views]. First, showing the meaning; second, first subverting the three names. That is to say, the various teachings...

Regarding what was previously stated—that the eighth is called *citta*, the seventh is called *manas*, and the first six are called *vijñānas*—this is not the case here, because there is no fixed restriction;

thus, they all interpenetrate one another. The text contains several sections: first, the lack of fixedness regarding their own names, meaning that *ālaya* is not restricted to being *ālaya* alone, and so forth, discussing their mutual interpenetration in isolation;
next, the mutual interpenetration between self and other, which has two parts, the first of which concerns the mutual [interpenetration] of the first two consciousnesses.
"Interpenetration" (*tong*) refers to the mutual inclusion of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), the manas, and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Since it is already fully established that the manas and the mental consciousness are of the same substance and without distinction, the treatise does not mention the interpenetration of the latter three consciousnesses.

This means that all three types of consciousness are designated as the "storehouse consciousness," and so forth. Question: Regarding the relationship between the storehouse consciousness and the manas, and the manas and the mental consciousness...
The treatises never state anywhere that the *ālayavijñāna* and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) mutually encompass one another;
how then could the three subtle states be called the *ālaya-vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna*? The answer is: because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not fixed, they may mutually encompass one another;
it is not permissible to restrict the *ālaya* and the mental consciousness to their own respective positions such that they do not interpenetrate. The treatise does not say so.

Since these cases should be understood as examples, the following passage further clears away the general designation by stating, "Furthermore, all are not," meaning that none are the *ālayavijñāna* and none are the *manas*,
and so forth. Second, regarding the section "In this way" and below,
which returns to the two truths (*satya*), the first part reveals the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), stating that "the absence of fixedness is precisely the suffering of shifting."

The characteristic of impermanence manifests the flow of transition; because these flowing characteristics are not real, there is no real characteristic of a self, as all are illusory transformations.

Thus, the characteristic of defiled delusion is empty. These various consciousnesses, through such characteristics, are mutually dependent and lack fixedness, being subsumed under conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
By means of illusion, one reveals ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); that is, through the emptiness of illusion, one brings forth true emptiness. This is liberation through emptiness.
Because their nature is empty, they are originally quiescent, without anything to be grasped;
the liberation of signlessness is itself quiescent, and even the mark of constant quiescence does not exist. Thus, there is nothing to be sought.
Through the gate of the three emptinesses, the self-nature of all consciousnesses is revealed as entirely true, and all are subsumed within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Secondly, because the "gold of the past" is cited as evidence that dependent origination lacks intrinsic nature, it is called "non-arising. Because its essence is entirely true, it is called "quiescent extinction.
Thus, by aggregating these seven, five, eight, six, and the nine aspects such as karma and transformation, they are found to lack substantiality; therefore, it is said to be "empty and non-existent.

There being neither existence nor non-existence, and neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, one repeatedly negates and sweeps away these layers until there is nothing to which one may cling. Thus it is.
Because all phenomena transcend the reach of mind and speech, the Buddha first praised them as "inconceivable.
Then, by negating all views, he declared that all things are unborn, signless, and nameless. All phenomenal characteristics are merely objects of perception;

all sentient beings are the very bodies upon which these perceptions depend. Since even these characteristics and bodies are empty and non-existent, how could there be any perceiving subject that depends upon them? How could such a thing possibly exist?

Regarding "Is there [existence]?"—this means that if one holds views, one falls into error and delusion. The scriptural text clearly demonstrates that while all phenomena are truly quiescent, within the process of their negation, conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is fully contained.

Second, regarding the section on the distinctions in the continuous activity of karma following the previous explanation, this part first concludes the preceding section and indicates what follows; here, it merely provides a brief summary.

The summary of the discourse on the aspects of the dependent *manas* according to the text, the sequential exposition of the three gates concerning the continuity of karmic activity, and the scattered explanation of the phenomena of the revolving of "mind-only" and the transforming characteristics of the *pravṛtti-vijñānas* shall now be clarified in due order; students should understand them all.

Second, the commentary on the root text, which has two parts: first, the recitation of the root treatise; second, the explanation of the text. Third, the initial section, which marks the divisions, has two parts.
First, the explanation of the characteristics [of the "meaning of not losing what was previously gathered"]. This reveals the function of continuous abiding and maintenance.
That which is able to produce and moisten—namely craving, grasping, and so forth—is like water that repeatedly irrigates the past ignorance.
The seed of karma causes its fruit to arise; following the perfuming and activation by this karmic seed, the function of grasping (*upādāna*) constantly arises in every moment.
Because it takes up that future fruit and brings it to maturity, it now receives the irrigation and sustenance of the water of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
This transforms the prior function of grasping into the function of yielding fruit, providing the power for that fruit to arise. Therefore, the treatise says: "And..."

Because it is able to bring about the power and function of accomplishing results, the meaning of the latter two [of the three characteristics] is the sense of the accomplishment of the fruition of results.
This continuous consciousness is further able to give rise to afflictions such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), which moisten the seeds of those results and cause them to manifest.

That is to say, the duration of time, the quality of the retribution received—whether good or bad—and the nature of the karmic fruit are all in correspondence; therefore, the treatise states that there is no discrepancy, as previously explained.
This clarifies that moistening karma results in moistened fruits because, within the constituent links (*aṅga*) moistened by it, both karma and its fruit are present.

Furthermore, while the seeds of karma and its fruit all pertain to the three time periods, what is being discussed here concerns how past karma sustains the fruit so as to manifest it in the present and future, thereby mutually revealing them.

Regarding the third point, the subsequent meaning refers to the sense of pervasive objectification (*sarvatraga-ālambana*) through false conceptualization; this means that this continuity (*saṃtati*) takes such things as its objective support (*ālambana*). However...
Not only does it maintain the maturation of past karma and its resultant retribution, but it is also capable of initiating ever-new faults.

Regarding objects of the past and present, it discriminates between the disagreeable and agreeable, giving rise to greed, hatred, and so forth; regarding objects of the future, it engages in false conceptualization, thereby increasing these faults.
Consequently, one wanders through birth and death in an endless cycle. Question: What is the essential nature of this evolving consciousness? Answer: It is the manas.

Regarding the question of why it is stated that those [afflictions] subsumed under the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) alone give rise to delusion and moisten karma: indeed, all eleven [afflictions] of the manas possess this function;

however, because they reside in the continuity following the manas and precede the initial stage of the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), their functional power is particularly strengthened.
Thus, the third section concludes the argument.

Second, the section on the teaching of the "Mind-Only Transformation of All Dharmas" has already been explained. This section consists of two parts: first, concluding the preceding and indicating what follows;

second, reciting the root text and providing an explanation. Regarding the second part, there are three sub-sections: first, reciting the root treatise; second, composing the explanatory text; third, the initial explanation of the general heading. The general heading states:

"Desire, form, and formlessness—collectively termed 'all such dharmas'—are entirely false and deceptive. This reveals that the previously mentioned *manas* (ego-consciousness) lacks any substantial reality.
The essential nature [of these objects] manifests solely through the fundamental mind turning and appearing under the influence of ignorance;
if one were separated from the fundamental mind, nothing would appear, as there are no other objects of the six sense-fields.

Second, the section on "the reason for" provides a definitive analysis and detailed explanation of two points: first, explaining the meaning of "mind-only," and second, clarifying the characteristics of the turning [of consciousness]. The former...

This means that if the mind exists, there are phenomena with temporal distinctions; if the mind does not exist, there are no phenomena with temporal distinctions. This explains and establishes the meaning of "Mind-Only" herein by showing that the arising of subsequent mental states causes the arising of phenomena, and the cessation of the mind causes the cessation of phenomena. It is not only that objects are unattainable apart from the mind; rather, if those mental phenomena (*cittadharma*) are likewise unattainable, then the mind itself would also not exist as a triad [of subject, object, and cognition].
To this, the text below raises an objection and provides an explanation: "Even non-existence is called 'mind'. This means:

if mental phenomena cannot be apprehended, how can the principle of "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*) be established? Therefore, the text explains: "This too is mind. Thus, it is not only when something is apprehended that one speaks of "Mind-Only."
Since this is the ultimate meaning of True Mind-Only (*cittamātra*), even the characteristics of the phenomena of consciousness (*vijñapti-dharma-lakṣaṇa*) must be explained as follows:

"When wisdom perceives no object whatsoever at all, one then abides in Consciousness-Only, free from the marks of subject and object. How much more so for the School of Dharmatā—how could there be any attainment?
Second, the passage beginning with "By what... cites scriptural authority to establish this, similar to the translation by Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of the Song Dynasty.

The first half-verse of the translated scripture states: "Observing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they are free from objective referents (*ālambana*); therefore, it is said that there is no mind.

Because the mind does not see the mind, no characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) can be apprehended. As for "the measure of the mind" (*citta-mātra*), this refers precisely to this state of no-mind, because it is the extent or dimension of the mind.

Second, next, the following clarifies the characteristics of the turning back (*parāvṛtti*). This has two parts: first, the turning back that results in difference; second, [the section on] how it is formed as empty and illusory through the turning back of the mind.
Within this, there are two sentences: the first is from the treatise (*śāstra*) and the second is from the sutra (*sūtra*).

Because the sutra and the treatise are in accord, it says "Great Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā*); the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* explains: "What is Great Emptiness? The eastern direction is empty of the characteristic of the eastern direction; it is not permanent."
Because it is neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why? Because its nature is inherently so. Regarding the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir:

the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir are mutually empty because they are neither permanent nor subject to cessation. Why? Because their nature is inherently so.

This is called "Great Emptiness" (mahāśūnyatā). As Nāgārjuna explains the meaning: "Neither permanent nor subject to cessation" means that if a person does not practice this emptiness, they will inevitably fall into the two [extremes].

The extremes are either permanence or cessation. Why is this so? If all phenomena were substantially existent, they would lack the principle of cessation and would fall into the extreme of permanence.
It is like a person who leaves one house and enters another; although the eyes do not see them [in the interim], it is not said that they are non-existent. Phenomena are likewise:
they pass from the future world into the present world, and from the present world into the past world. If it were as [you suggest]...
This [nature] is thus eternally abiding and indestructible; now, by stating that it is not eternal, one avoids that fault.

Furthermore, because conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*) is afflicted by existence, one uses emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to destroy the mind of existence. Yet, those who value emptiness and become attached to it fall into the view of annihilationism.

Now, by stating that it is not annihilated, one avoids this error. Because one is free from these two extremes—neither eternal nor annihilated—this is the esoteric teaching of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Because all phenomena enter into True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are all said to be empty. This treatise explains that the three realms are false and illusory, yet not separate from the true mind;
therefore, it is said to be signless (*animitta*). Accordingly, the treatise states: "By means of the phrase 'the mind cannot be apprehended,' the meaning of Great Emptiness is established.
It then cites a scriptural passage to demonstrate the point of the treatise: "The mind does not see the mind. Since this mental dharma follows conditions, [it is thus empty].
Since that which appears lacks any visible characteristic and even its manifestation is false, it is swept away into emptiness and illusion, wherein nothing possesses true reality;
therefore, it is said that by means of the phrase "the measure of mindlessness," the meaning of the various distinctions of illusion is established.

Second, furthermore, the following section reveals the principle of the Dharma through the turning of the mind. First, regarding the meaning of the "Great Emptiness" whereby delusion is established based upon the True [Suchness]:
this implicitly reveals that the essence of True Suchness transcends all marks, being neither permanent nor subject to extinction;

it is precisely this awakened mind (mūla-jñāna) as clarified here that enables all phenomena to be established—meaning that all phenomena, such as the false and deceptive dharmas of the triple world, depend upon the essence and function of emptiness to exist.
The manifestation is also like molding clay into a vessel: when it is empty, it possesses the utility of a vessel.

This explains the main treatise’s statement that "the mind arises and phenomena arise" because all phenomena are generated from the Great Emptiness and the True Mind. Next, by relying on the delusory to manifest the true, one realizes that illusions are not the reality of True Emptiness;
only then does the truth become manifest, just as when the snake and the ghost have vanished, the rope and the stump appear. This explains the main treatise.
When the mind ceases, phenomena cease; because the true mind is immovable, all illusions are extinguished, and the principle of the single flavor of emptiness (*ekarasā-śūnyatā*) finally manifests.

Second, from "Furthermore" (*punar-aparam*) onwards, "mutual dependence is quiescence" (*sāpekṣa-praśama*); the character *xiang* (相) is pronounced level-tone (*ping sheng*). "Contemplation" (*guan*) refers to contemplative practice (*bhāvanā*), which is what was explained above.
True mind and delusive objects are established through mutual dependence; because they depend upon one another, meanings such as "one" and "two" are entirely indeterminate and cannot be established.
Establishment and non-establishment are likewise mutually dependent.

Since there is no establishment that serves as the object of dependence, how could there be non-establishment that serves as the subject of dependence? The characteristics of mutual observation are primordially quiescent.
Third, as in the section below, the conclusion exhorts one to contemplate.

Second, from "already explained" onwards, is the section on the gate of the evolving characteristics of the *vastu-vijñāna* (object-consciousness). This has two parts: first, the conclusion of the preceding and the presentation of what follows;

second, the citation of the root text followed by its commentary. Regarding the first, there are two: first, the citation of the root treatise; second, the composition of the explanatory text. Regarding the second, there are two: first, the division of the categories; second, following [the previous] with the section beginning "discriminating."

Explanation of the Four [Sections]: First, the Section on Distinguishing the Provisional Entities of the *Sabhāgatā* (Homogeneity). Regarding these three types of provisional entities, the first comprises the entire group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*).

Because they have not yet been able to generate the factors of practice (*caryā-dharma*), they are said to be "rootless. Because they lack the "Dharma-eye" of the Mahāyāna wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), they are said to be "blind.
The second comprises the entire group of those who are not fixed (*aniyata-rāśi*). Although they cultivate the ten mental states (*daśa-citta*), they still advance and retreat.
It is indeterminate, like a hair on a path blown by the wind; therefore it is called "Hair-tip" (*vālāgra*).

Because its position has not yet been established due to this instability, it is termed "Difficult-to-Subdue" (*durjayā*). Furthermore, "tip" (*aṅga*) means contention; it shares the same meaning as "struggle.

Having first generated the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), one startles and agitates the hosts of Māra; because the struggle with Māra is extremely difficult to advance through, the third stage then encompasses the "Right" (*samyak*).

A small portion of meditative concentration arises from the three stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) through mastery over the emptiness of persons; it is of the same nature as the qualities of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), being adamantine, firm, indestructible, and free from decline or change.

Second is the gate of the transformational aspect of the arising of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*); third, although ordinary people initially lack the faculties [of the noble ones], these various defilements—both coarse and subtle—[are thus addressed].
All [beings] possess [this], but it is spoken of only in relation to the *vastu-vijñāna* (object-consciousness) because it occurs at the very end.

If we consider the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are like fine hairs, even though Bodhisattvas at this stage have realized that karmic results are certainly unwholesome, they still do not give rise to non-conceptualizing wisdom regarding the emptiness of birth;
because the fundamental mastery [of that wisdom] has not yet manifested, they still conceive of a self in relation to objects and the parts of the body.
Regarding the three types of "mine" (*mama-ātmīya*), if we consider the stage of ordinary beings below the diamond-like [samādhi],

although these bodhisattvas have already cultivated the skillful means of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the fundamental true wisdom (*mūla-tattva-jñāna*), the latter has not yet manifested before them. Consequently, they give rise to mental clinging and discursive thoughts regarding phenomena,
which obstructs the principle of equality.
Section Three: The Gate of Establishing the Distinctions of Names. Part One: Indicating the Names. Part Two: Explaining the Meaning of the Names. Section One: The Subtle Names Based on the Support.
This name is established based on the subtle faculties of the support, namely the mind (*manas*);

because it is the consciousness of the mind, it is called "mind-consciousness" (*manovijñāna*). Section Two: The Grossly Manifest Names Based on the Support. This [name] is established based on the support... [text continues].

The coarse and manifest sense organs (rūpīndriya) are used to designate its name, because it is the consciousness depending on the eye that discerns form, and so on, up to the consciousness depending on the body that discerns tangibles.
Originally there is only a single consciousness; however, when its functions are divided, it depends separately upon each organ and apprehends each object separately.

This "separation" refers to the fact that the substance of consciousness maintains distinct functions; thus, the separated consciousnesses are distinguished by their respective organs and objects. (3)
The subsequent section is titled "Conforming to Objects. This name is established merely in accordance with the objects themselves;

it is still coarse and active, as one has not yet attained true realization, but rather gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding phenomenal appearances. Fourth, this reveals the basis for the establishment [of these views]:
coarse views are discriminative (*vikalpita*), while cultivation consists of the innate (*sahaja*). These innate afflictions have been false and delusive since beginningless time.
Because they arise by the power of the internal cause of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they are always present with the body;

since they operate spontaneously without depending on false teachings or false discrimination, they are called "innate" (*sahaja*) conceptual afflictions. As for the internal cause, it must necessarily be present.

Furthermore, because they arise by the power of external conditions in the present, they are not present with the body and only arise after depending upon false teachings and false discrimination; therefore, they are called [acquired].
Due to these two delusions, the *ālayavijñāna* (fundamental consciousness) is perfumed, whereby it undergoes transformation and gives rise to the *vikalpavijñāna* (discriminative consciousness);
that is, the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) assist the power of the mind-king (*cittarāja*), causing it to become more intense and flourishing.
Second, the characteristics of the excellence of causes and conditions from above and below. This has two parts: first, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one;

second, reciting the root text and providing an explanation. Regarding the second part, there are three sections: first, reciting the root treatise; second, composing the explanatory text; third, dividing the categories.

First, following the explanation of the first category: fifth, the section that cites persons to demonstrate excellence. This has three parts: first, stating the heading and posing the inquiry; second, explaining the characteristics, starting with "The first... and so forth; third, [the sub-section].

Regarding the simultaneous cessation of both the partial and the complete: because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles have not yet cultivated or realized either the causal portion or the resultant portion, they are said to be "simultaneously ceased.
Because the ignorance of ordinary beings is profound and the wisdom of those of the two vehicles is inferior, they are unable to perceive or awaken to the consciousness arising from ignorance.
As for the "partial" and the "complete": the fifty stages of the causal position of humans are called "partial" because the fruit has not yet been realized; thus it is so described.

It is called "Non-Fullness" (*aparinispanna*). From the initial stage of right faith, which is the level of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one arouses the mind and engages in observation, which is the level of the three worthies (*tri-satpuruṣa*).
If one realizes the Dharma-body and attains partial knowledge, this refers to the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) up to the ultimate stage of the Bodhisattva, which comprises the remaining stages.
Although the causal factors are cultivated in these aforementioned levels, the fruition is not yet fully attained because residual obstructions still remain. Therefore, regarding...

The consciousness arising from ignorance cannot know the exhaustion [of suffering]; because those who have fulfilled existence (bhava-pūrṇa) realize the ultimate fruit, they are called "fulfillers of existence" (bhava-pūrṇa).

In contrast to those previously mentioned who possess portions, these are called "portionless" (apūrṇaka). Only the Buddha alone, through the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) manifesting universally, is able to exhaustively comprehend this;
thus, "three" concludes the enumeration of names.
Second, the section already explained, which displays the profound conditions to resolve doubts, has two parts. First, the section summarizing the headings and dividing the gates;

[in the Yan edition, "profound conditions" (shen yuan) was erroneously transcribed as "defilement" (ran)]. Second, the section explaining the characteristics according to the gates. This has two parts. First, the correct exposition of the two gates. First, the gate of the permanent and the impermanent:
because the self-characteristic of original enlightenment (*prakṛti*) does not change, it is called "permanent"; it is not that there is no non-existence.
Because it is both eternal and subject to transformation, it is described by the two terms "eternal" and "non-eternal. Regarding the gate of non-eternity within eternity:
this originally awakened mind is eternally constant yet non-eternally changing; therefore, it is called "non-eternal. Because it is neither permanently abiding nor immutable, it is called "eternal.
The aforementioned eternity and non-eternity refer to that which is undefiled yet defiled, which is difficult to comprehend. This [is] non-...
It is constantly stained yet unstained, which is difficult to comprehend; therefore, it is called "manifesting the profound condition" (1).
Thus, the following summarizes the excellence: because the characteristics of these causal conditions are so excellent, this meaning is concluded as being knowable only by a Buddha (2).
From here on, the preceding meaning is explained again; this consists of the sense of the passage rather than being restricted to the literal phrasing.
The sequence proceeds from the latter to the former as follows: because the nature of the mind is eternally free from thought, it is called "unchanging";
this phrase explains the preceding term "eternal-constant. Because one does not penetrate the single Dharma-realm, thoughts arise suddenly in a manner dissociated from the mind;
this is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*), and this phrase explains the preceding term "constant-unconstant."

Third, the section on the gates of "indicating hindrances through downward elevation" and "showing remedies through appropriate application," which has already been explained. Part Two: First, the summary that points out and divides the gates;
second, the explanation of the characteristics according to the gates, starting from "following the turning. Regarding the first, the positions of the fundamental and subsequent remedies:

within the gate of the stages of the positions of following and applying remedies, taking the arousal of the mind as the beginning, this refers to the fulfillment of faith. Since the ten stages of faith only suppress [the afflictions], they are not included here at the outset. First.

The nature of the defilement associated with attachment (*saṃprayoga-kleśa*) corresponds to these two types of distinct characteristics; its attendants likewise extend to both karma and its retribution.

Otherwise, karma and its retribution would not be objects to be abandoned. The stage associated with faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*) refers precisely to the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śukla*) and the ten kinds of faithful mind already accomplished.

Thus, in the *Dìlùn* (Treatise on the Stages), those from the tenth stage of understanding (*daśa-vyākhyāna*) onward are collectively termed "Bodhisattvas of Faithful Practice" (*śraddhā-carita*). This is as stated in the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-śāstra*.
The same applies here: the second, the defilement associated with non-interruption (*anuccheda-samprayukta-kleśa*), is the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*);

the third, the defilement associated with discriminative cognition (*vikalpa-jñāna-samprayukta-kleśa*), which the three stages of worthiness (*tri-vidha-pudgala*) suppress and the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) can eliminate, is the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṣa*). From the second stage up to the tenth stage, one attains ultimate detachment;

yet for a Bodhisattva on the seventh stage, there still remains the application of effort (*prayoga-prayukti-kriyā*) within signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*), because [of the absence of]... [the signless].

When observing characteristics (*nimitta*), there is still the alternation of entering and emerging; because the eighth stage and beyond consist purely of the state of signlessness (*animitta*), this [seventh stage] is called "skillful means" (*upāya*).
Furthermore, signlessness is the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), while skillful means is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*);

because within this stage one can, by means of the wisdom of skillful means that is itself empty, initiate the sublime practices within existence (*bhava*). Fourth, the defilement of non-conformity with the manifestation of form; these are the latter three [defilements].

The seeds are precisely the three subtle states; because Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage attain mastery over the transformation of physical marks and lands according to their minds, they manifest these signs through such mastery so that they cannot act as obstructions.

Fifth, the mind of seeing that is dissociated from outflows [is present] in Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage who occupy the rank of Dharma Masters; they skillfully know the dense forest of sentient beings' mental activities, and their wisdom-vision is unimpeded.
Because of obstruction, the mind lacks mastery and is unable to abandon the characteristic of transformation.

The six fundamental karmas, the non-associated defilements, and so forth, are abandoned in the Bodhisattva’s diamond-like mind; they are entirely abandoned in the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*) because one has realized the nature of the mind and reached the state of non-conceptualization.
Second is the section on the stages of the fundamental antidote: the great power of ignorance has both coarse and subtle aspects in its essence and function;
its subtle essence is that which is fully perfected [only by the Buddha], while its coarse and manifest function is gradually eliminated during the causal stage.

Through the comparative contemplation of the Three Sages, one observes the root of all defiled ignorance, subdues its force, and causes it to become increasingly attenuated; this is called "learning to sever."
Having entered the stages (*bhūmi*), one gradually distances oneself from [ignorance] part by part until, upon reaching the fruit of *samyaksaṃbodhi*, it is entirely and suddenly exhausted.

Question: Ignorance (*avidyā*) is extremely subtle; how can it be suppressed? Answer: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 97, states that there is not only one way to destroy ignorance.

There is "destruction" in the sense of obstructing it so that it does not arise; there is also "destruction" in the sense of attaining the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. Furthermore, regarding this ignorance...

The categories [of ignorance] are very numerous: there are those to be eliminated by Bodhisattvas, those to be eliminated by Buddhas, those to be eliminated by lesser Bodhisattvas, and those to be eliminated by great Bodhisattvas.
From this, one should know that powerful ignorance pervades both the coarse and the subtle, as well as the two stages of suppression and abandonment.

Regarding the distinction between the primary and secondary afflictions (*mūla* and *anubandha*) and their respective antidotes, first, this section directly clarifies the stage of *pramuditā* (the Joyous).

Thus, the distinctions in meaning regarding the derived [wisdom] (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) and the fundamental [wisdom] (*mūla-jñāna*) are explained as follows: Derived wisdom correctly takes conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛti-viṣaya*) as its object, while fundamental ignorance is fundamentally deluded regarding these phenomena;

because their respective antidotes and objects are contradictory, derived wisdom eliminates that [ignorance]. Fundamental wisdom correctly takes ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as its object, while the defiled phenomena associated with appearances are fundamentally deluded regarding this truth;
because their respective modes of activity (*ākāra*) are contradictory, correct wisdom eliminates both. As stated below, it refers to this.

For example, as it is with the first stage (*bhūmi*), so it is with all subsequent stages; although within these various stages there are distinctions between the meaning of the union of the ultimate and conventional truths and that of obstacles and wisdom, they do not overlap or confuse one another.

Fourth, having already explained the preceding section, this is the section on the distinction between what is appropriate and inappropriate. It has two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the explanation beginning with "How... and so forth.

Regarding the two aspects of "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*), first is the meaning of correspondence itself. Second, regarding the meaning of the distinct natures [of the factors involved]: because their essential natures are different, they correspond.

The category of the mind (*cittapakṣa*) corresponds to the aspect of Original Enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). When it refers to the mental king (*citta-rāja*), its meaning belongs to the aspect of Original Enlightenment. When it refers to mental states (*caitta-dharma*), its meaning belongs to the aspect of Non-enlightenment (*an-awakening*).

Thus, these two types each have a distinct essence. The category of the mind serves as the primary factor because it is capable of leading and guiding; the mental states serve as its companions because they are capable of assisting and supporting it.

Therefore, because they mutually provide support for one another, they are said to be "associated" (*saṃprayukta*). Regarding the two mental factors of mindfulness (*smṛti*), their characteristics are identical;

thus, they are associated. First, the formal question and answer: Suppose there is a doubt as to why it is said that mindfulness forms the meaning of association when the defiled mind and the pure mind differ in their distinctions.
The commentary explains: It is because the aspect of the cognitive mode (*ākāra*) and the aspect of the object (*ālambana*)—these two pairs—are identical. Thus, they are called associated.
Question: It is said that the "corresponding" [nature] is achieved only when the mind-faculty (citta) and mental factors (caitasika) are a synthesis of the true and the false.

Why, then, is it now stated that the mind-faculty is exclusively true and the mental factors are exclusively false, yet they are called "corresponding"? Answer: In reality, both the sovereign (the mind) and its objects (the mental factors) possess aspects of both the true and the false.

However, this statement is made based on their primary and dominant characteristics. It is just as the characteristics of consciousness are established as distinct based on their predominant features. What are these two?

The third section, the detailed explanation of the sub-section on "Turning," has two parts: first, the explanation of the two types of "sameness" (sādharmya). First, regarding the sameness of wisdom (*jñāna-sādharmya*):

it refers to the non-separation of mental attention and its harmonious integration. This means that the sovereign mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its associated mental factors (*caitta*), whether wholesome or unwholesome, are necessarily concordant.

Because the aspects (*ākāra*) of these two dharmas are similar, they are called "same. Next, regarding the sameness of the object (*ālambana-sādharmya*): it refers to the commonality of the focal object.

Regarding the "commonality determined by the sovereign object" (*viṣaya-rāja-niyata-sādharmya*): this means that when the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) takes form and so forth as its object, the mental factors (*caitta*) necessarily take those same form and so forth as their objects;
thus, the two primary bases are identical. Regarding the citation of scripture from the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* to prove the three types of commonality:

it refers to the fact that among the three types of associated defiled dharmas (*saṃprayukta-kleśa-dharma*), both the "characteristic of cognition" (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the "characteristic of the object" (*ālambana-lakṣaṇa*) are identical. Regarding the establishment of commonality through difference: this refers to the identity of essence (*svabhāva*) between the sovereign [mind] and its [mental] factors.

If their natures were each distinct, they could only achieve the realization that the conditions (*ālambana*) are identical; if their substance (*svabhāva*) were not different, with respect to what would one speak of identity?

If they were both identical and non-identical, this would conversely clarify the preceding meaning: namely, if the mental states and phenomena were identical, one could not say that the realization of the identity of conditions constitutes the meaning of association (*samprayoga*).
Furthermore, this single phrase doubly concludes the preceding meaning: that is, if the realization of the identity of conditions [is established].

Because their essential natures are different, they are called "associated" (*saṃprayukta*). Alternatively, this phrase may be explained separately as referring to three kinds of non-associated defilements:

first, the mind's lack of awakening is termed "non-identity" (*asamatā*); second, because the aspect of the knower and the aspect of the object do not possess a similar nature, it is termed "non-identity";
and third, since the mind and its mentation are one and there is no distinction between the knower and the object, how could they be said to be identical? If one relies on this...

Regarding the statement above that there are three types, this reveals both the "associated" (*samprayukta*) and the "non-associated" (*viprayukta*); specifically, two [of these] correspond to the associated, while one corresponds to the non-associated.

If this is so, the following section below reconciles apparent contradictions in the texts. If it is said that these three know the object (*ālambana*) and have the same aspect (*ākāra*), they are termed "associated";

why then does that sutra speak of them as "functioning in opposition"? That is because it intends to reveal how these three types of coarse defilements (*dausthulya-kleśa*) oppose the aforementioned functioning.
The sublime state of virtue is not characterized by the contradiction between the two aspects of the object of knowledge and its conditions; rather, it signifies their mutual non-correspondence.

Since this is merely the reverse of what preceded, it is termed "contradiction. As this has been explained only briefly and without further distinction, I urge you to examine it with careful scrutiny.

Fifth, the section on establishing the distinct functions of the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) has already been explained. This section consists of two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the explanation of their characteristics.

Regarding the second part, there are three sections, the first of which is the specific clarification of the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Within this, there are six types of defiled mind called the hindrance of afflictions;

the wondrous wisdom that illuminates quiescence and accords with reality is called fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Coarse and subtle defiled mental states are characterized by a predominance of distraction and movement.

Because it can truly obstruct that state of tranquility, it is called an "obstruction. Second, because that wisdom and inferior wisdom obstruct the fundamental and derivative ignorance, they are called "obstructions to knowledge" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

The wisdom that penetrates conventional truth according to its measure (*yathāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*) is able to contemplate the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the application of the faculties, and the constant quiescence of all phenomena;
therefore, it is called the "wisdom of spontaneous activity" (*anābhoga-karma-jñāna*). All [of these] are non-existent.
Because it clarifies the nature of the obscure and dark, and because it is precisely able to obstruct that nature of clarity and intelligence, it is called an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*).

Now, this [text] merely distinguishes two types of obstructions based on their fundamental and derivative roots: the defiled mind that arises is categorized entirely under the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), without distinguishing between its coarse and subtle aspects;
and the ignorance that gives rise to it is categorized entirely as the obstruction to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), without distinguishing between its branches and roots.

1. Regarding the different categories of what is subsumed: various teachings name [the obstacles] based on the two types of grasping—grasping at persons and grasping at phenomena—which give rise to the two hindrances.

This point generally indicates the causes and conditions; it demonstrates that the defiled mind, which is the dependent, and ignorance, which is its basis, are each designated by the term "obstruction" in relation to their respective objects of obstruction.
2. Regarding the section below on the two hindrances, which provides a detailed analysis and encourages contemplation: there may be those who harbor doubts regarding "obstructions."
Regarding the question of what distinguishes these two names, the present commentary explains:

The establishment of the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*) is explained solely in terms of their being severed by the noble path (*āryamārga*) which acts as their antidote; thus, the establishment of the hindrances is entirely based on their respective stages (*avasthā*).
As for the establishment of the two obstructions (*vibandha*), it applies to both meanings, namely, severance and...
Regarding the statement that "the non-interruption is not interrupted," this is based on the functional activity of the dharmas that arise.

Because the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) opposes the nature of equanimity, it gives rise to all dharmas of inequality; because the hindrance of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) opposes the nature of clarity and sharpness, it gives rise to all dharmas of profound obscurity.
For these reasons, the two hindrances are largely not understood in terms of their sequential order of abandonment. This is truly because...
All teachings encompass two meanings: namely, the sequential order of arising phenomena (*utpatti-krama*) and the sequential order of antidotes (*pratipakṣa-krama*).

The two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are restricted solely to the latter [the order of antidotes], whereas the two hindrances (*āvara*) also apply to the former [the order of arising]. For this reason, there is no confusion between "obstacles" and "hindrances.

Furthermore, according to the Dharma-character school (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*), the two obstacles are exclusively false defilements that must certainly be severed; however, in the present Dharma-nature school (*dharmatā-yāna*), the two hindrances are established as being false...

Because it is truly such, it is not definitively subject to severance; thus, the faults and hindrances are established separately. Three [categories] are connected through the upper and lower [stages].
The fourth fascicle of the Treatise ends here.

Composed by the Great Master Puguang of the Huáng Sòng Dynasty, Wú Jì Dàshī.
Part Three: Revealing the Characteristics of Arising and Ceasing. First, the general indication: this commentary establishes the text by stating, "This is the arising and ceasing of the mind."

Within the "characteristics of causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*), the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the universal substratum upon which the single gate of arising and ceasing depends—namely, the mind’s arising and ceasing (*citta-utpāda-nirodha*).

The "dependent specific characteristics" refer to the characteristics of causes and conditions; these "causes and conditions" designate that which is required for arising and ceasing, for it is by virtue of these causes and conditions that arising and ceasing are established.

These characteristics represent the distinctions between the coarse and the subtle, which differ from the single flavor of *tathatā* (suchness), which is beyond dependence and devoid of characteristics.

Regarding their characteristics, the phenomena of arising and ceasing possess distinctions due to mutual dependence; that is, intrinsic awareness (*jñāna*), affliction, purity, internal results, and so forth, are termed "characteristics.
However, this fundamental treatise, among all phenomena, reveals their characteristics by relying solely on the six types of affliction.
This means that by citing the middle [afflictions], it encompasses the beginning and end: intrinsic awareness and ignorance, along with their karmic results, constitute the beginning and the end.

Because the root and the branches are fixed as following one another. Second, the chanting and explanation of the two [sections]: First, the chanting of the root treatise; second, the composition of the explanatory text. Second, the initial division of sections. Regarding the phrase "The statement below follows the explanation," there are five parts.

First, the section on the simultaneous establishment of both by indicating their characteristics. Third, the explanation of the meaning; second, the citation of the sūtra; third, the correlation with the root text.
Regarding the first of the two [sections] in the middle [of the preceding], there is a general explanation of the three [aspects of] "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) and so forth:

because the three types of afflicted mental states (*citta*) associated with them involve distinct attachments and views that are intensified; regarding the three [aspects of] "subtlety" (*sūkṣma*) and so forth, they are not associated with the mind, and because their faults have not yet been differentiated, they remain hidden.

Second, "How so? and below is the specific explanation of the two; within the section on coarseness, there is an interrogation and an explanation of these two matters, namely, their essential nature (*svabhāva*) and...
Because it is associated with the three [aspects of] association and is the most subtle among the subtle within the defiled [manas], it is called "subtle-subtle" (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma*).

Furthermore, because it is associated with the wisdom that corresponds to the *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and is not severed, it is also associated with the manas; since its substance is identical to the *vastu-vijñapti* (object-consciousness), either term may be used to denote both.
Why is it called "subtle"? It is because this is the "subtle" aspect of the fundamental [manas]; thus, it is simply called "subtle" when referring to it in relation to the three stages.
Regarding consciousness and its non-associated [factors], second, Māngala cites a sūtra below; third, first, he raises a question to introduce the topic;
second, he cites a sūtra to establish the point. First, the first sūtra has two parts: first, the two types of non-associated [factors];

second, they are called "non-associated" because, being extremely subtle, although they possess the characteristics of arising and ceasing, these aspects are not manifest, as their meaning consists solely in a subtle vibration and a hidden flow; therefore, they are so named.

The continuous flow of birth and so forth, along with its three corresponding characteristics of arising and ceasing, clearly manifests as the aspect of the "characteristic of production" (janmalakṣaṇa) and so on;
these two [aspects] are further divided into superior and inferior, and within each there are two types of continuity and flow, though their meaning is not different.
Furthermore, in the Great Sūtra, the two kinds of three grades of subtle consciousness follow their respective order.

That is to say, the transformation of karma into manifestation is the subtle arising and ceasing of the preceding flow; the pervasive discriminative consciousness consists of the three types of coarse and defiled phenomena.
Each relies separately upon its sense organ and each separately apprehends its object, just as an image appears when a mirror faces a face.
Now, these three coarse and defiled phenomena are likewise so; therefore, the treatise describes them as being like the separation of the face and the mirror, and such other dharmas.
Because they flow continuously and always coexist with their characteristics, all are said to be not apart from arising and ceasing.
Thirdly, below this, the meaning is pointed out through these three sūtras to reveal that the coarse and subtle aspects of arising and ceasing differ, each being opened into two kinds:
"conforming" (kai) means corresponding, which refers to coarse arising and ceasing; "non-conforming" (fei-kai) means non-corresponding, which refers to the meaning of subtle arising and ceasing.
Third, "as in the original" [refers to] the section below that merges with the original text.

Second, "already explained" [refers to] the section below that enumerates the mutual connections; this corresponds to the gate of the provisional person (*pudgala*). Part two: first, the summary and indication of the divisions;

second, the explanation of the textual meaning. Third, "non-retrogressive ordinary beings" refers to the three levels of the inner ordinary beings of the stage of semblance (*sambhāra-mārga*), who possess semblance-awakening (*tadākāra-jñāna*).

Because one is able to correctly understand that the dream-like state associated with the defilement of attachment is what is to be abandoned, among these two [defilements], the "purification of the lower part of the person" refers to the first stage, the Pure Ground (*śuddhabhūmi*), within the ten stages; it can correctly counteract the non-interruption of the associated defilement.

From the second stage through the seventh stage, there is a gradual treatment of the defilement associated with cognition. At the eighth stage, there is the manifestation of forms, and at the ninth stage, there is the capacity for vision.
Within the fundamental karma that is the object of antidotes for the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the coarse portions are combined into three;

those that are subsequently purified at the lower limit are combined with the movement common to both cause and fruit; the severance of the Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) includes the coarse within the ten stages;
and the severance of the Subtle belongs to the present fruit-stage, as it is exclusively subtle when acting alone. Therefore, it belongs entirely to the fruit.

Third, having already explained the preceding section, this part now reveals the gateway of the basis for the coarse and the subtle. It has two parts: first, the summary and indication of the sections;

second, the detailed explanation of the textual meaning. Third, the initial explanation of the meaning. Regarding "common" (*sādhāraṇa*): it means that the aforementioned two types of arising and ceasing—the coarse and the subtle—share ignorance as their common basis.
Consequently, through this ignorance, [the mind] is able to produce both the non-associated [formations] and the fundamental [consciousness].
They are distinct because they are universal causes; that is to say, each of the two types—arising and ceasing—possesses its own respective causes and conditions.
Specifically, the three types of non-associated defilements take inconceivable perfuming as their cause and inconceivable transformation as their condition.

The three types of associated defilements take the perfuming of false conceptualization as their cause and various objective realms as their condition. Thus, the two sets of causes and conditions for each are distinct from one another.

This is stated according to the scriptural passage cited below; if one relies on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* (the Root Treatise) to clarify the characteristics, the "affliction of non-concomitance" (*viprayukta-kleśa*) speaks only of the dependence on causes, whereas the "affliction of concomitance" (*samprayukta-kleśa*) speaks only of the dependence on conditions, and thus they are called distinct.
As in the Root Text below, in the combined section of the main body, first the common basis of the former two types is revealed, and next...
This means that what follows clarifies the distinct meanings of their two types of bases:
