second, the perfuming of karma; and third, the two sounds [of the terms], which may be understood respectively according to the sequence.

Second, the section explaining the gate of the mutual permeation (*vāsanā*) between the lower [defiled] and the white [pure] dharmas having power. This has two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the detailed explanation. Regarding the second, the detailed explanation, there are two parts:

first, the general question and general answer that clarifies the tenet; second, the specific explanation. Within the first part, the general question and general answer that clarifies the tenet, there are two sections: first, the general question, which arises as a preliminary to clarifying the upward-turning permeation of pure dharmas;

second, the general answer from this point forward. Within the first of these, the summary reference and enumeration, there are two points: first, the summary reference; second, the enumeration. [The enumeration begins with: "Beginningless..."
The following commentary establishes two points. First, it provides a general demonstration that the fundamental cause and fruit are established through beginningless perfuming:

because of the power of internal causes from time immemorial, one is fully endowed with the causal stage and the merit of the fruit. Second, it demonstrates that the initial cause and fruit are established through the power of external conditions arising at the beginning:
by relying on the power of external conditions such as spiritual practice, one is then able to manifest those inherently existing causes and fruits.

Second, the detailed explanation of the two causes below. First, the *Maulī Bhūmi* (Basic Section). First, the exposition and explanation. Based on the cessation of beginningless perfuming, the fundamental cause and fruit are established.
Now, there are three types of perfumers and only two types of objects to be severed: namely, true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*), suchness (*tathatā*), and the first fruit-mind (*phala-citta*).
These three act as the perfumers, while the two kinds of ignorance—the fundamental and the derivative—constitute that which is severed. This is due to the perfuming of the ten [factors].

The ten stages (*bhūmi*) are established based on the various branches and extremities of ignorance (*avidyā*), while the state of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is established based on a single type of fundamental ignorance.
Although within the three stages of the worthy ones (*tri-śaikṣa*) both the fundamental and the permeating ignorance are present, the latter is somewhat diminished;

nevertheless, because this contemplation has not yet been able to correctly remedy the subtle obstructions and defilements, it is for this reason that the "one dharma-realm mind" is not mentioned—referring to the aforementioned ten kinds of suchness (*tathatā*).
Because true wisdom is quiescently illuminating and undifferentiated within the reality of the central essence, it is called the "One Dharma-realm Mind.

Furthermore, because the manifold dharmas entered therein are unified within a single mind, and because the fundamental ignorance has been severed through beginningless perfuming, it is also called the "One Dharma-result Mind.
If this is so, since the previously mentioned One Dharma-realm Mind possesses two types of mastery, why is it merely that which is perfumed?

Now it is said that [the dharmas] also act as perfumers; however, this fundamental dharma provides the awakening and power for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) to perfume those conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena, causing their afflictions to cease;
and it provides the power for the conditioned to perfume those unconditioned phenomena, causing them to become obscured and abandoned.
Since its essence is dependent upon function, how could it not be a perfumer? As for why it was not mentioned previously, it is because the perfumed (*bhāvya*) is predominant among all phenomena.

Because they rely [on this], there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Second, "as in the original" refers to the three characters "the Dharma of True Suchness" (*tathatā-dharma*) in the main text;
these are displayed in their respective order as the three types of perfuming agents from beginningless time.
The first two are the power of practicing according to reality within the "characteristic of the purity of wisdom," while the last one is the power of the perfuming of the Dharma.
By means of these two powers, one counteracts the two types of non-awakening, both fundamental and derivative.

Regarding the second [power], the initial cause, from the lower stages of the ground, the first part explains that the causal conditions for initial awakening are established through the power of fundamental perfuming.

Starting from the group of those fixed in error (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), one arouses a sense of weary detachment and enters the group of the undetermined (*aniyata-rāśi*). Initial awakening, supported by its conditions, gradually ascends through the stages. Third.
From the ten stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sages, up until finally attaining the fruit of wondrous enlightenment, their application remains unceasing throughout the future.
These two [stages] correspond to the original text below. If one causes the deluded mind to give rise to weary seeking, this is the group of those in false concentration (*mithyā-samādhi*).

When this deluded mind reaches the point of self-conviction regarding its own nature, it is the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). At this stage, the practitioner realizes that the mark of cessation is the ultimate.
It is said that within one’s own body, the true nature is inherently present, endowed with immeasurable virtues and lacking nothing;

yet, out of a sense of weariness toward the conditions for seeking [enlightenment], one repeatedly practices the cultivation of *tathatā*. However, according to the fundamental position, the true is the perfuming agent (*pariṇāmanaka*) and the deluded is the object perfumed (*pariṇāmya*).

Here, the statement that one "perfumes *tathatā*" refers to the locus of reliance—that is, the original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*) perfumes the delusion by relying upon the principle of suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, it may also be understood that the treatise relies on both powers simultaneously: first, the power of the deluded mind’s weary seeking;
second, the power of the permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā*). This indicates that [the stage] also relies on True Suchness as the active agent of permeation.

Furthermore, within this stage, although True Suchness is predominant as the permeating agent, it does not preclude its simultaneous possession of the nature of the permeated object. Thus, one knows that the deluded movement of the mind corresponds to the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).
In this stage, one first perceives the Dharmakāya as quiescent and eternally extinguished;

because all movement of thought and cognition is seen to be illusory, there are no external objects before one—this is the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-pratipatti*), wherein one cultivates various supreme practices to counteract the perception of differentiated characteristics, and through the skillful means of realizing the emptiness of phenomena, one understands that objects are empty, thereby cultivating the Dharma of detachment.

This is the stage of the Ten Transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), wherein, in accordance with the cultivation of supreme deeds, one dedicates them toward the three spheres; thus, one is able to distance oneself [from attachments].

Because one abandons inverted seeking, seeking for difference, and various mental engagements (*manasikāra*), through knowing things as they truly are (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), one reaches the state of non-grasping and non-recollection, thereby entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

As for "the power of long-term perfuming" (*vāsanā-bala*), this refers to the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) from the second stage up to the tenth stage, which is the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because ignorance has ceased, the mind does not arise; this is due to the fundamental [cause].
Because ignorance is exhausted, the deluded mind of karmic consciousness never arises again. Because it does not arise, its objects of perception likewise cease.
When the sixfold winds of sensory dust and their corresponding causes are all extinguished, and both causes and conditions have perished, the mental characteristics are entirely exhausted.
Thus, coarse and subtle defiled marks are extinguished without remainder; being vast and utterly pure, it is said that one has attained Nirvana, and so forth. Thus it is.
Both cause and effect are manifested through the power of cultivation.
Second, having already explained the general summary, there follows the section on specific and detailed exposition. This section has two parts: first, the conclusion and indication of the divisions;

second, the explanation based on the gates, beginning with the defiled dharmas. Regarding the first, the gate of the perfuming of delusory defilement, there are two parts: first, the heading and indication; second, [the explanation] starting from "the mental consciousness... and so forth.
The second section, "Explaining the Accomplishment," consists of two parts. First, regarding the forty mental states (*citta*) that are perfumed by the first consciousness (*manovijñāna*):

these refer to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and the three stages of worthiness (*kṣānti*). This so-called "consciousness" refers to the coarse aspect external to the *manas*; it corresponds to the *manovijñāna*, which belongs to the stage of grasping and calculating the characteristics of names (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).

Such a consciousness is established through the conjunction of two types of "vitality" (*vāyu*): that of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and that of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Although its portion belonging to fundamental awakening...

Although delusion arises in accordance with conditions, its intrinsic nature is luminous clarity and can never be obscured by darkness. Since beginningless time, this has inwardly perfumed the portion of ignorance, causing it to subside.
It is like fire within wood: although the element of fire combines with the other elements to form wood, its inherent nature is to burn;
from the very moment it is produced, it begins to consume the wood until it is finally reduced to ashes. Therefore, to slander the sutras is [to deny] this.
Though one slanders the Buddha, it is like planting the supreme seed of the vajra; by means of this very seed, one will ultimately achieve liberation.

Although the external object is merely a pretext, the reality depends on the slanderous mind; thus both the true and the false are established. Through the power of this habitual perfuming, wholesome roots such as non-attachment arise and function together;
through revulsion for the false and the seeking of the true, one progresses through successive stages toward the path of Buddhahood.

The twenty-first [verse], the latter part, states that the *manas* perfumes the manifest; the Sūtra says that the *manas-vijñāna* possesses eleven meanings because the five aspects of fundamental ignorance and the five consciousnesses together constitute these eleven.

Thus, through the mutual perfuming of the real and the false, and by virtue of their commonality in mode of activity, they become distinct according to their coarseness and subtlety, or their superiority and inferiority.
If this is so, since it is said that the Real is the perfumer, it should not be opposed to the false defilements.
Furthermore, what further distinction is there between the subsequent pure dharmas? Indeed, the true nature is of a single flavor and fundamentally lacks both defilement and purity;

it is only by following [the influence of] functional activity that distinctions are established. That is to say, by following defiled conditions, all defiled dharmas are formed, arising in conjunction and evolving together—neither identical nor different.
Therefore, when awakening follows along with delusion, they are both termed "delusory defilement," just as fire within wood is collectively termed "wood. Furthermore...

There exists a superior function that sustains all meritorious qualities—namely, the practices such as the six perfections and the fruits such as the three bodies—all pure virtues rely upon true awakening;
because awakening follows from these virtues, both are termed "truly pure.
Just as fire in the realm of space is not found solely in wood, such functions, whether general or specific, are utterly distinct and should not cause confusion.
Second, the section on the gate of the perfuming of the lower pure dharmas already explained, which has two parts: first, the summary and classification of the sections;
second, the general heading followed by the explanation of the characteristics according to the gates. Regarding the first, the general heading section, there are two parts:

first, the opening and explanation of the gate; second, the specific clarification of perfuming. Regarding the first, the specific clarification of perfuming, there is the gate of the natural perfuming of the Dharma-body.

This means that within the three self-natures (*trisvabhāva*), the two meanings of perfuming (*vāsanā*) regarding essence and characteristics correspond respectively to the "characteristic of pure wisdom" (*jñāna-viśuddhi-lakṣaṇa*) within the category of following defilement (*anuvyañjana-kliṣṭa*), and the "mirror of causal perfuming" (*hetu-vāsanā-ādarśa*) within the category of purity (*viśuddha*).
Because this nature-wisdom is originally untainted (*anāsrava*), it perfumes sentient beings; thus, these two [meanings] are as stated below.

Next is the gate of the constant nature-perfuming of the manifested and transformed [bodies]. Within the three self-natures, the meaning of the self-use perfuming corresponds to... [the category of following defilement].
The inconceivable aspect of activity within the defiled state and the mirror-like aspect of the perfuming of conditions within the purified state arise from this awakening-function;

it either manifests as clouds of bodies or acts as objective realms, causing all practitioners to perceive these signs and engage with various objects, such that all their diverse activities become the work of a Buddha, functioning without substitution throughout the limits of the future.
Therefore, the subsequent treatise states: "Constantly and eternally perfuming. (2)
Thus, the preceding section generally reveals the power and function. These two gates refer to the essence, characteristics, and the perfuming of function;

because they are mutually identical, they are not separated from one another. Alternatively, it may be that both gates collectively refer to the perfuming of the deluded mind by True Suchness (*tathatā*); there is no contradiction in this principle.
Because it reaches the utmost limit throughout the three periods of time and pervades the ten directions without interval or deficiency, it is called "eternal" (*nitya*). That is to say:

By the power of constant and perpetual perfuming, it causes the practitioner to give rise to the ten faiths, produce the ten understandings, establish the ten practices, and perform the ten dedications;

with a mind like a diamond, they never regress. Upon fulfilling the stage of the three worthies, they enter the ten stages (*bhūmis*), whereby they penetrate the realms of both the ultimate and conventional truths through both fundamental wisdom and subsequently attained wisdom, thereby fusing them.

Returning to a single mind so that there are no obstructions corresponds to what is stated in the *Benjue* (Awakening of Faith): "To have self-confidence that one's own body possesses the *tathatā*-dharma.
This refers precisely to the arousal of the mind during the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), which belongs to the level of the three worthies (*tri-kṣānti*).

As for the practice, it refers to the practice of actualization within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Therefore, this section below concludes by demonstrating that these two meanings arise from the process of perfuming (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, it is clearly and manifestly evident that the Dharma-body’s manifestation for the sake of sentient beings inherently possesses such principles. III.

Having already explained [the above], there follows the section on "Initiating Questions and Answers to Resolve Doubts," which has two parts: first, the summary indication; second, the explanation of the characteristics, beginning with "This resolves...

Part three of this [second part] first sets forth the intended meaning to reveal that the teachings and principles are even more profound and subtle, and further provides a detailed exposition to clarify them.
Regarding the opening and elucidation of the two meanings of the definitive selection (*viniścaya*) for those below: first, the general presentation of the two meanings.

First, the presentation of the existence and non-existence of the principle: all sentient beings, when compared with the original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*), universally possess both the sense of existence and the sense of non-existence.
If they exist, they all exist; if they do not exist, they all do not exist. Thus, both existence and non-existence possess profound principles, unlike [the teachings of] expedient means (*upāya*).
The teaching that there is definitely existence and definitely non-existence, each being distinct from the other, serves as the basis for establishing the meaning of existence and non-existence.

To prove the point at hand, one cites what the Buddha taught to validate the established thesis: "If the dharmas of the gates are explained individually, then there are persons and there is cognition;

if one abandons the gates and enters the dharmas, their functional utility returns to the essence, which is the single flavor of the Mahāyāna dharma, wherein no further arising or cognition is spoken of."

Furthermore, regarding these distinctions: based on the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), all possess original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*); whereas based on the gate of suchness (*tathatā-mukha*), none possess original enlightenment.

Although they are endowed with the inexhaustible virtues of nature as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they are solely of a single flavor, for there is no distinction between delusion and awakening based on their mutual dependence.

2. Second, the detailed explanation of the two gates based on the preceding [section]. 2.1. First, the gate of having awakening (sajñāna). 3.1. First, the arising of awakening. 3.2. Second, returning to the source through question and answer.
3.3. Third, resolving doubts by building upon the preceding. Within the first [of these], there are two parts: 3.3.1. First, posing and explaining the questions regarding identity and difference.
3.3.1.1. First, the formal question and answer. 3.3.1.1.1. First, the general question: "All sentient beings possess original awakening (*mūla-jñāna*); is the awakening they possess identical?"

If they are identical, then a single awakening would pervade the entire substance of the realm of birth without distinction; if they are distinct, then many awakenings would each pervade the realm of birth with different substances.
As stated in the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda once posed this question:
"Is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings possessed by all in common, or is it possessed individually? If it were possessed in common..."

If one person attains the fruit, all should attain it simultaneously; if each were to attain it individually, one should not say that all Buddhas are equal, nor should one say that Buddha-nature is like space.
In that sutra, Buddha-nature is precisely this original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*);

here, in response to sentient beings, its identity and difference are questioned. The intent of this present inquiry is entirely the same as that sutra. [The section] "Second, all... below distinguishes [the two].

Answer: Because all sentient beings possess a single awakening—since the nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is without differentiation—the wording of this treatise’s response is identical to that sutra.
That sutra’s response to the preceding question contains two points. First, it establishes the principle of identity:
the Buddha said, "Good son, the buddha-nature of sentient beings is neither one nor many; the equality of all Buddhas is like space. All.
That all sentient beings possess this in common establishes the principle that the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings is identical;

this dispels subsequent doubts regarding such identity. As the Sūtra says: "If there are those who can cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, you should know that these persons shall clearly perceive [the Truth].
This addresses the previous doubt: if [Buddha-nature] were shared in common, then when one person attains the fruit, everyone should simultaneously attain Buddhahood. Now...

Answer: Although that nature is one and common to all sentient beings, because it can be clearly perceived through the cultivation of the path, one should not raise the objection that everyone must attain it simultaneously.

Second, "If that were so," etc., provides a further inquiry and explanation. First, the inquiry regarding whether the innate awakening (*mūla-awakening*) is one or many: [The opponent asks] if the fundamental awakening is but one, how can there be many...?
Because many [phenomena] arise, they follow one another; thus, it is difficult to reconcile the one and the many. From the perspective of arising, they should be one rather than many;

from the perspective of awakening, they should be many rather than one. Regarding these matters, there are two parts: first, explaining the equality and difference of the inferior and superior; second, establishing their identity and difference. First, as for establishing identity and difference:
since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is distinct in each case, how could they be uniform? Yet the awakened mind is equal and cannot be divided into differences.
Why would one confuse the distinctions among sentient beings and force them to be identical? [The two positions] cannot both be maintained:
the single awakened mind cannot be of diverse kinds, and therefore it must be one; the nature of birth cannot be of a single kind, and therefore it must be many.
For this reason, one should not follow [the opponent's logic] and raise such objections.

Second, "If that were so," and below, is the section reconciling contradictions with the scriptures. This has two parts: first, citing the contradictory passages, which consist of four verses in total; second, specifically clarifying their two meanings.

The first two verses clarify *mūla-āśraya-jñāna* (fundamental awakening), and the latter two verses clarify *avidyā* (ignorance). Each begins with a metaphor followed by the application to the dharma. Since fundamental awakening is singular, it correctly accords with the preceding meaning;
these are cited here as a convenient segue and do not constitute a contradiction. However, that [previous] ignorance is contrasted with the present [discussion].

There is a different [interpretation] that should properly be reconciled with what was previously stated: because all sentient beings possess distinct natures, they cannot belong to the same species (*eka-jāti*).
Does this not contradict the meaning of the *Mysterious Text* (*Xuanwen*), which states that ignorance (*avidyā*) is one and constitutes a single species?

This is because even when a single fragment of cloud covers the moon, a thousand vessels are simultaneously obscured; when a single delusion perfumes the mind, the myriad spirits are all darkened. How much more so is this true for the substance of ignorance itself!
Because they are one, the vessel is used as a metaphor for the various classes of sentient beings; because the moon is like the original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) obscured by ignorance.

Second, "There are two" and below provide the reconciliation and explanation. Part three, "First, establishing the principle," also has three sections. First, the heading; second, "The words 'by themselves'" and below cite and explain.
First, regarding the demonstration of the meaning of the same single continuum within our own school: all sentient beings are the same.

Because they are of one essence, the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) are equal and singular; all phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) are entirely formed by encompassing this principle.
Therefore, from the moment sentient beings exhaust their lives throughout the ten directions until the end of existence within the three realms (*tridhātu*), they are all solely this one [essence].

Regarding the subsequent demonstration of the meaning of the continuity of differentiated phases within the process of attraction and inclusion: because the bodies of all sentient beings are each distinct, they are defiled by hearing the substance of phenomena.

Because it distinguishes the purity of the stages and exerts effort in cultivation and abandonment to guide and sustain sentient beings who are indolent, it is said that ignorance has distinct individual entities.
Third, in the *Xuanwen lun* (Treatise on the Profound Text), the meaning of being within the same continuous stream is demonstrated;
therefore, it is said that ignorance is a single entity without duality. This is what the *Qixin lun* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith) demonstrates regarding their differentiation.

Because they refer to the meaning of distinct continuities, it is said that all sentient beings possess immeasurable and boundless ignorance, which has been differentiated by its very nature from the beginningless past and varies in its thickness and thinness;
this is stated for the purpose of providing skillful means to guide and gather them.
Thus, since these two treatises each rely on one specific aspect of meaning, they do not contradict one another.

Second, for this reason, the following citation of scripture establishes the two points. First, the treatise proves the distinction [between the two] with two verses: the first provides the analogy and the second applies it to the Dharma.
The lotus leaves are used as an analogy for ignorance (*avidyā*), each being distinct; the vessel represents the individual essence of sentient beings.

The moon-disk covered within them represents the original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) remaining in bondage; the other vessels represent the Buddhas, in whom the moon-disk is not obscured, representing the original enlightenment that has emerged from bondage.
The *Awakening of Faith* is precisely identical to that text in its demonstration of the meaning of the continuity of differentiation.
Second, below the "next" section, the sutra clarifies the two aspects of attraction and inclusion: first, the citation of the text; second, the explanation of the meaning of this text.

First, the clarification of the establishment of distinctions: first, regarding the increase of indolence upon hearing [the teaching] of oneness; within this, the primary clarification states: "Upon hearing that sentient beings are the same..."
First, regarding ignorance: there are already many people who have cultivated their minds and refined their conduct such that they are fully capable of eliminating and severing it;
why, then, must I now exert myself in the arduous task of cultivation and severance? This is as illustrated by the following example:

for instance, if many people hear of an enemy and are able to kill him through their combined efforts, what need is there for me to personally inflict punishment upon him? For this reason, [I let go].

The mind does not diligently recollect the Path; this second point is intended to explain below that there is much and long-lasting vigor. This is taught in order to remedy sentient beings who are as aforementioned lax.
Ignorance is boundless and immeasurable; upon hearing this teaching, one should apply oneself with diligent vigor and seek the means for its abandonment as if putting out a fire on one's head.
This second section clarifies the underlying intent (samdhāya) by showing the commonality with the explicit text of the sutra, even though it has already been stated.
The fundamental intention of the Buddha of Infinite Origin is simply that there is but one ignorance; therefore, the meaning of the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) is established.

Third, "If this were so" and below extensively explains the preceding meaning in two parts: first, the arising of delusion; second, whether it is one or many. Regarding the first, the investigation through advancing and retreating contains three points:
first, it means that the substance of ignorance is one, such that when one person severs it, all are severed; next, it means if...
To say that others cannot sever [ignorance] because they have not yet practiced it would mean one could not say that ignorance is a single entity.
Furthermore, if one were to grant that by severing one, all are severed, then the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) would become utterly annihilated.

It is by means of ignorance that the realm of birth is sustained and never perishes; if, as you claim, they are now equally exhausted and the realm of birth is thus severed, a great error would follow.
Second, the detailed explanation of this matter in terms of "one" and "many," which has two parts. First, the refutation of the incorrect view:

regarding the previous objection that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a single entity and thus involves three faults, that is not the case. Second, the establishment of the correct view, beginning with "ignorance," which has two parts:

first, establishing the principle and raising the inquiry; within this, first the establishment of the principle states: although all instances of ignorance are one, they are capable of producing the distinct continuities of sentient beings.
However, although all sentient beings each take the nine aspects as their essential substance, the auxiliary characteristics they apprehend differ from one another;
this constitutes the sense of distinction within the commonality. Next, a further inquiry is raised, which leads to the subsequent response and explanation.
The two verses provide an answer by means of an illustration. The first verse contains four lines: the first two lines illustrate delusion;

the next line contains two characters that signify awakening; and the final three characters encompass both of the preceding meanings. The prose commentary has two parts: first, the illustration of delusion. 1. The illustration of delusion:

Darkness can universally represent ignorance. Since the ten rooms are distinct, they represent [the various states of existence]. [Note: The provided text fragment appears to be a structural outline or commentary on a Buddhist philosophical text, likely concerning the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its manifestations.]

Sentient beings each give rise to different delusions; because the relationship between the one and the many differs, it cannot be said that one gives rise to many delusions or that many give rise to one.

This is because, just as there cannot be one darkness in one room and ten darknesses in ten rooms simultaneously, so too, if one were to awaken from the darkness of a single room, how could the darkness remain in nine other rooms? It would be like being born while still dreaming.

To say that when a person holds a bright lamp within a single room, the darkness inside the room is completely extinguished without remainder is a metaphor for how enlightened wisdom destroys and exhausts ignorance.
The nine rooms remaining dark is a metaphor for sentient beings who have not yet severed ignorance.

When the Buddha and sentient beings face one another, their states of delusion and awakening are entirely different; it cannot be said that the delusion of sentient beings is the same as the delusion of the Buddha, nor that the severing of delusion by the Buddha is the same as the severing of delusion by sentient beings.
As with the "extinction of one" and the "extinction of nine," since it is impossible to speak of "nine existences" or "one existence," Lord Chongluo said:

"I have examined the old edition of the *Śāstra* and found three additional phrases totaling thirteen characters, namely: 'clarifying perfection' up to 'without remainder. Examining this meaning in detail, 'non-existence' is already manifest;

to add 'existence' would involve redundancy and prolixity. Furthermore, I suspect these were errors occurring during the process of carving the woodblocks or transcribing the text. Thus did the commentator explain the text at the outset.

Regarding the statement that "darkness is exhausted and extinguished within emptiness," this is a general interpretation of the preceding verse. The subsequent thirteen characters, beginning with "the brilliance is perfectly manifest" (*ming yuan xian deng*), are intended to clarify that the darkness within the nine chambers has not yet been extinguished;
therefore, they cannot be treated as analogous [to the former case]. For this reason, the meaning is restated. This principle can also be applied to the two types of ignorance (*avidyā*);
the application to the phenomena below [ignorance] can be understood accordingly.
Third, therefore, the subsequent section concludes based on the meaning: the delusions of all sentient beings are identical while their bodies differ.

If one possesses the path of cultivation and is able to sever ignorance, or if one has not yet cultivated the cause and ignorance remains intact, it cannot be said that when one sentient being severs [ignorance], all are severed.
This is merely a point concerning the distinction between the essence of ordinary beings and Buddhas from the perspective of a single gate.

Second, if [the nature of awakening] were identical upon descending into birth, there would be two points: first, the difficulty regarding the distinction between being entangled and free from entanglement;

second, the initial presentation of the intent, which follows upon the previous discussion of whether ignorance is severed or not, to explain the meaning of this doubt. The intent is as follows: the nature of awakening is one and universal throughout both those who have not yet severed [ignorance] and those who have already severed it.
In those who have not yet severed it, the nature of awakening is obstructed; in those who have already severed it, the nature of awakening... [is unobstructed].

Regarding the two states of being unobstructed and free from obstructions: how can it be said that they are of one essence and non-dual, pervading the realm of birth, when there is a distinction between these two positions—one being free from obstructions by emerging from the entanglements, and the other being obstructed while remaining within them?
Regarding the response to the two points concerning original enlightenment, the single flavor, and the non-differentiation of the single characteristic: first, the response by means of principle.
First, establishing the correct principle: Original enlightenment, the Buddha-nature, possesses four great meanings;

it is equal to empty space, pervading everywhere within the realm of sentient beings, reaching every part of the realm of the two vehicles, penetrating throughout the realm of bodhisattvas, and extending to the realm of the Tathāgatas.

The realms (*dhātu*) have nothing to which they do not correspond; furthermore, in this passage, although the phrasing varies through pervasive reaching and universal correspondence, there are in fact only two meanings:

namely, vast containment and universal pervasion. Because they universally reach and pervade all other phenomena within themselves, and because their own phenomena enter into others, they correspond exactly.
Thus, it possesses both meanings; though dual, it is without duality, thereby dispelling delusion.
The nature of the obscuring ignorance is precisely the nature of the *dharmadhātu* when it is bound; the nature that is outside of being bound is precisely the state of being free from bondage.
To hold such a view is merely an object perceived by the deluded mind, and not the true mind that is free from extremes.

Therefore, the following section concludes based on the meaning of the second [verse]. Furthermore, the following section cites the teachings to establish the point: "The moon arises at the edge of the heavens, its perfect brilliance reflecting in the clear sky."
The clarity and obscurity appearing within the vessel [of water] are like the nature of awakening in sentient beings;
how could the difference between clarity and obscurity cause the original moon to become something else?

Second, "All things below" refers to the section on returning to the source through question and answer. First, within the actual question and answer, first, the question: first, the statement of the intent.
Next, why are there three points for raising doubts below? First, the doubt that the speed of attaining the fruit differs;

second, the doubt that there are differences in the nature of diligence or indolence; and third, the doubt that the faculties of the vessels are each distinct as either sharp or dull. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "immeasurable distinctions," this refers by analogy to other meanings.
Later, the conclusion of the difficulty states: "Since fundamental awakening (*mūla-avabodha*) is one and not different, then all..."
When sentient beings give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, their cultivation of practices and their attainment of the Way should all be equal and without distinction.

Next, following the section on Original Enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*), the answer is given: because of the manifold aspects of the single mind, there is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) sovereign activity of Original Enlightenment, and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) sovereign activity of Ignorance (*avidyā*).
From the very beginning, the Buddha-nature of Original Enlightenment has been [obscured] by the power of that Ignorance.

Regarding the distinction of inferiority: from the very beginning, due to differences in the thickness or thinness of that fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), sentient beings come to possess many distinctions.
If awakening is strong and afflictions are thin, then their faculties are sharp, their nature is diligent, and they swiftly attain the Buddha-way.

If awakening is inferior and afflictions are thick, then their faculties are dull, their nature is indolent, and they slowly attain the Buddha-way. Second, if one speaks of the downward-turning [aspect]:
In the initial inquiry within the commentary: If one says that there are distinctions between the strength and weakness of Buddha-nature, such is not the case.
Because Buddha-nature is perfect and complete, with merits exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges, it neither increases nor decreases.

If there were now strength and weakness, there would necessarily be increase and decrease—meaning that where there is increase, merits are many, and where there is decrease, merits are few. Since this is so, how can it be called "equal" and "of a single flavor"? If...

Regarding the statement that there is a distinction between the thickness and thinness of ignorance (*avidyā*), this meaning is not so. For the Noble Ones have taught that fundamental ignorance is abandoned upon seeing a single point;

if there were degrees of thickness and thinness, there would necessarily be differences in the amount [of what is abandoned]. That is to say, if it were thick, the faults would be many and thus abandoned across all stages;
if it were thin, the faults would be few and thus abandoned in only a single stage. Since this is the case, the principle is that it is abandoned instantaneously within a single stage.

This cannot be established. Following this, the text below explains that the *tathāgatagarbha* (original awakening) of sentient beings is in reality devoid of increase or decrease, yet manifests distinctions based upon ignorance (*avidyā*).

It means that since ignorance is thick, the nature of awakening is correspondingly inferior; although the nature inherently possesses merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, because the obstructions are profound and heavy, liberation is somewhat difficult to attain.
This does not mean that the number or names of the merits have decreased, but is spoken of in this way [due to the state of obscuration].
For those of inferior capacity whose ignorance is thick, the arousal of the bodhicitta is extremely difficult; it is like accumulated hard ice that is hard to melt even with a gentle breeze.

Through the long-term internal permeation of the fundamental awakened nature (mūla-bodhi-citta), it gradually becomes thin and subtle. Furthermore, when aided by the external conditions of the Buddhas, one may arouse the mind, yet progress remains unstable.
Externally, the Compassionate Father does not abandon them, and internally, the fundamental awakening constantly permeates them; thus, after passing through further time...

Over a long period of time, as one gradually becomes compliant through the perfection of causal practice, one directly perceives that the fundamental ignorance within the single mind of the Dharma-realm can finally be severed instantaneously.
Since this severance does not occur merely because of "thickness," how could it be validly objected that [the severance] cannot be achieved in a single stage?
Furthermore, what distinct causes lead to the unequal thickness of the ignorance created within the single mind of the Dharma? [Answer: ... [The answer follows].

Since it is logically appropriate that such distinctions exist within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), just as one cannot fathom why the wind moves the earth despite its solidity and capacity for resistance,
how much less can one hastily confuse the mind regarding the realm of the Buddhas?
Third, if it is as stated below, it follows from the previous section on dispelling doubts. Part two: first, a general explanation of the methods of the remaining gates. Section four:
first, an inquiry and explanation regarding practitioners who have attained full purity. Subsection one: first, an inquiry based on both dharmas. This means:

if it is said that although the essence of ignorance is one, because the continuums are distinct, there are cases where it is severed and cases where it is not—just as for various practitioners who sever evil and cultivate good, such that causes are perfected and fruits are fulfilled.
In this way, for the practitioner, "clarity" (*vidyā*) is not definitively established because the darkness within the remaining chambers has not yet been extinguished;
nor is it "lack of clarity" (*avidyā*), because the darkness within one chamber has been extinguished without remainder. Thus, below, the explanation concerns only lack of clarity:
although the afflictions of a single body have already been severed, the lack of clarity in sentient beings continues on as before, like the orb of the moon.
Being solitary and luminous, it does not illuminate the Cakravāḍa mountains; being like a solitary black pearl, its light shines only within the seas.

Therefore, although it is said that there is awakening and understanding, one still remains within the stage of ignorance. Furthermore, because these practices and virtues are established as provisional expedients and have not yet reached ultimate, true perfection, they are said to be not within the stage of clarity.

2. If that is so, [the text] below interrogates and explains the pure *amala-vijñāna* (fundamental awakening). This section has two parts: first, the interrogation regarding the pure fundamental awakening.
It is inherently endowed with virtues exceeding the sands of the Ganges; it is neither established as existent nor denied as non-existent.

It transcends the four verbal formulations—existence, emptiness, and so forth—and is free from the five extremes such as increase and decrease. It is naturally pure, beyond the reach of mind and speech, and detached from such purity.

Regarding the statement "Awakening is explained as the two, clarity and non-clarity," the subsequent explanation means that although such pure original awakening (amala-jñāna) functions solely as the fulfillment [of reality], it is established in relation to its counterpart;
and although it is permeated solely by virtue, it is established in relation to illusion.
Because it is established in mutual dependence upon that non-awakening (a-vibodha), it is called the "domain of non-clarity" (avidyā-pradeśa).
Third, if that is so, [the text] below raises an inquiry and provides an explanation regarding the "One Dharma-realm Mind" (eka-dharmadhātu-citta). First, the inquiry:

Among the eight fundamental dharmas that constitute the entry [into the state], one essence and one mind are termed the "One Dharma-realm. Alternatively, it refers to the one mind realized by the prior original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*).

Because this is extremely subtle and difficult to manifest, it is displayed through the skillful means of negation (*apavāda*) and affirmation (*samāropa*); thus, this very one mind is that which is beyond the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*).
That which cannot be called "not-thousand" is what is meant by "that which cannot be. Although this is nominally called "middle," its nature is actually neither middle nor not-middle.

Although these are nominally called "the first principle" (*paramārtha*), they have from the beginning always been free from both "heaven" (*deva*) and "non-heaven" (*adeva*). Regarding the phrase "flowing water" (*yan-shui*): "flowing" (*yan*) means to stream;

it refers to speech that is as rapid as a cascading river, hence the metaphor of "feet" (*pada*) is established for the meaning of "speech. As for "feet" (*zu*): [Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on Buddhist terminology, likely concerning the *padaparama* (foot-syllable) or the nature of linguistic expression. The final sentence is incomplete.]
Regarding the phrase "such as hoofprints and tracks," "deliberation" (*samīkṣā*) and so forth refers to the measure of precise and discerning reflection.

The mind’s ability to apprehend objects is established through the metaphor of the hand; just as a hand picks up an object, it is like the "hand of faith" (*śraddhā-hasta*) or the "hand of instruction" (*anuśāsana-hasta*).
Because verbal discourse is exhausted [in silence], the feet cease their movement; because mental objects of thought have subsided, the hands come to rest. Thus it is one.

The mind is both luminous and non-luminous; thus, the following passage explains that although this single mind reaches the ultimate limit of its causal seeds, it is still not yet perfectly luminous within non-duality, and is therefore designated as the "state of non-luminosity."
Regarding the four [sections], the third consists of three parts: first, the general inquiry; second, the specific analysis; and third, the summary. First, the general inquiry:

Because those dharmas are manifested through the gate of the basis (*āśraya*), they are like a Wheel-Turning King who is designated by his wheel. Now, it is said that the three bases and the single mind are manifested through the gate of the means of entry (*praveśa-mukha*).
Therefore, it is stated that "one cannot be one" and that "the one is manifested through the means of entry," and so forth. Thus, there are three [points].
From the perspective that the fundamental dharma of the single mind is profoundly remote and transcendent, [the distinction between] enlightenment and non-enlightenment is thus clarified.
Below, this is explained by establishing it through the mutual dependence of the "enterer" and the "entered"; therefore, it also belongs to the domain of non-enlightenment.
Second, the section on "Non-duality" specifically clarifies the dharma of non-duality. This means that this Mahāyāna dharma of non-duality is most supreme and perfectly consummate:
as a cause, it is the cause; as a fruit, it is the fruit; as a phenomenon (*dharma*), it is the phenomenon; and as a principle (*artha*), it is the principle.

Within all various dharmas—such as defilement and purity, principle and phenomena, stages of practice, and mind and objects—it lacks any characteristic of relative distinction; therefore, it is solely non-dual.
Regarding these two Mahāyāna dharmas—such dharmas as these, within the duality of clarity and non-clarity—how are they subsumed?

The Master of Exegesis, wishing to demonstrate that this dharma is profoundly deep, most mysterious, uniquely honored, and supreme, [teaches] because it transcends the capacities of sentient beings and because it transcends verbal instruction;
thus, although there are interrogative words, there are no responsive utterances. Furthermore, because the essence of the non-dual Mahāyāna is itself both clarity and non-clarity.
The fourfold and sixfold propositions regarding clarity, non-clarity, and ignorance are all inclusively subsumed;
the questions and answers differ neither in wording nor in meaning, as they manifest directly as non-dual and without distinction.

Second, it has already been explained that the sentient beings of the lower realms who lack awareness, as well as awareness itself, are established based on the differentiated functions of the single mind.
Now, in this present section, the differences are reconciled and returned to their unity; as function is dissolved and the essence remains, there is only the equal, single-flavored *dharmadhātu*.
How, then, could there be any distinction between subject and object, or between the arising of awareness?

Third, this section concludes by connecting [the text] to the treatise; that is, by means of the two approaches of "with cognition" and "without cognition," one thoroughly penetrates the profound purport of the questions and answers in the root treatise, so that all doubts may be resolved and cleared without obstruction.

IV. Having already explained the preceding section, this section provides a detailed exposition on the conditions for raising questions and the opening of the discussion. It consists of two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the sequential explanation of the subsequent sections. Regarding the second part, there are two sub-sections:
first, the general indication of the rules for the gate of determination; second, the specific explanation. Within the first sub-section, there are two parts:

first, the formal presentation; second, the citation and explanation of the text. Regarding the third part, the explanation of the nature of phenomena: if the dharmas of all Buddhas were to be established only by depending upon causes and conditions, they would differ from those of the non-Buddhists.

Because the Way exists spontaneously, the nature-seed of original enlightenment is called the "cause"; this refers to the "correct cause" (*samyag-hetu*), which is also termed the "generative cause" (*janaka-hetu*) because it is that which truly gives birth to all Buddha-dharmas.

The distinct functions of the provisional and the real—namely, the six perfections, the myriad practices, and the function of initial enlightenment—are called the "conditional cause" (*pratyaya-hetu*);
they are also termed the "revealing cause" (*vyañjaka-hetu*), as they assist the correct cause to bring it into manifestation.

Therefore, the second section explains the subsequent metaphors. This consists of two parts: first, a general clarification; second, a detailed exposition. Regarding the first part, there are two sub-sections: first, the citation and indication; second, the application of the explanation.
Regarding the first [of these], there are four sections, beginning with the metaphor of wood. Within this, the first is the illustrative metaphor, namely, the *āliḷada*.

The term for "shrouding the corpse" is translated as "dragon-tongue" (*nāgajihvā*); in this land [of China] as well, there is a base and filthy wood that serves as a dwelling place for venomous insects.
Regarding the two types of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the lower dharmas within the synthesis: first is the individual synthesis, and subsequently are the four general syntheses.
Second, regarding the metaphor of the fire from below: first, the illustration shows that the fire within this wood arises simultaneously with the wood itself, burning the wood from within.

It is just as original enlightenment (mūla-bodhi) functions together with afflictions, internally perfuming those afflictions; thus, when the two types of original enlightenment are joined with the dharmas below them, there are six.
Therefore, according to their respective order, these are joined with the seven preceding matters. As for the perfuming of defiled dharmas until they reach extinction:
it is like fire within wood until the wood is consumed. As for the flow of receiving perfuming: it is like fire causing the wood to grow and flourish. This is inconceivable.

The deliberation on this is like fire within wood; because its location is unknown, the original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) is obscured. It is like fire hidden in wood that emerges without remainder.

Just as the flame appears when the fire is brought out, so too does defilement manifest according to whether it is present or absent in relation to the twofold union. When defilement resides in enlightenment, it is made manifest; when defilement perishes, enlightenment is concealed.
Third, the analogy of the inferior person has two parts: first, the illustrative analogy. *Bharadvāja* (translated as "Possessing Skill") refers to [the sage] Mahā-bharadvāja.
*Upāya-nāśitāra*, translated as "Lacking Skillful Means. Regarding the five matters known by the foremost person:
first, there are those capable of emerging [from suffering], yet without wood there is no fire; there are those capable of being transformed, yet without birth there is no Buddha.

Second, by using what is appropriate for drilling, one obtains fire; by imparting the teaching according to the faculties and relying on study, one realizes the nature. Third, it refers to the ability to know.

Regarding the wood, one observes the speed with which it catches fire; regarding the root, one examines the suitability of its nature and the sequence of its manifestation—this constitutes the fourth [point], namely, knowing which part of the wood the fire resides in, because this serves as the basis for realizing the emptiness of the five aggregates. The fifth point is knowing the sequence of the fire’s emergence and its accomplishment:
first, one uses a spark to draw forth the momentum, and subsequently, one continues the flame with dry leaves; likewise, when realizing the nature, one first uses...

After the fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) has merged with the essence, its function is then activated through skillful means (*upāya*). As for the second person, who lacks such skillful means, he will ultimately fail to obtain fire;
that is to say, the ordinary and ignorant person, lacking skillful means, seeks erroneously and seeks diversely, and thus never perceives the nature.

The fourth [section], "The Analogy of Burning from Below," consists of two parts: first, the illustrative analogy; second, the application to the three matters. First, the illustrative analogy... [let it be known].
Having abandoned their function of being swift, sharp, and piercing, they become dull objects incapable of harming persons or other things;
that is to say, by the power of the path of remedy (*pratipakṣa-mārga*), their obstructive and defiled functions—which produce moisture and intense activity—are caused to be relinquished.
Because they no longer possess such activity, they cannot obstruct practitioners; thus, on the Path of Application (*prayoga-mārga*), the various seeds are suppressed so that they no longer exist.
For this reason, [the fire] causes the branches, trunk, flowers, and fruits to abandon their distinct characteristics of dullness and become uniformly reduced to ashes;

likewise, by the power of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it causes all obstructive defilements to abandon their various distinct characteristics of aversion and attachment and become uniformly extinguished within the single flavor of the true principle (*tattva*).
This is because the Path of Non-interruption (*ānantaryamārga*) is able to sever all seeds of darkness within the true principle; thus, thirdly, it causes the ashes to return to their source.

Their fundamental identity is established in the ground; through the power of the path of cultivation, the principle realized is brought back to accord with the fundamental mind, such that there is no longer any separate entity.

This is because, via the path of liberation, one abandons habitual tendencies and unifies with the single mind. The same principle should be understood by analogy for the lower dharmas of the two paths of cultivation.

Third, the explanation of the concordant conditions has already been stated; this section consists of two parts: first, the summary reference, and second, the detailed explanation following the summary.

Regarding the second part, there are two sections: first, the general statement, and second, the specific explanation. Within the specific explanation, there are three parts: first, the indication; second, the citation and explanation of the deficiency of conditions;

and third, the gate of the single cause being powerless due to the deficiency of conditions. This means that although the internal fire—the primary cause for burning wood—is present, it lacks the human effort required for its application.

Just as fire can ultimately not be obtained from wood-drills and other conditions, so too sentient beings, though possessing the correct cause of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), cannot ultimately obtain the fruit if they lack the conditions such as the good friend and initial awakening (*ādi-awakening*).
This is the "Gate of the Powerlessness of Lacking Either Cause or Condition.

That is to say, even if one possesses human effort and conditions such as the wood-drill, if the primary cause of fire is lacking within the damp wood, fire can ultimately not be obtained; likewise, although the practitioner possesses [the necessary factors],...

If one practices while lacking the conditions for practice, one will ultimately fail to attain the fruit because of the absence of the power of the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) as the primary cause.
Since this internal permeation of fundamental awakening is never absent, we provisionally posit "no cause" only in contrast to the deficiency of conditions.

This means that even if one were to undergo cultivation and seek the Way through many kalpas, one would ultimately not attain the Path without the power of this primary cause; furthermore, this applies to those of the icchantika class who have severed their roots of goodness for long kalpas.

If the internal reduction of the power of perfuming is not sustained, it is called a deficiency in the primary cause; even if one is able to exert oneself in cultivation, one will ultimately fail to attain Buddhahood, because the mind is entangled in false views and one pursues a perverted course.

When these three causes and conditions are fully present, this is the gate of perfect accomplishment. Through the complete presence of the internal and external perfuming and supporting causes and conditions, the virtues of the causal and resultant fruits are thereby perfected.

Second, the section on the gate of generating understanding through the detailed exposition of the characteristics of downward-orientation already explained. This has two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the sequential explanation based on the general outline.

Regarding the second, there are two parts: first, the general statement; second, the specific indication and explanation. Regarding the second, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the citation and explanation. Regarding the first, the "capable object" (ālambana):
the statement in this treatise regarding "perfuming" (vāsanā) refers to the Buddhas of the Response and Transformation bodies, who are the capable subjects—that is, their inconceivable karma.

The mirror-like arising of the perfuming of mutual conditions and the manifesting function of the perfuming of appearances present all objective realms, constantly and without rest, drawing in and guiding what is appropriate for the faculties.

Regarding the two terms "that which is below" and "the object of perception," the realm of objects of perception extends throughout the three categories of beings. Previously, the responsive and transformational Buddha was the principal transformer;
this realm of sentient beings is the retinue to be transformed. In the treatise, it is stated that the power of external conditions is precisely [this].
Regarding the subject that acts as the perceiver, it is cited here according to the convenience of the text for inclusion within the object of perception;
because it internally perfumes the essence and characteristics of the fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), this is described as the power of external conditions.

Second, concerning the specific [explanation], there is a separate exposition of two parts: first, the heading that assigns the divisions to the fundamental [awakening]; second, the detailed explanation following the gates.
Second, the initial section on discerning conditions has three parts. First, the differentiation between the subject that perceives and the object perceived.

Third, the initial indication of that which possesses discernment—this refers to the meaning of "differentiation," meaning that the functioning of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) manifests various forms before ordinary beings and followers of the Small Vehicle, each being distinct.
This differentiation is the very essence, sustenance, and function of the conditions. Furthermore, the mental activities of those prior to the stages [of the Bodhisattva path] are not...
The distinction of the same name is established based on the objects to be converted; thus, there are two types of objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Regarding the first type of objective condition, the text first poses a question and then provides an explanation, demonstrating the sequence and boundaries of the objective conditions.

This means that from the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) until the attainment of the fruit, [the bodhisattva] acts as a condition for sentient beings throughout the entire process; it is not only upon reaching the final fruit that this occurs.

Regarding the section on the "active subject" (*ālambaka*) followed by the "object" (*ālambana*), first there is the inquiry and then the explanation. The two groups—the erroneously fixed (*mithyā-niyata*) and the indeterminate (*aniyata*)—completely encompass [all beings].

As for the correctly fixed group (*samyak-niyata*), only the three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the Three Virtuous Stages) are taken, as they are subsumed under the equal object-condition (*sama-ālambana*) throughout the ten stages of the *aśaikṣa*.
Regarding the phrase "these persons, etc.," it demonstrates the superior conditions upon which the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) relies, from the initial resolve until its attainment.

The Buddha clarified that regarding the stages and positions traversed during the cultivation of causes—whether through vision or mindfulness and so forth—there are many kinds of differentiated conditions encountered while practicing these causes that serve as transformative catalysts.

For instance, he may manifest as a kinsman, parent, or relative, demonstrating loving-kindness to inspire the aspiration for enlightenment; or he may manifest as a servant, appearing in a lowly position to assist and support the path.

The mind may act as a friend, manifesting as a companion to infuse [the practitioner] with the conduct of incense and rue; or it may act as an enemy, appearing in a threatening and fearful guise to coerce them into entering the Path.
Or it may employ the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to ensure they never regress and to cause them to transcend other classes of beings. Therefore it is said:
"Even through immeasurable activities and conditions, all who see or hear [them] shall obtain benefit. From this point onward, the roots of goodness [are established].
Regarding the distinction between the mature and the immature, "attaining deliverance" (pāra-gata) refers to crossing over birth and death to reach the stage of non-retrogression;

it does not necessarily mean that one must achieve Buddhahood to be called "delivered. From this point downward, there are two pairs concerning the near and the distant, distinguishing cause and effect.

That is to say, within the two conditions of the distant and the near, both are capable of increasing the two stages of cause and effect. Because the practices of the ten stages increase through both the near and the distant, they are categorized as "near."
Because it causes the fruit of Tathāgatahood to grow over a long period, it can only serve as a supporting condition for that [fruit] and not as a specific condition;
this is because those who have already entered the stages and so forth have already entered the subsequent gate.
Second, regarding the two types of non-discriminative objects already explained, first is the summary: "non-discriminative" means the sense of equality.

This refers to the functioning of original enlightenment (mūla-awakening) which accords with the bodhisattvas; it manifests only a single class of the physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) and marks of the Buddhas without distinction, and is therefore called "equality.

Equality is precisely the essence, sustenance, and function of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Furthermore, because this [state] belongs to the stages above the ground (*bhūmi*), it is its domain.
Because they are all equally cultivated through the conditions of profound samādhi-equality, and because they are named according to those conditions upon which they rely.

Second, the general exposition followed by the detailed explanation. First, the general exposition. Third, within the section on the conditions of compassionate vows, first, the citation and reference to the various [vows].

The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all vow to deliver sentient beings; this is the original arousal of the great mind (*bodhicitta*). Through the power of their vows, they impartially permeate [sentient beings] and do not abandon them;
thus, in accordance with their vows, they give rise to conduct characterized by compassion and impartiality.

This refers to the subsequent explanation of how the causal power of the compassionate vows of all Buddhas and Bodhattvas constantly and eternally permeates the bodies of sentient beings at all times and in all places, [thereby nurturing] the goodness obscured by ignorance.

Because the root-faculties (*indriya*) are manifested through their differentiation and are always accompanied by goodness, they are called "not abandoning. Furthermore, because the compassionate vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas never cease, it is called "always not abandoning.

Second, regarding the shared lower true wisdom (*tathatājñāna*), in the first part [of this section], it cites and points to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who, through the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūtajñāna*), perceive that self and others are originally of one essence; by the power of this wisdom, in accordance with...
Because the faculties (*indriya*), manifested signs, and activities all accord with the nature (*dharmatā*), they are called "actual practice" (*satyācaryā*).

Next, the lower [explanation] clarifies the names of the Dharma-body and Reward-body Buddhas as being "responsive transformation" (*nirmāṇa*). When the superior faculties have matured, it is called "responding according to the time"; when it manifests at the place where it is perceived, it is called "appearing according to the location.
Teaching according to the faculties is called "according to suitability" (*yathārha*); acting in accordance with what is appropriate is called "according to the matter" (*yathārtha*).

Causing their aspirations to arise is called "conforming to delight. Such sovereign and unimpeded functions all proceed according to what the practitioner delights in, for there is nothing that does not accord with the principle of *tathatā*.
Regarding the eight types of activity: they manifest the eight signs, such as the descent from the womb and so forth, throughout the realm of birth;
therefore, it is said to be "without remainder. Thirdly, regarding the lower samādhi, its object is the middle [realm].
First, the summary and indication: because one sees the Buddha-dharma-body by relying on samādhi, it is called "contemplating the true dharma of the Buddha.
Next, the explanation and establishment: regarding the phrase "hair between the horns," the "horns" are the vessels that hold the hair, and the "hair" is a metaphor for its extreme abundance.
Although the number of Buddhas appearing in the world is boundless, if one does not cultivate the gate of *śamatha*, by what means could one see them? Therefore, the Bodhisattva...
By the power of samādhi, Śākyamuni beheld that the Buddha’s Dharma-body is equal and without distinction;
if there are sentient beings who perceive it differently, this is merely due to the false perceptions of their own minds, for my own body is fundamentally without differentiation.

Second, having already explained the general [classification], there is now a specific explanation in two parts: first, the summary introduction; second, the explanation of the characteristics, beginning with "How so...

Part one, regarding those who have not yet entered the stage of correct determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), has two sections: first, the presentation of the meaning; "The ten faiths," etc., refers to the forty mental states prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva-citta*).

"And furthermore, the two vehicles" refers to those who have not yet attained [the higher realization]; that is to say, although they have already attained mastery over the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), they have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Because one has not yet entered the realization of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) subsequent to the fundamental emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*), it is as stated below in the main text of the treatise:

regarding those who are perfumed by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it was previously explained that the manas-consciousness perfumes [the seeds] only from the stages of the Bodhisattva onwards;

however, how could there be perfuming by the mind (*manas*) prior to these stages? Furthermore, this meaning of the perfuming of the manas also encompasses three levels: coarse, subtle, and intermediate.
