Narrated by the Great Master Puguang of the Unbounded Majesty of the Imperial Song Dynasty.
The third [section] is the analysis of the characteristics of setting forth upon the path. Part two: first, connecting the preceding with the subsequent.

This refers to the very act of generating the mind and setting out toward the path traversed by all Buddhas. Because cause and effect are distinct, the "characteristics of the path" (mārga-lakṣaṇa) are so named;

yet because the essence and function maintain the identity of the path, "setting forth" is itself the characteristic of the path. Furthermore, since the path and its characteristics are both that which is to be traversed, they are the "setting forth" of the characteristics of the path.
Because the objects and practices differ, their meanings and principles are distinguished and differentiated;

therefore, it is called "discrimination" (*vibhāga*). Part Two: The Commentary on the Text. This has two sections: First, the recitation of the root treatise; second, the explanatory commentary. The latter has two parts: First, the heading that divides the sections; second, the detailed explanation following the headings.

Regarding the first, the general heading for the "Gate of General Exposition," there are three parts: First, the path of conforming to the characteristics of the Buddha's stages; Second, the three periods of time; Third, [the explanation of] the *śloka* verses.
The vows made by all Buddhas are the causes and results of the vows that have been generated; these constitute the path of self-benefit.
The ocean of disciples to be transformed constitutes the path of benefiting others. All Bodhisattvas are those capable of generating and proceeding [upon these paths].

The repetition of the word "like this" (evam) refers to the aforementioned ocean of vows and so forth, which are all entirely in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*); thus, they are practiced and realized through corresponding cultivation.

Furthermore, because the sequence of time, kalpas, numbers, stages, and levels does not exceed its proper order within that [process], and because in the second instance—the path of the Buddhas which transcends signs and is realized by all Buddhas—all things are entirely free from conceptualization, one has no dwelling or attachment toward self-benefit, benefit for others, and so forth.
Because there is no dwelling or attachment, there is no movement toward anything; such is the state of being free from signs.
The Buddhas follow the true path, and all Bodhisattvas emulate the former Buddhas; because they practice within the purity that is free from signs, it is called "setting out" (*prasthāna*).
The three [points] below correspond to the main text of the treatise as in the original.

Second, the section on the detailed explanation of the sub-classifications already mentioned, which consists of two parts: first, the summary reference and exhortation to reflect; second, the analysis of the characteristics according to the gates.
Third, the section on the three types of arousal of the mind, which has two parts: first, the general classification and reference; second, the detailed explanation of the first gate.
First, the gate of the arousal of the mind through the accomplishment of faith, which has three parts: first, the heading and division; second, "The first," etc. [and so forth].

The explanation of the three [sections] consists of: (1) the section on the initial setting forth that opens with questions and provides a general outline; (2) the section on the detailed exposition that displays the answers and explanations;

and (3) the section on initiating questions and answers to resolve doubts. Of these first two sections, they are combined and divided into two parts: first, the two types of sections for the first cycle;
second, within the first "opening question" section, the explanation of the meaning, the synthesis, and the conclusion are to be understood; second, the subsequent "answering and explaining" section.
Regarding the two parts of the introduction, first is the general and specific presentation of the divisions; by means of these six gates, the four preceding questions are answered.

First, the gate of the "provisional" answers the first question concerning the person who practices. Second and third, the gates of "perfuming" and "cultivation" answer the second question concerning that which is practiced.
Fourth and fifth, the gates of "temporal measure" and "causes and conditions" answer the third question concerning the attainment of accomplishment. Sixth... [text continues].
Because the sixth stage provides a superior answer regarding the fourth stage’s characteristics of excellence and progress.

The two terms clarify the characteristics of the subordinate gates of sequential interpretation; first, the individual explanation of the two gates, and second, the general clarification of the remaining meanings.

Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, answering according to the sequence of the questions, and second, the explanation of the gate of the six. Although the gate of the provisional practitioner who manifests practice...
Regarding those beings to be transformed, they are immeasurable; however, those who can now practice are comprised solely of those prior to the stage of the ten faiths.

In the context of the causal conditions previously discussed, this was explained solely based on the stage of the accomplishment of roots of goodness, referring exclusively to the superior grade. Since the present case encompasses both the primary and the secondary, it includes all three grades.
Second, the gate of natural, original perfuming: within the bodies of sentient beings, the originally awakened treasury (primal awakening) is the Buddha as the direct cause of Buddhahood;
because the roots of goodness such as faith constantly perfume from within, they cause [the awakening] to gradually increase.

Third, the section on the gate of manifesting the merits of practice: those who practice the ten stages of faith, through the power of internal permeation, bring forth initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), cease evil, perform good, grow weary of suffering, and rejoice in awakening;
by encountering a Buddha and receiving his personal instruction, the efficacy of their practice becomes increasingly sublime.
Fourth, the section on the time required for the accomplishment of the fourfold faith: first, the heading that poses the inquiry; second, from "First," below, the citation of the sūtra.
The explanation of the three [stages] begins with the citation of fifteen sūtras. Regarding the first part, the citation of the first five sūtras:

the first two both state that the accomplishment of the ten faiths (*śraddhā*) leads one to enter the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), as indicated by the term "proximate" (*upaniṣad*). "Delight" (*preman*) refers precisely to faith;

the "Vajra Stage" (*vajrabhūmi*) refers to the ten abodes themselves, because within the Mahāyāna position, one never regresses and is as firm as a vajra. The subsequent three [sūtras] clarify only the accomplishment.

Because it concerns oneself, the two [phases of] subsequent advancement are not mentioned. Regarding the sixth point, the middle section cites five sūtras, and the seventh explains that the roots of goodness are like parents and heaven and earth;
these metaphors are employed to manifest the merit of faith.

This means that because of faith, one can give rise to all manner of wholesome qualities, just as in the world, based upon parents and heaven and earth, one is able to abandon the state of icchantika, lack of faith, and heterodoxy.

Because one perceives stumps and logs, it is said that the ground of faith is level and free of weeds. Regarding the first moment among the eight [stages], "the perfection of faith," this refers to those of the highest sharp faculties;

that is to say, from the very beginning, when the subtle veils of ignorance are thin and the excellence of original enlightenment (prakṛti-vijñāna) manifests, they immediately achieve accomplishment at the moment of the initial resolve (prathama-cittotpāda).
Alternatively, because the first moment and kalpas are mutually interpenetrating, even though a long time may pass...
At that time, one does not depart from the initial thought, because a single thought-moment is itself immeasurable eons; thus, immeasurable eons do not depart from a single thought-moment.
Among these, the three great immeasurable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) of the nine stages refer to those of the most inferior and dull faculties.

This means that for such individuals, ignorance has been thick and heavy since beginningless time while original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*) has been weak; only after long cultivation and refinement is realization finally accomplished. Alternatively, this may refer to the Esoteric [Vehicle].
It is said that faith encompasses all stages; thus, throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, it is fully established as the thirty-one [stages].

Furthermore, the subsequent five sutras and the eleventh [verse] among them state that "contemplating Sukhāvatī" means that through the perfection of faith, one focuses the mind and contemplates with supreme love and joy upon the Mahāyāna path.
Regarding the thirteenth [verse], "neither distant nor near," etc., it is because through faith, the entire body is entirely the True [Dharma].
Because it is free from various differentiated characteristics, herein the Dharma is briefly shown through ten pairs: first, there is no characteristic of temporal duration such as long or short;
second, there is no characteristic of increase or decrease, or of annihilation or permanence; third, there is no characteristic of distinction between high and low;
fourth, there is no characteristic of cause and effect, or of agent and object; fifth, there is no characteristic of arising, ceasing, or flux; sixth, there is no superior... [and so forth].

10. Because it eliminates various distinct characteristics—such as (7) the inferiority and superiority of the lower [stages], (8) the distinction between kalpas and non-kalpas as well as truth and falsehood, (9) the exclusion of states and stages from descending signs, (10) the nature being neither defiled nor pure, and (11) the fundamental transcendence of gain and loss—it is concluded that this is named "True Faith.
14. Regarding the "Ten Faiths": these ten faiths encompass all dharmas through the faculty of faith.
There is no dharma that is not faith; therefore, the ten faiths encompass all stages, even including all dharmas of the stage of false certainty.
Furthermore, because the essence of this faith is *tathatā* (suchness), it can pervade all stages and all dharmas.
Second, this is the conclusion of the section on the distinctions of names. Among such sutras, there are those that are extremely concise, referring to what is called "a single thought-moment."
There are those who extend for an exceedingly long time, passing through the remainder of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, while others experience durations that are not fixed;

furthermore, there are cases where the duration is not mentioned at all. This is truly because the mental dispositions (*citta-prakāra*) of sentient beings are boundless; therefore, what is taught in the various sūtras differs.
It is also due to this that truth and falsehood mutually support one another: while falsehood varies in its duration—being either extended or brief—truth fundamentally lacks any division of time.
Because such profound principles are the domain of the noble ones (*ārya*), students should carefully examine and discern them. Now, hereafter, the text correctly clarifies what is to be grasped:

namely, the fifteen sūtras cited previously. This treatise, for the time being, relies upon the exposition in the *Ratnavali* (The Jewel Garland) regarding the five gates of revealing the causes and conditions for generating the resolve [for awakening].
First, it indicates the intent and marks the divisions; second, from the words "I exhort" onwards, it relies upon those markers.

The explanation of the three types of exegesis: First, regarding the cause and conditions for the initial request, "the stage of non-fixed ground" refers to the domain where faith is unshakable, which indicates the stage of abiding.

Second, regarding the cause and conditions for deliverance, because sentient beings of the six realms are submerged in the ocean of suffering, one gives rise to fierce compassion with the desire to extract them and enable them to attain peace and happiness. Third, regarding the cause and conditions for protecting the Dharma, it is said that...
Regarding "various skillful means" and so forth: if one does not employ skillful methods and expedients, even with the desire to support [the Dharma], it may instead increase its decline.

Therefore, protecting the Dharma requires that one act in accordance with what is appropriate for the faculties [of beings], ensuring that it is consistent and fitting; that at whatever time or place there is no deficiency or omission;
and that one exerts effort and capability to ensure the long-term endurance of the Dharma. For these reasons, one generates the Great Mind (mahācitta) to rectify and uphold it.

The collapse of the net does not allow for the immediate extinction [of the teaching]; the former represents great compassion benefiting and bringing joy to all classes of beings, while this represents great wisdom maintaining the bequeathed Dharma.

Within the section on the superior gate of the stage of attaining benefits, first there is the heading and inquiry, next the enumeration and demonstration, and finally the synthesis by means of ten points.
Having refined one's faith through a thousand kalpas and attained maturity, one enters the initial stage of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*) of the Mahāyāna;

this is called the "Assembly of Right Certainty" (*samyaktvaniyatarāśi*), wherein one attains the stage of non-retrogression. The ten names possessed therein form five pairs: first, the pair of being free from fear and attaining bliss; second, the pair of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This means that faith serves as the hands and feet while wisdom serves as the lamp; relying on faith to give rise to wisdom is like holding a lamp with one's hands.
Relying on faith, one traverses the realm as if walking along a long road; the three [stages] are like entering the ocean. Regarding "the house" (*gṛha*) in contrast to the "home" (*agāra*):

it carries the sense of continuous succession and inheritance, and thus there are many kinds, namely: the house of the objective realm, the house of practice, the house of the Dharma, the house of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and so forth.
Now, having entered and dwelt in this [house], one perceives the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), enters the Tathāgata’s chamber, dons the Tathāgata’s robe, and walks the path of the Tathāgata.
Because it continues without interruption, it is said that one dwells in the family of the Tathāgata. Fourth, regarding the separation from ordinary beings and the emergence from obstacles;

fifth, regarding the gathering of sentient beings without hindrance: this means that by the power of faith, one gathers others to follow oneself, such that immeasurable humans and devas all respectfully comply;
whatever transformations one performs according to one’s will are sovereign and entirely without obstruction.
Second, the section on generating understanding by citing the inferior to reveal the superior, already explained in two parts: first, the summary reference;
second, the citation of the inferior followed by the detailed explanation. Regarding the first, the section on citing the inferior to reveal the characteristics of inferiority:

when roots of goodness are extremely slight, one cites their inferiority as small seeds of goodness, further revealing their inferiority by stating that because these roots of goodness are inferior, even though they encounter a Buddha and offer worship...

Nevertheless, they still seek the realms of humans and devas in a perverted manner and seek the inferior fruits of the paths of the two vehicles; they have not yet been able to advance toward the sublime practices of the Mahāyāna. This section consists of two parts:

first, the formal explanation of the "gate of manifesting excellence by means of excellence," which refers to those who seek the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna—because their seeking mind is excellent and the Dharma sought is excellent—it is called "manifesting excellence by means of excellence. Second, [the illustrative examples]. Regarding the first: the formal explanation.

Those who seek the profound and wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna possess an excellent seeking mind and seek an excellent Dharma; therefore, it is said that they "manifest excellence by means of excellence. Second, if...

Regarding the first question and subsequent answer within the section on "not falling into obstructive hindrances," there are two meanings: first, looking toward one's own object; second, looking toward the objects of others.

Second, from this point downward, the remaining meanings are explained in general. Third, first, it clarifies that there is no fixed time for faith; second, first, the heading is presented. Second, [the explanation follows].

The so-called "lower explanation" establishes this: excluding the *ratnāvalī* (necklace), among the remaining fourteen [verses], the most distant [time] is three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, while the most near is a single thought-moment;
the extension and contraction in between are as previously cited. Regarding the phrase "according to conditions," when the causes are complete, faith matures without requiring a long duration;
if the causal conditions are lacking, faith will not arise even if many eons pass.

Second, from here below, the explanation of the causes and conditions for generating the mind [of awakening] has two parts: first, the heading and inquiry; second, the enumeration and explanation, which consists of four sections.

First, the cause and condition of seeing the Buddha: By contemplating the wondrous marks [of the Buddha], one knows there is a distinguished cause; yet, because I do not delight in cultivation, how could I possibly attain it?

It is for this reason that, with vigor and courage, one gives rise to the Great Mind. Second, the cause and condition of making offerings to the Saṃgha: This refers to the field of merit providing secret assistance, thereby causing one to generate the Great Mind.
Because it is mental, the three causes and conditions for shame and remorse are narrow and inferior in the Hinayana; since one does not rely on them now, one generates the Great Mind.
Fourth, the causes and conditions are concurrent, meaning that one generates the mind of enlightenment spontaneously based upon the teachings of others.
Third, from here below, the indeterminate characteristics are shown in two parts: first, the general indication; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "By what...
The term "conducive" (śūnyānukūla) means that when one encounters favorable time and place, as well as excellent teachers, friends, and complete requisites, one will not regress;
conversely, to encounter the opposite is "adverse."

Second, having already explained the first [section], there follows the second section on the two types of gates. This has two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the detailed explanation following the statement "Furthermore," which consists of: first, the gate of opening the inquiry;
second, the gate of answering and explaining following the statement "Briefly stated," which consists of: first, citing the number and posing the question;

second, the analytical explanation according to the meaning following the phrase "From this point onward," which consists of: first, the heading; second, the sequential explanation following the statement "The correct..."; third, correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*).

Regarding the gate of skillful means, "direct mind" refers to being free from crookedness; that is, by means of this direct mind, one takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object, and through this skillful means, one gives rise to right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
Regarding the gate of the fulfillment of the two merits, "profound mind" refers to the great vows;
by means of this skillful means, one accumulates the sublime qualities of merit and wisdom. Regarding the gate of the accomplishment of peace and bliss, by...

Because the mind of great compassion uproots the suffering of sentient beings, bestows happiness upon them, and enables them to attain peace and security—this has already been explained in three ways.

Second, the section on the "Gate of Resolving Doubts through Questions and Answers" initiated below: first, the summary of the divisions; second, the explanation of the characteristics according to those divisions.

Within the first part, the "Gate of Questioning regarding Contradictions between Prior and Subsequent," there is first the heading and inquiry, followed by the citation and explanation of the text. Regarding the latter: [The text continues with the specific analysis of the contradictions.]

Since the preceding text states that the dharmakāya of original enlightenment is of a single aspect and non-dual, the subsequent text should simply involve taking the suchness (tathatā) as its object with a direct mind;
it should not further speak of accumulating goodness with a profound mind, for this would later contradict the conclusion of the text.

The second [section], the section on the sequential explanation and resolution of difficulties regarding the subsequent teaching, has two parts: first, the section marking the general and specific gates; second, the section explaining according to the sequence of analogies, which has seven parts.
The third part is the section directly answering and resolving those difficulties, which has three parts: first, the section opening the metaphors; second, the section indicating the presentation;
third, the section explaining the characteristics, which has four parts: first, the analogy of the jewel; second, the analogy of intrinsic purity; third, the analogy of defilement.
The analogy of the four groups of people illustrates the explicit text of the *Mūla-śāstra*, which clarifies only indolence;

however, the Master’s commentary reveals that its meaning also encompasses diligence, as this is shown by implication within the *Mūla-śāstra*. Second, "Having already explained... introduces the section on the correspondence of the explanation. This section has two parts: first, the summary reference;
second, from the "analogy of the two jewels" onwards, the actual correspondence. Within this text there are also four segments, which correspond to the preceding text and are clearly visible.

Third, the section on the teaching of the lower dharmas has already been explained. This section has two parts: first, the summary that exhorts reflection; second, the application and return to the source as in the original text.

Second, the section on the benefits gained by practitioners who cultivate wholesome deeds through the lower teachings: this refers to how, by means of the practitioner’s abandonment of evil and cultivation of goodness, [benefits are attained].
The Dharma accords with true spontaneity, thereby accomplishing the profound samādhi; by the power of this samādhi, one is free from doubt and fear.
Third, the section on the skillful means for practicing the lower [stages] is explained in two parts: first, establishing the four gates; second, explaining the characteristics of their meanings.
Regarding the first gate—the fundamental gate of all practice—it is divided into two sections. First, the classification of the gates; second, the explanation of "pāramitā" (perfection).
The second part, the explanation of the characteristics, has two sections. First, the individual explanation of the meaning and characteristics. Second, the section on the gate of *prajñā* (wisdom).
This means that by means of *prajñā*, one realizes that all phenomena are without arising or ceasing and are originally quiescent; thus, one does not dwell with attachment in birth and death.
This is the entry from the conventional into emptiness, taking the ultimate truth as the object. If one does not realize the true nature of phenomena, one will falsely cling to the mundane world.
Through inversion and delusion, one undergoes various great sufferings of body and mind; now that the truth has been seen and delusion abandoned, one therefore does not dwell in saṃsāra.
This refers to the second gate of great compassion: by means of great compassion, one observes that all phenomena arise through the convergence of conditions and that karmic fruits are never lost;
thus, one likewise does not dwell in nirvāṇa. This is the process of entering the provisional from emptiness, conditioned upon—

If one does not contemplate the conventional truth—that phenomena arise through dependent origination—one becomes attached to the empty stillness of *nirvāṇa* and falls into the deep pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the two vehicles.
Now, observing that karmic fruits do not perish, one gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to gather and transform beings.

"Great" compassion is distinguished from "small" compassion; while ordinary compassion provides only temporary relief and cannot be a true salvation, great compassion provides eternal rescue and never ceases.
Although there is renunciation, there are eight differences as explained in the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*. Regarding the two preceding gates, they mutually support and guide one another:

although one knows that phenomena are empty, by the power of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one does not abandon sentient beings; although one knows that phenomena exist, by the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not dwell in saṃsāra.

When emptiness and existence are unimpeded, taking and abandoning occur spontaneously. This is the contemplation of the Middle Way, for it contemplates conditions in terms of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); thus, there is no [duality].

Abiding in the Path is the root of practice. Second, by following the general indication of causes and conditions through the nature of conformity, the two practices of wisdom and compassion previously cultivated are thereby accomplished.
Regarding the "two gates of subduing evil karma so that it does not arise," each of the three gates below consists of two sections:
the demonstration of the meaning and the conclusion of the connection with the text, which can be understood from the words themselves. Now, within this gate, it refers to relying upon—
Second, the gate of the two dharmas that restrains and halts evil karma so that it does not arise;

third, the gate of producing and increasing roots of goodness, which means diligently cultivating the five practices to increase faith; fourth, the gate of boundless and impartial vows, which means that vows and practice rely upon one another to encompass and produce the attainment of results.
From here below, the section on manifesting excellence begins with a brief indication, followed by [the detailed explanation].
Why is it said that its essence and nature are vast and boundless? Because horizontally they encompass the ten directions.
Why is it said that its characteristics and functions are unimpeded and without beginning or end? Because vertically they penetrate the three periods of time.

This is intended to cause practitioners to accord with the *dharmatā*, so that their aspirations may be vast, their resolve profound, and their activities—refining their conduct and delivering sentient beings—be inexhaustible throughout the ten directions and across the three periods of time.

Because [the previous section] has been exhausted, the fourth section explains the gate of manifesting the merits of generating the bodhicitta. This means that a Bodhisattva abiding in the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-avasthā*), relying on this contemplative mind, partially perceives the *dharmakāya* of True Suchness (*tathatā*);
relying on their vows, they initiate practice and are able to manifest the eight phases of enlightenment.
For the sake of benefiting the multitude.

Fifth, having already explained the selection of the lower [stages], there follows the manifestation of the distinct gates between the upper and lower, which has two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the statement that selects the lower, followed by the explanation establishing it.

Within the first part—the gate of selecting what differs from the stages above—there are two: first, the heading that marks the selection; second, the subsequent explanation establishing it through its subtlety.

Because the suffering of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) flows continuously through conceptualization, this section distinguishes [the Bodhisattva] from those still bound by fetters (*sambandhana*).

Although a Bodhisattva at this stage carries the karmic fruits of beginningless outflows (*āsrava*), because they lack the karma that binds one to causal retribution, they do not experience it as fixed.
Rather, through the power of great vows and skillful means, they take birth with sovereign mastery, free from fixed limits and without the burden of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).

Included within the bonds of karma. Regarding the six [points], the first has already been explained. This is the section on the definitive resolution according to the scriptural texts (*sūtra*). It consists of three parts: first, the summary and the indication of the topic;

second, "First," the citation of the scripture followed by its explanation; and fifth, the *Mañjuśrī-sūtra*, which first cites the text and subsequently demonstrates its meaning. The remainder follows.

These four sūtras all contain these twenty stages (*bhūmi*). Because the Bodhisattva personally realizes *tathatā* (suchness) and never regresses, they are called the "stages of certainty" (*niyata-bhāga*).

Although the preceding forty minds—faith, understanding, practice, and orientation—have already achieved mastery over the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), because one has not yet attained the correct wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), one cannot exercise mastery over the various dhyānas, such as the bliss of the present life (*dr̥ṣṭa-dharma-sukha*), and so forth.
Because it manifests through the power of fortune, it is called the "regressive portion" (*hānabhāgīya*).

In the *Dvibodha-mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, all four stages are termed the "regressive portion" because, at the very beginning of each of these four positions, one is able to regress from and relinquish the obstacles of the preceding stage. Thus, the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) is the "indeterminate group" (*aniyata-rāśi*), as it can initially regress from the obstacle of the *icchantika* who are fixed in error.

The initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) marks the first entry into the stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*), where it can initially regress from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Now, because the obstacle of "clinging to a self" (ātmagrāha) exists, as soon as the pure mind enters the initial stage of the noble state (*ārya*), one is able to eliminate the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) within the three realms;
likewise, at the stage of the "vajra-mind," at the initial entry into the fruition, one is able to eliminate the subtle obstacles of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).
Thus, these names are all designated based on what is eliminated. Furthermore, these four stages cannot arise spontaneously from beginningless time without being [overcome] by the four...

Because they are subject to regression due to hindrances, and because these four minds are initially the most inferior in their mode of activity according to their respective stages, they regress and abandon the initially inferior dharmas as one gives rise to the vast, perfect, and boundless superior dharmas of subsequent stages;

since they are abandoned at each successive stage, they are called "stage-regressions" (*khaṇḍa-vivarta*). Those states in between are called "non-regressions," which refers to the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) and the subsequent dwellings.

The three stages prior to the abiding in the subsequent ground—namely, after the pure mind (*śuddhacitta*) and before the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*)—are called "non-retrogression" (*avaivartika*).

This is because, in each of these initial stages, one remedies the obstacle of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya-āvaraṇa*), the mode of activity (*ākāra*) is particularly sublime, and one has not yet immediately fallen back or abandoned [the path].

In reality, there is also the sense of retrogression during the intermediate stages; however, because the signs of retrogression are obscured by the maintenance of the initial resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*), they are not mentioned.

The meaning of "abiding in peace through the realization of the three great [aspects]" refers to the fact that within this mind, one perceives the Dharmakāya and never again deviates from or loses the Mahāyāna stage.

The *Sūtra on the Clarification of the Fourth and Fifth [Dharmas]* states that there is neither regression nor progression, because the fruition is perfectly accomplished and thus lacks increase or decrease;

there is neither coming nor going, because its nature is eternally abiding and thus lacks arising or ceasing; and there is neither exiting nor entering, because its quiescent function is without [limit].

Because there is no fixed distinction between obstruction, dispersion, and concentration—meaning one is free from the characteristics of exiting concentration and entering dispersion—the *Ten Abodes Sutra* speaks of the fulfillment of the fruit within the stage of the ten abodes.
This is because, by seeing the Dharmakāya, there is nothing lacking; because a single stage is all stages; because one knows that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind;
and because the primordially endowed wisdom-body is not something realized through another. The *Five Adornments Sutra* refers to this as the seventh [stage].

Only when the mind abides is it called "non-retrogression," for one has then attained the stage of non-retrogression within the Mahāyāna and will never again fall back into the stages of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

Because the preceding states of mind had not yet reached a fixed position, they were termed "parts subject to retrogression. Now, in this section below, the meaning is reconciled with the original treatise;

according to the intention of the *Śrīgarbha-sūtra* (or *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*), those who have entered the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) of a bodhisattva are said to have "perfected their faith" (*śraddhā-sampanna*).
Regarding the statement that there is regression from the stages of abiding as explained in the sūtras upon generating the mind of enlightenment:
this was taught to protect beginners with weak faculties by instilling fear and awe, thereby causing them to become courageous.

Seventh, the section on praising the difficulty of generating the mind of enlightenment, which is explained last; first, the specific manifestation of its characteristics, followed by the generation of fear.
"Fear" refers to the arising of dread regarding the inferior paths of the two vehicles; "arising of fear above" refers to the arising of dread regarding the sublime realm of the bodhisattvas.

Since one is now able to remain far removed from these two fears during the stage of generating the mind through the perfection of faith, [the text] concludes the causal conditions with the second point: by knowing that all phenomena are originally quiescent.
Because they are extinguished, one is freed from the various delusive fears.

Third, regarding the sequence from above to below: having already explained the "Gate of Accomplishing Faith" by means of the initial binding of the fingers, what follows below provides a brief indication without further detailed explanation of the remaining gates.
Now, presenting a general outline according to this fundamental treatise, there are two gates.
The first section clarifies the two types of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*). This consists of two parts:

(1) the gate of clarifying the generation of the resolve through practice based on understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), and (2) the gate of clarifying the generation of the resolve through realization (*praveśa-bhūmi*). Within the former gate, there are again two sections:

(1) the gate of praising the excellence of the general presentation of practice based on understanding, and (2) the gate of praising the excellence of specifically following the Dharma at the appropriate time. Regarding the first gate, it asks: "What is meant by 'precisely by means of this practice based on understanding'?"

Having generated the aspiration and looked toward the preceding stage of the fulfillment of faith and entry into understanding, one now, within this stage, fulfills practice and enters toward the deeper generation of the aspiration;
therefore, it is said: "One should know that it becomes increasingly superior. Next, there are two gates:

first, the gate of manifesting superiority by citing the time [of its commencement], which refers to these bodhisattvas from the initial stage of right faith—that is, the stage of the accomplishment of faith—up to the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*), meaning from the fulfillment of faith.
Because one has arrived here, the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is about to be completed;

that is, at the moment immediately following the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), all these stages up to this point are called the "first resolve through practice" (*adhimukti-caryā-pratipatti-citta*). Since this is adjacent to the first stage (*bhūmi*), it is said to be "about to be completed.

Second, regarding the section on "Manifesting Excellence by Citing the Dharma Below Reality," there are two parts: first, the general, and second, the specific. Within the general section, concerning "Reality":

The manifestation of a profound understanding in accordance with the Dharma refers to the excellence of understanding; being free from signs in what is cultivated refers to the excellence of practice.

Within each of the six perfections, both of these are present. Knowing that the nature [of the mind] is non-attachment refers to the excellence of understanding; practicing in accordance with the perfection of generosity refers to the excellence of practice.
The remaining perfections should be understood as following this same pattern.

The second section, the gate of realizing the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), contains three parts: first, the gate of the causes and conditions for arousing the mind; second, the gate of the characteristics of the arousal of the mind;
and third, the gate of the fruits and rewards of the arousal of the mind. In the first gate, there are again three sub-sections. First is the gate of indicating the stages (*bhūmi*).

From the Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddhacitta-bhūmi*) to the Ultimate Stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*), by citing the beginning and the end while skipping over the intermediate ones, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are subsumed. Second... [text continues].
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one realizes the extent of the stages traversed from the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

Second, regarding the gate of determining the object and wisdom below: when the fundamental wisdom (*maulajñāna*) realizes *tathatā*, the mind and its objects merge in profound stillness, becoming equal and of a single flavor;
thus, it is impossible to clarify any distinction between the mind and its objects. What is being discussed here, however, is the realization of the object.

Those who resolve their minds based on the *dhātu* (element/realm) make this statement by relying on the subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) that arises simultaneously with the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).

When this wisdom reflects back upon the principle previously realized—which pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* and serves as the actual nature (*bhūta-svabhāva*) of all phenomena—one is able to obtain hundreds of gateways of clarity and various merits.
Because of this, immeasurable joy and bliss arise; such is the object [of this realization].

The arousal of the aspiration within the realm (*dhātu*) that accords with its nature, which is a vast ocean of vows, and which at the appropriate time and place honors the Buddhas and engages with sentient beings, is called the "vow-attaining" arousal of the mind.

Question: Since the two types of subtle consciousness and mental activity have not yet been differentiated, how can it be said that they function simultaneously during the state of post-meditative attainment (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)? Answer:

Although it is said that [the wisdom] functions simultaneously with [the consciousness], because it is extremely subtle, they cannot be distinguished. Even though the specific objects of the sovereign [wisdom] and the distinct wisdoms differ, the wisdom is also consciousness; it is consciousness.

It is also wisdom. Therefore, one should know that the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) possesses no distinct characteristics of subject and object.

Furthermore, since the evolving consciousnesses—the seven evolving consciousnesses—are the consciousnesses that differentiate phenomena, once subject and object are distinguished, the subsequently attained wisdom arises simultaneously with them.

As this subsequently attained wisdom is subsumed under "initial awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*), how could it arise in conjunction with defiled consciousness? Nevertheless, it is formed through the influence of pure perfuming.
Regarding the qualities (*guṇa*), there is no loss in explaining their simultaneous arising.
Third, "This is the Bodhi... is the section revealing the superior function (*viśiṣṭakārya*). Fourth, within the initial "Compendium of Dharmas" (*dharmasaṃgraha*), there are two parts:

first, the actual explanation of the request for the Dharma; second, "Only for... which reveals the intent of the request. Second, "Alternatively, showing... concerns the extension or abbreviation according to the faculties (*indriya*). Among these...

Third, the first [section] is brief while the second is extended; both first present the application and subsequently reveal the underlying intent. The latter [section] can demonstrate the conclusion of these three.

As for "In reality... and below, the actual practice is not different. Within this, there are four equalities: first, equality of cause; second, equality of practice; third, equality of realization; and fourth, equality of time. Fourth, "But according to...
refers to the differentiation of practices according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Secondly, regarding the gate of the modes of activity for generating the resolve [for enlightenment] below, there are three kinds of mind: first, the true mind, which is far removed from false and delusive discriminative views;
that is to say, it is great wisdom (*mahājñāna*). Second, the mind of skillful means, which universally cultivates merit and wisdom to benefit all sentient beings;

that is to say, it is the great vow (*mahāpraṇidhāna*). Third, the mind of karmic consciousness, which relies upon the subtle karmic consciousness born of the mental faculty to give rise to the superior mind.

Therefore, it is said that this very great compassion manifests that the bodhisattva still possesses the burden of subtle arising and ceasing, which differs from the purely pure merit of the stage of fruition.

Third, within the section on the retribution of the initial arousal of the mind, there are two parts; first, the general overview, which has two sub-sections; first, the cause-stage reaching its ultimate limit.

Next, regarding the manifestation of the fruits and virtues below the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*): when a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) is about to achieve perfect enlightenment, they receive a great office (*mahā-adhikāra*) in that celestial realm.
The world they manifest is peerless, and their name is called "Supremely Great. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"Because of the benefit of present retribution, one receives the rank of Buddha; because of the benefit of subsequent retribution, one is born in the abode of the wisdom of Maheśvara."

The second refers to the two [aspects] within the intermediate section of the latter part. First, it clarifies the practice for one's own benefit: "instantaneous correspondence" (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta*) refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).

This means that through initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*), one approximates fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); being closest to the fruit, it is called "corresponding wisdom" (*samprayukta-prajñā*).

At this point, ignorance is suddenly exhausted, which constitutes the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Fundamental ignorance, along with its independent and karmic aspects, is entirely severed and exhausted, thereby manifesting and illuminating all phenomena.

Therefore, it is named "All-Knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*). Next, following the natural [sequence], the section on revealing the virtue of benefiting others begins; this concludes the gate of clarifying the two kinds of arousal of the mind.
Second, the explanation of the gate of the two layers of question and answer has two parts. First, within the gate of initiating questions and answering to resolve doubts, there are two sections.
First, the opening of the gate of questioning, which takes up the previously mentioned All-Knowledge as the subject of inquiry. First, the doubt is set forth: it is said that there is empty space.
Wherever there is a location, there is a world; wherever there is a world, there are sentient beings; and wherever there are sentient beings, there is mental activity.
Such boundaries of these realms are difficult to know. Next, the section beginning with "If there were none" formally sets forth the objection:

not only is it difficult to know the boundaries of external objects because they are infinite, but furthermore, if one exhausts all internal mental conceptions, how can [the object] be apprehended? Next, the response says:
The answer provided below within the section on the Śramaṇa school consists of three gates. First is the gate of establishing the principle as the correct response:

it is solely because one has internally exhausted the mind of false conceptualization that one can externally and extensively know objects; though objects are boundless, they do not transcend the single mind.

Since one has realized the source of the mind, what is there that is not understood? The realm of true mind is free from forgetfulness; therefore, only by exhausting all conceptual thoughts can one finally come to know it. Second...
In the section on "The Gate of Revealing Loss by Citing the Multitude of Inferior [Views]," first it clarifies that the realm of deluded vision is limited;

next, with the phrase "by means of delusion," it explains the reason for not seeing, thereby clarifying that because there is deluded vision, there is something that is not seen. Third, in the section on "The Gate of Manifesting Attainment by Citing the Buddhas," it says:
"Being free from the marks of vision, there is nothing that is not pervasive. This means that because there is no deluded vision, there is nothing that is not seen.

Regarding the phrase "not seeing the truth of the mind" and so forth: the Buddha-mind is free from delusion; its essence is the one mind, which fundamentally lacks any distinction between original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) and subsequent awakening (*anubodhi*), and is therefore called "true reality.
However, because this original awakening serves as the substance of deluded phenomena within the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*), it is said to be the nature of all dharmas.
All deluded phenomena are thus the manifestations of the Buddha-mind, the original awakening; since these manifestations have appeared...
Since its own essence illuminates its own characteristics with its very substance, how could it be difficult to understand them such that they remain unknown?

Therefore, it is said that "the essence illuminates and manifests," and so forth. In the preceding section, the functions of the Buddha’s recompense and transformation bodies were analyzed as being within the minds of sentient beings;
now, the delusive phenomena of sentient beings are analyzed as being upon the Buddha-mind. This is because the source of the mind is non-dual.
Therefore, this is so because, by means of the power of the wisdom of the same essence (*samatā-jñāna*), one gives rise to superior skillful means (*upāya*) to gather and transform sentient beings;
thus it is said that "there is great wisdom," and so forth.

Second, regarding the section beginning with "Again, he asked": this is a question-and-answer exchange arising from the preceding discussion. First, the opening of the inquiry: this refers to following immediately upon what was stated before.
Spontaneously, through inconceivable activity, he poses this question. First, he states his doubt; next, from "How so? onwards, he formally sets forth his objection.
Second, from "He replied" onwards, is the answer and explanation. Within this, the textual structure of the dharma, the metaphor, and the application is clear and understandable.

The Seventh Treatise concludes. Part Three: The Section on Cultivating Faith. This has two parts: first, summarizing the section and delineating its divisions; second, the actual cultivation [of faith], which is explained sequentially below. Part Seven:

First, the Gate of the Correspondence between the Remedy and that Which is to be Remedied. This has two parts: first, citing the heading and raising the inquiry; second, proclaiming the root text and providing the explanation.
II. First, the initial recitation of the root text; second, the citation and explanation. II.A. First, the classification of the subject and object. Within this: first, a general indication;

next, "the objects to be converted" and below, a specific pointing out. In the previous section on causes and conditions, it was taught only for the middle grade of those to be converted, as it is revealed from the perspective of the primary [path].
II.B. Second, the determination of what accords with reality. Within this: first, the heading and inquiry; second, "those who desire" and below, the detailed explanation. Within this: first, faith.
The practice of the two groups [of the wrongly fixed and the indeterminate] is distinguished; this section fully explains the four faiths and five practices.

It causes those in the wrongly fixed group to cultivate the four faiths and those in the indeterminate group to cultivate the five practices. This is because the two groups differ by nature in their lack of faith and non-cultivation.
Furthermore, in the second instance, the lower stage of faith-practice benefits both groups, as both types of persons universally cultivate the nine dharmas.

Second, having already explained the categories and divisions of the "Chapter on Inferior Faith," there are two parts: first, the section summarizing the reference (or alternatively, the section of analysis);

second, the section of the formal exposition. First, the formal recitation of the root text; second, the commentary upon it. First, the heading indicating the divisions; second, the direct explanation following [the headings].
Third, first, the direct inquiry into the categories of the "Chapter on Faith"; second, the direct inquiry into the categories of "Practice"; third, regarding the subsequent...
A Brief Response Displaying the Gateway of Faith, Part Two: 1. Initial Division of Categories; 2. Explanation of the Characteristics, Part Two:
A. General Response; B. General Inquiry; C. Extensive Response, Part Two: 1. Presentation of the Divisions; 2. Sequential Explanation, Part Four: First:
The Gateway of Faith as the Foundation that Renders the Mind Equanimous. This refers to faith in *tathatā* (suchness) as the root of all dharmas; it is the foundation...
The name "faith" is established based on its object, and it is also for this reason that faith is the most supreme among all [mental states], as it gives rise to the others;

thus, faith is the root. These names are established according to their functions. All mental states—namely, the karmic consciousnesses and so forth—arise through the power of ignorance and thus manifest such distinctions.
Now, they are all brought together and unified into a single flavor, the undifferentiated True Suchness (tathatā).

From the perspective of principle, there are three types of faith: first, the gate of rejoicing in the Buddha’s meritorious qualities, which means believing in the Great Awakened One and joyfully seeking all the immeasurable, supreme merits of the state of fruition;

second, the gate of faith in the Dharma and diligent cultivation, for the Dharma has four aspects—teaching, principle, practice, and fruition—and because the Buddha exists by relying upon the Dharma, all Tathāgatas together revere it as their father, mother, teacher, and elder, as vast as space.
Because the nature of the vajra is eternally firm, it cannot be destroyed, nor can it arise or cease; for this reason, it is called the "Immovable Rule.
Such a rule brings great benefit that transcends the reach of mind and speech, and is therefore termed "Supreme.

To practice the various perfections (pāramitās) in accordance with all times and places, thereby assisting in the accomplishment of the path to enlightenment, one must have faith and apply oneself to the Dharma; these are the four types of faith in which one abides.

The Sangha instructs the mind in the gate of non-contention. Because one admires virtue and relies on a person to seek the Dharma, once the Dharma has been heard, one must certainly study it so that the mind may be harmonious and free from discord or strife.

Third, having already explained the two gates of skillful means for the lower stages of practice: first, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent; second, citing the root text and providing an explanation.

Regarding the second [citing the root text and providing an explanation]: first, citing the root text; second, providing the explanation. Regarding the second [providing the explanation]: first, indicating the divisions;

second, explaining the characteristics in detail. Fifth: first, a general indication that answers the previously asked questions; second, thoroughly penetrating the questions stated in the general inquiry; third, a brief answer establishing [the response].

Regarding the establishment of the number of gates and the sequence of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*): it is because each preceding one induces each subsequent one, and each subsequent one maintains and purifies each preceding one;
furthermore, they follow a sequence in which the preceding is coarse and the succeeding is subtle, and where the former is easier and the latter more difficult to practice.

Now, by combining the final two into a single category, they are called the "five practices" (*pañca-caryā*). Those treatises that expand them [into six] do so based on the distinction between the essence and function of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the specific obstacles to be remedied.

Because the fruits induced by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and their respective benefits differ, this treatise combines them; for when they mutually assist and stimulate one another, their functional power is superior, and when concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are practiced in tandem, all hindrances are abandoned.
The fourth section, the "Gate of Brief Questions and Extensive Answers with Dispersed Explanations," has two parts: first, the general and specific classification; second, the sequential explanation.

Regarding the first [the Gate of Giving], there are two parts: first, the gate of brief questions; second, the gate of extensive answers. Regarding the second [the gate of extensive answers], there are three parts: first, the heading and division;

second, the explanation of the characteristics, beginning with the words "As for material wealth..."; third, the actual explanation of material giving, which itself has two parts. Regarding the first of these [the actual explanation], there are further two parts. First...
Being able to give with a mind free from stinginess is based on those of superior faculties; therefore, it is said that they "give everything.

Since the root treatise generally encompasses those of middling and inferior faculties as well, it states instead that one gives "according to one's power. Second, regarding the distinctions among the objects given by those of inferior faculties, there are two parts: first, a general indication of the two categories;

second, a specific explanation of the two characteristics within the category of internal objects. Regarding the first, the giving of internal material things—that is, the consciousness—is as follows:
When the mind and intellect are made to serve others, devising strategies and schemes solely for the sake of another’s affairs, one no longer applies the mind and intellect with full concentration;
because they have become subordinate, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "While solid food may be given as a gift, other foods that are not material cannot be transferred.
Why, then, is the formless also given here? The answer is: that [text] was addressing a situation where the seeker's hunger and deprivation were truly extreme.
First, giving face-to-face, one speaks only of material food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) and other such things, as there is nothing else with which to bestow;

this is explained clearly in the text. Second, regarding external material wealth, it is as stated in the root text. Regarding the two types of giving: first, giving according to what is appropriate, which means removing their suffering and distress and causing them to attain security—this is the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*).
Third, the gift of the Dharma (*dharma-dāna*), which means teaching the Dharma for them to sever their doubts.
Because it removes affliction, increases wisdom, destroys evil, and causes one to proceed toward the fruit.

Second, the section on the gates of morality (*śīla-mukha*). This has two parts: first, the summary index and the division of sections; second, the explanation according to the gates. This has four parts. First, establishing the characteristics of morality and the gate that sets forth the fundamental tenet:
this means using the ten wholesome paths of action to prevent and prohibit killing and so forth, thereby ensuring they do not recur. Second, the accomplishment of the categories of morality.
The gateway of the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) is to dwell in seclusion, free from clamor, so as to fully attain the precepts;

the gateway of not disparaging the three types of complete precepts is that one must certainly respect and cherish the various articles of the monastic code (*śikṣāpada*) established by the Buddha and practice them.

The gateway of guarding the four [precepts] so as not to incur slander is that by guarding what is established by the Buddha, one fulfills one's own benefit, and by avoiding worldly reproach, one fulfills the benefit of others.

Regarding the first four gates, the first corresponds to the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint); the second corresponds to the *kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precept of gathering wholesome dharmas);

and the last corresponds to the *sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla* (precept of benefiting sentient beings). Furthermore, the first three gates are all subsumed under *saṃvara-śīla*: the first clarifies the characteristics of the precepts, the second concerns the conditions for upholding them, and the third concerns the mind that guards them.
As for the *kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*, since it is not separate from the two accumulations (*saṃbhāra*), it is omitted here.
The Three Gates of Patience, Part Two: First, the summary of the headings; second, the explanation according to the gates. First, the Gate of Briefly Patience and Subduing the Self:
The meaning of this gate corresponds to the patience of enduring injury and harm. Because one sees adverse conditions and subdues the mind so as not to retaliate, it is called "subduing the self.
Second, the Gate of Extensive Patience and Non-self: This gate possesses both the patience of accepting suffering and the patience of discerning the truth (*dharmānupaśyanā-kṣānti*).

The patience of examining phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā-kṣānti*) arises from contemplating the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Seeing neither self nor person, one does not rejoice upon encountering pleasure nor feel sorrow when meeting suffering;

thus, within the eight kinds of phenomena—both adverse and favorable—one examines them with discernment and accepts them calmly, so that the mind remains unshaken. Therefore, it is said: "Lack of self. To have wealth and honors that benefit oneself is called "gain" (*lābha*);

to suffer loss, depletion, or insult is called "decline" (*alābha*); to be surpassed or slandered is called "disparagement" (*nindā*); and to surpass others in virtue or reputation is called "praise" (*praśaṃsā*).

To "exclaim" (*taṇhā*) means to praise based on actual virtues; to "extol" (*vaṇṇa*) means to laud based on actual merits; to "discourse" (*vāda*) means to criticize; to "afflict" (*upaghāta*) by invading the physical form is called "suffering" (*dukkha*);
and for the mind to be at ease and joyful is called "pleasure" (*sukha*). Because these do not stop at eight, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is added.
IV. Entering the Gate (2): First, the Section on Binding the Fingers; Second, the Explanation According to the Gates (2). First, a General Demonstration of the Gate of Diligence (*vīrya*).
In treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, it is taught that there are five types of diligence, which are subsumed under five modes of practice:
(1) Armor-like Diligence (*saṃnāha-vīrya*), which refers to donning the armor before seeking to defeat powerful enemies—this is the cultivation of the initial generation of the bodhicitta.
1) Because of applying effort with great vigor through the diligence of application (*prayoga-vīrya*), one practices for a long duration;
2) because of increasing one's courage and sharpness through the diligence of non-depression (*anavalīna-vīrya*), one does not disparage oneself or allow oneself to become low-spirited;

3) because of practicing without interruption through the diligence of non-retrogression (*avivarta-vīrya*), one is able to accomplish what is wholesome and does not yield even when encountering suffering; 4) because of practicing with earnest intensity through the diligence of non-contentment (*atṛpta-vīrya*), one remains firm.
Because one firmly delights in cultivating the profound and supreme fruit and does not give rise to complacency through minor virtues, there is no cultivation that is incomplete;

thus, the present treatise encompasses the aforementioned five types. Regarding all virtuous activities—namely, donning the armor, generating the resolve, cultivating virtue, anticipating the encounter with Māra and enemies, and donning the mail—because the mind does not slacken or retreat, it simultaneously demonstrates both the absence of regression and the absence of indolence in application (*prayoga*).
Thus, because his actions are unhurried, he does not abandon his tasks when they recede; because of his application (*prayoga*), he does not slacken in what he undertakes;

and because there is no regression, he does not forsake his work. He is firm in his resolve, meaning that his aspiration is steadfast and his character is robust, for he is never satiated in benefiting himself and others.
He is free from cowardice, meaning that he possesses no inferiority complex.

Because one understands the vast and profound, inclines toward the sublime and great, and is free from all inferior and narrow-mindedness. Second, the detailed explanation of the gate of diligence (*vīrya*).

First, the classification of the gates; second, the explanation of their characteristics. First, the gate of being without obstacles: this means that by being able to exhort oneself to diligence, one fulfills both self-benefit and benefit for others;
thus, when cultivating the causes and adorning the fruits, they are easily accomplished. Second, the gate of having obstacles: this refers to the influence of past karma which drives one's conduct.
Because progress is difficult, skillful means are shown to cause them to leave behind hindrances; this is for the sake of beginners of inferior capacity.

Fifth, the gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Part One: Summary and Sectioning. Part Two: Explanation of the Characteristics according to the Gates. Fourth: General Indication and General Explanation.
Regarding the gate of the wheel of *śamatha*, which abides in a single state of tranquil nature: "gathering the mind" means to collect it within a single flavor (*ekarasa*).
Because the tranquil nature of *tathatā* (suchness) does not allow one to emerge toward other objective marks, it is designated as "stopping" (*śamatha*).
*Tha* means "master" and *artha* means "companion. Stopping and concentration are the master, while insight is the companion; they rely upon each other.

*Śamatha* is translated as "stopping" (*zhi*), because concentration also possesses the function of observation. Therefore, it is further called "observation" (*vipaśyanā*) in meaning. These two constitute the general designation.

The explanation of the gate of contemplating the wheel (*cakravibhāga*) means that one observes the arising and ceasing of dependent origination and thereby penetrates and fully knows the characteristics of all phenomena.

This refers to the aforementioned reversal where insight (*vipaśyanā*)—translated here as "contemplation" (*guan*)—takes wisdom as its primary factor and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its companion, functioning through mutual support.
Third, the brief explanation of the gate of conforming to decisive discernment (*viniścaya-anuloma*) means that the two factors of concentration and wisdom proceed in equal measure.

Calm abiding (*śamatha*) can still the discursive thoughts, while insight (*vipaśyanā*) can give rise to wisdom. Because of the stilling of thoughts, the winds of distraction cannot cause it to waver;

because of the arising of wisdom, who could obscure the stains of ignorance? Since these two mutually accord with one another, it is said that they are "endowed with" and "not separated from" [each other].
Thus concludes the first section: the detailed explanation and determination of the gateway to the wheel of calm abiding. Part Two: The Classification of Categories.

Second, the explanation of the characteristics according to the subsequent section, which has three parts: first, the enumeration of the number of conditions; second, the demonstration of the characteristics of the conditions, beginning with "As for abiding...

and so forth; and third, [the conclusion]. Within the first part, there are fifteen sections. Regarding the first, "a secluded place" (*śūnyāgāra*): "secluded" (*śūnya*) means being free from all clamor and bustle; "secluded" (*agāra*) means ceasing all worldly affairs.
Although one may be fully endowed with internal causes, one must also have an external environment that is empty and quiet; the noise and confusion of the marketplace must not disturb one’s *dhyāna*.
There are three conditions for easily giving rise to stillness in a quiet place, and four types of quiet places.
As for the three: first, deep mountains, rocky gorges, and perilous ravines where human tracks are forever severed; where praise and blame do not reach and profit and fame are kept at a distance;

where one concentrates the mind on the Way and maintains one’s resolve to cultivate dhyāna—this place is considered supreme. Second, secluded and silent places within a few li of a city where social interactions are rare; these serve to refine away hindrances.

To settle the mind in this place is the next [level]; for the third, the *saṃgha* supervisor dwells alone in a single room, unmixed with other affairs, sitting cross-legged in right mindfulness—this place is the lowest.
This is based on the places where an ordained bodhisattva cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).

As for those who are householders, they eliminate greed and anger within and cut off forms and sounds without; thus, wherever they may be, it is difficult to strictly fixate upon a specific location due to the constraints of their worldly duties. Fourth:
First, the condition of livelihood through commerce: one becomes entangled in every encounter, discarding the little for the much and replacing the old with the new;

since the body itself is already unstable, how can one attain peaceful meditation? Second, the condition of social affairs: attending to congratulations and condolences, auspicious and inauspicious events, and welcoming or seeing off guests wastes one's undertakings and squanders one's efforts.
If even worldly duties hinder one, how could one establish oneself in the Way? Third, the condition of technical skills...

Medicine, divination, archery, charioteering, lute-playing, chess, painting, pharmacology, incantations, and technical crafts—though these are called worldly talents, they are in truth excrescences upon the Holy Path.
Furthermore, the pursuit of the four branches of learning involves reading, reciting, and debating the sutras and treatises;

this exhausts one's strength and tires the mind, obstructing dhyāna and wasting the Way. Therefore, the Perfect Man rests his thoughts, the Accomplished Scholar maintains his simplicity, and the Gentleman...
Seal your speech; though the Śrāvaka’s knowledge of cessation and inferior paths still rely upon tranquil, profound dhyāna, how could they be mixed with clamor?
It is like when the wind is stilled and the waves are clear, and the stars and moon shine forth brilliantly.

Take for example Devadatta: although he recited sixty thousand sūtras, he could not escape his retribution in hell. This was because although his mouth recited the scriptures, his mind constantly deviated from the Way. If one can [truly practice...]
It is not prohibited that the teaching which illuminates the mind serves as a model for meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Regarding the second point:

it is permitted for a beginner practicing meditation to dwell together with teachers and friends; however, once their practice has been refined, this is generally not allowed, though in small measure it does no harm. Now, based on those of superior capacity, they remain entirely alone. Regarding the third point:
the rising of the sun in the east symbolizes the numinous clarity of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-āmalā-tathatā*), while the setting of the light in the west symbolizes its disappearance.

Just as the darkness of ignorance must now be dispelled so that the practitioner may contemplate the truth to remedy delusion, it is said that the southern region is extremely hot with many mosquitoes and fleas, while the northern region is bitterly cold with frequent wind and snow;

thus, it is difficult to cultivate concentration (*samādhi*) when increasing discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*). According to ancient teachings, *vitarka* and *vicāra* are termed "awakening" (*vitakka*) and "observation" (*vicāra*); because they are restless and unstable, they are likened to a wheel.
Regarding the four types [of food], the *vīṇā* insect is not well understood. Among the five, *gaṇḍakamodaka* is translated as "composite," referring to steamed or pasted foods;
*pānīra* is translated as "dispersed," referring to soups and stews.

Those possessing a nature like that of a *ṛṣi* can support meditative concentration (*samādhi*), just as ginseng, astragalus, and *śuāngzhì* (aconite) aid in stabilizing the will, while garlic and leeks increase anger.
If such things as these, though called "insentient," can cause the mental consciousness to experience fluctuating joy and anger and receive food at specific times—
since those who eat beyond the midday hour have no fixed schedule, or because [the food] is received according to the desires within one's own mind to sustain the body—
it should not be restricted to a fixed rule. Thus, for these two reasons (the fourth and fifth), clothing serves to cover [the body].

The physical form wards off cold and heat, while food fills the belly to relieve that which is emaciated and weak. Once clothing and food are secure, one may apply oneself to *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Furthermore, it causes the practitioner to keep the "represented" in mind, taking shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*) as their clothing, and the joy of meditation (*dhyāna-prīti*) and the joy of the Dharma (*dharma-prīti*) as their food.
However, because the faculties and natures of practitioners differ, they are roughly divided into three grades. The first is the superior faculty (*adhimātra-indriya*), which remains hidden...

Dwelling among crags and gullies, they do not involve themselves in human affairs; they thatch grass for mats and tie weeds for clothing, relying solely on sweet fruits and clear springs, or perhaps consuming pine and cypress as food, devoting themselves single-mindedly to meditative stillness with no other concerns.
Those of the second grade, the middle capacity, wear only the three robes, neither exceeding nor accumulating them;
they emerge from the villages and enter the mountains, their attire always neat and orderly, seeking alms through the practice of *piṇḍapāta*.
Regarding the three types of practitioners, it is permitted for those of inferior capacity to receive offerings of alms, clothing, and food;

however, they must not seek much or accumulate excessively, as this would hinder their own practice and disturb the faith of others. They should focus solely on sustaining the body, always knowing contentment.
The present treatise allows the use of two kinds of food and three colors of clothing for all three capacities, ensuring that no requirement is lacking. VI.
The causes and conditions for establishing the boundary within [the monastery] rely on the power of divine mantras to protect the concentrated mind so that malevolent spirits cannot enter.

One *krośa* refers to the distance of one "cow-bellow" (*go-ruta*). However, as the words and phrases of the mantra contain repetitions, there are instances where a single character exceeds ten syllables;

many such examples exist today. According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks Who Sought the Dharma in the Western Regions of the Great Tang*, Master Śīla was particularly proficient in the *mantra-piṭaka*.
At that time, there was a disciple named Nanda, who was intelligent and widely learned.

Fearing that the clarity of the mantras in this scripture might be lost, he compiled approximately twelve thousand verses, establishing them as his own distinct tradition. Within each verse, he combined and separated the texts of the mantras and mudrās;
although the words and characters remained the same, their meanings and applications were distinct. This could not have been achieved by anyone other than [him].
"Transmitted face-to-face and bestowed from heart to heart, [Dignāga] truly realized that there was no cause [for his insight].

Later, when the Master Dignāga saw that his compositions were so exquisite and surpassed human intellect, and that his thoughts reached the ultimate limit of emotional refinement, he sighed over the scroll and said:
