When compared to that Buddha, whose virtues are supreme, non-duality is the "general" (the subject), and therefore serves as the agent (*kartṛ*);

whereas the various Buddhas are the "particulars" (the objects), and therefore serve as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Thus, the general is the support for the particular, and the particular is what is accomplished by the general; this is the relationship between the general and the particular.
When comparing their relative superiority and inferiority, they are separated; because the inferior is set aside to manifest the superior, "non-duality" (advaya) is thus adopted.

While the substratum of Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is collectively termed "non-dual," it is spoken of as "the Buddhas" from the perspective of the superior.

Furthermore, the text below cites scriptural authority to establish this, stating that it is due to the power of the non-dual Mahāyāna *dharmatā*, whose virtuous qualities are all-encompassing and perfect.

Fully equipped, profoundly endowed, and extensively established, it is designated by the name "Ocean. Because it completely encompasses the remaining gateways of the Dharma and now transcends them, it is further called "Perfect" (*pari*).
This Dharma is supreme; "attaining all Buddhas" carries the sense of "attaining accomplishment.
Since this Dharma is all-encompassing and total, one is able to accomplish all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth. However, the essence of this Dharma is fundamentally...

The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is not established by means of cultivating causes or severing hindrances; rather, it is realized by the Buddhas yet cannot be attained [as an object] by them, while the deluded ordinary beings fail to realize it yet do not lose it.
This is because people possess only a slight and inferior capacity regarding the Dharma.

Second, "If that were so" and below reconciles contradictions. First, the contradictory text is cited; here, the passage concerning "encompassing and sustaining" is raised to challenge the meaning of the previous "establishment.

Since all phenomena are fully encompassed by the three worlds—namely, principle and phenomenon, cause and effect, person and dharma, and the environment and its inhabitants—all things, including the ocean of perfect circles, are likewise not separate from these three worlds.

Since Vairocana subsumes all things and is further able to take the three periods of time as his essential body, why was it previously stated that the Buddhas cannot achieve the "perfectly perfect ocean"?
Regarding this, there are two sections for providing a detailed explanation of what is subsumed and what is not:
first, the gate of differentiation and equality; second, the gate of the support and achievement. What is the first gate?
This refers to the first, the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), which is the supporting retribution;

the remaining two worlds, the sentient-being-world (*sattva-loka*) and the wisdom-enlightenment-world (*jñāna-bodhi-loka*), which are the supported primary retributions and their auxiliary companions, respectively.

Although these supports and primaries, and the principals and attendants, are each distinct, the Buddha is able to universally govern them all, which is termed "encompassing the three periods. Furthermore, these three periods are fundamentally interfused as one.

The equality of flavor is eternally dependent and eternally correct; being without dependence and without correctness, it is simultaneously the principal and the attendant, yet neither principal nor attendant.

It is sovereign, unimpeded, non-dual, and undifferentiated; one cannot speak of a distinction between the capacity to grasp and that which is grasped. The Great Root [text] relies on what follows, while the Branching Flow [text] employs what precedes;
therefore, the texts of these two do not contradict each other. Regarding the latter gate, what is meant by the "first vessel-world" (bhājanaloka)?
The Buddha is able to rely upon and sustain the other two worlds because he maintains himself and others through the virtues of compassion and wisdom.

Furthermore, these three worlds of vessels arise from karma; their individual delusions are all produced by ignorance’s confusion regarding the truth, rather than being created or established by the Buddhas.
This is because the extensive and abbreviated sūtras each follow a different perspective, and thus they do not contradict one another.
For this reason, because that Buddha accords with the distinctions of the three worlds and serves as their support, it is called "comprehensive" (*saṃgraha*) due to its equality and its fulfillment;

it cannot be called "comprehensive" in the sense of encompassing different branches (*pravibhāga*). This is because, according to the preceding *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it is comprehensive when viewed from the perspective of what follows, whereas the treatise states that it is not comprehensive when viewed from the perspective of what precedes.

The second explanation of the two characters "profound" (*shen*) and "deep" (*shen*) is as follows: they are called "profound" (*shen*) because they are subtle and reach the ultimate limit; they are called "deep" (*shen*) because they cannot be measured or fathomed.
This means that because the fundamental Dharma encompasses all phenomena and subsumes the ten directions, it constitutes the source of the minds of all sages and the ocean of wisdom of all Buddhas.
It transcends the path of language and is extinguished from the sphere of mental activity; thus, each manifests its own gate of profundity according to its respective category.
The third [section] explains the meaning of "vastness" through sixteen gates that can manifest the fundamental dharma; these serve as the names and meanings for that fundamental dharma because,
since the fundamental dharma is subtle and extremely profound, it cannot be vast or self-magnified by itself,
but can only manifest the vast meaning of the dharma it enters by means of the gates of entry.

Second, having already explained the preceding section, this part now displays the gate of the characteristics of the syllables that constitute the speaker. It has two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "I say. The latter has two sub-sections:
first, the citation and attribution of the characteristics of the syllables; second, the interrogation and explanation of the underlying reasons, beginning with "For what reason? etc.
Second, having already explained the section on expanding the merit of the lower *kaṅkṣā* (stretching/extension), there are two parts: first, the summary of the index;
second, the explanation of the expansion. Regarding "second, the explanation of the expansion," there are two parts: first, clarifying the dedication (*pariṇāmanā*);

second, based on the meaning, revealing the causes and conditions for dedication to the three objects—this corresponds to the verses where each character of the term *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is treated individually.

When the single True Suchness is itself illumination, it is the quiescent Original Enlightenment; when Original Enlightenment is itself quiescence, it is illumination. Thus, the mind’s quiescence and illumination flow as a dual current within a single mind.
Furthermore, this single mind is the fundamental Dharma that is entered (*praveśya-dharma*); its awakening is the gate through which one enters the Dharma (*praveśa-mukha-dharma*).

This is because one desires to enable sentient beings to rely upon the gate to enter the Dharma. Second, regarding the section "Thus" and below, which distinguishes the benefits, there are three analogies, namely: first, the dust...
All that rests upon the earth is due to its merit of providing a thick support; a single stream entering the sea shares equally in the virtue of moistening and benefiting.

The small merges with the vast without any distinction of measure, and the one and the many enter into each other without obstruction—this is the core intention preserved by the Master of the Treatise.

Third, the section on the universal benefit of bestowing gifts upon sentient beings has already been explained. This consists of two parts: first, the summary reference; second, the detailed explanation.

Third, the section on stimulating the flow and circulation [of the teaching] has two parts: first, the general exhortation by citing persons and dharmas; second, the specific exhortation by distinguishing between benefit and harm.

Within the former, there are two parts: first, citing the person to manifest their rank; the "Joyful Great Being" (Muditā-mahāsattva) is the Master’s own reference to his own position as being at the first stage.
Upon first attaining the nature of a sage on the [First] Ground, one is fully realized in the two kinds of emptiness and is able to benefit both self and others;

thus, joy arises. However, could one not be boastful in recounting what one has realized? To encourage others and inspire faith, it is necessary not to conceal these matters. Prior to this stage, during the ten levels of faith, the faculties are not yet fixed;
therefore, they are likened to the tip of a hair. From the three stages of worthiness onward, one is within the Mahāyāna ranks, and thus it is designated as such.

Following the stage of the "Horn" (*viṣāṇa*), there are four stages of application (*prayoga*), namely: Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
These are established by the names "Attainment of Clarity," "Increase of Clarity," "Sealing Accordance," and "Uninterrupted Manifestation of Merit.

Furthermore, being adorned with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and distinguished by the title of "Flower," and because the Teacher Śākyamuni has already transcended them, it is said that one has "already surpassed" [them]. Having entered this stage, one has already completed the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.

Because it takes an eon (*kalpa*) to reach the coarse fullness, one must proceed through the stages of the second incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeya-mahākalpa*); thus it is said that he has "just begun to enter.

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* provides the proof for this, stating that in the kingdom of South India, there was a bhikṣu of great fame and virtue named Nāgārjuna, who attained the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). This is precisely that evidence.

Second, the specific praise of the main text from the perspective of the author’s own experience, which has two parts: first, "I have extensively gazed upon the Dragon Palace," describing how the author personally examined ten billion scriptures;
second, "In this manner," showing that the precious volumes fully encompass the meaning, such that there is nothing prepared here that is not complete.
